plain: A startup making human-shaped robots intended to help in homes as well as workplaces.
snappy: Humanoid-robot startup building Neo (home) and Eve (commercial) bipeds.
detail: 1X Technologies develops the Neo home Humanoid robot and the Eve commercial platform, emphasizing safe, soft-bodied designs for Human-robot interaction in Service & Consumer settings. The company stresses Teleoperation-assisted data collection and Imitation learning to bootstrap Manipulation skills, then refines them with a learned Policy. Its consumer focus puts a premium on Compliance and lightweight actuation so a Neo robot is safe to be around people at home.

plain: Finding objects and working out their real-world size, position, and which way they face, not just where they appear in a flat picture.
snappy: Detecting objects with their 3D extent, position, and orientation in metric space.
detail: 3D object detection outputs a 3D bounding box with dimensions, location, and heading, giving the metric geometry a planner needs to predict motion and keep clearance. Autonomous vehicles fuse LiDAR point clouds with camera images (Camera-lidar fusion) to produce these boxes, often projected into a Bird's-eye-view representation. It extends 2D Object detection and complements an Occupancy network for full Scene understanding.

plain: Turning sensor data into a full three-dimensional model of a scene or object that you can view from any angle.
snappy: Building a 3D geometric model of a scene or object from images, depth, or lidar data.
detail: 3D reconstruction fuses many observations into a single model that can be a Point cloud, a Mesh, a Voxel grid, or a learned representation like NeRF or Gaussian splatting. It is produced by methods such as Structure from motion, Stereo matching, or registering lidar scans, and is used to build a Map for navigation or a Digital twin of a Space asset or a Service & Consumer environment. Quality depends on accurate Camera calibration and clean Point cloud registration.

plain: Designing a robot's electrical system around 48 volts so it can deliver more power through thinner, lighter wires.
snappy: A power bus built around 48 V, which lowers current for a given power level and so shrinks wiring, losses, and heat.
detail: Because power equals voltage times current, raising the bus to 48 V (the 48V system, or high-voltage bus) lets actuators pull the same power at a quarter of the current a 12 V system would need, cutting copper weight, resistive loss, and Thermal management burden, while staying below the 60 V safety threshold for extra-low voltage. It has become the default for a Humanoid robot and high-torque Quasi-direct drive joints, where a Brushless DC motor and its Motor controller benefit from the headroom. Stepping down to logic rails still needs a DC-DC converter, and the bus is fanned out through the Power distribution board.

plain: A more detailed kind of car radar that also senses height, painting a dense 3D picture of the scene.
snappy: High-resolution automotive radar that adds elevation as a fourth dimension and outputs a dense point cloud of the scene.
detail: Where classic Automotive radar gives range, azimuth, and velocity, 4D imaging radar adds elevation and many more antenna channels to produce a Point cloud approaching the richness of LiDAR while keeping radar's all-weather and Doppler-velocity strengths. This makes it attractive for a Vision-only autonomy team wanting depth redundancy, or as a Camera-lidar fusion supplement in a Self-driving truck needing long-range Perception. It feeds 3D object detection and a Bird's-eye-view representation in the Self-driving stack.

plain: A method for finding the shortest route through a network of connected points by always heading toward the goal while keeping track of distance already travelled.
snappy: A best-first graph search that expands nodes by path cost plus an admissible heuristic estimate of remaining cost.
detail: A* search ranks candidate nodes by the sum of the known cost so far and a Heuristic function estimating the cost to the goal, which lets it find an optimal path while exploring far fewer cells than uninformed search. It is the workhorse Global planner for grid-based mobile robots, running over an Occupancy grid or Cost map, and is a special case of Graph search that reduces to Dijkstra's algorithm when the heuristic is zero. Variants tailored to vehicles include Hybrid A*, which respects nonholonomic turning limits, and D* algorithm for efficient Replanning.

plain: The robotics arm of the engineering company ABB, which makes factory robot arms and automation gear.
snappy: Industrial-robot division of ABB making articulated arms, cobots, and factory automation systems.
detail: ABB Robotics is one of the 'big four' Industrial robotics suppliers, building the Industrial robot arm for Manufacturing and Logistics & Warehouse applications plus a Cobot line such as YuMi for Collaborative robot tasks. Its portfolio spans Robotic welding, Pick and place, and Palletizing, paired with the RobotStudio offline programming and Robot simulator environment. ABB integrates its arms with a Robot controller, vision, and broader Industrial automation systems.

plain: A position sensor that always knows exactly where a joint is pointing, even right after power-up, without having to move first.
snappy: An encoder that reports unique absolute position and retains it across power cycles, needing no homing.
detail: An absolute encoder assigns every shaft angle a unique code, so a robot knows its true Joint position immediately on startup. This contrasts with an Incremental encoder, which only counts relative motion and must perform a homing move to find a reference. Absolute encoders are favored on a Servomotor or Joint of an Industrial robot arm where unexpected power loss must not lose track of Pose; alternatives include the Resolver.

plain: A sensor that measures how fast something is speeding up, slowing down, or being tilted by gravity.
snappy: A sensor that measures linear acceleration, including the constant pull of gravity, along its axes.
detail: An accelerometer senses linear acceleration along one or more axes; because gravity reads as a steady acceleration, a stationary accelerometer can also estimate tilt. It is one half of an Inertial measurement unit, paired with a Gyroscope, and most modern units are a MEMS sensor on a silicon chip. Robots use it for Balance control, vibration monitoring, and as one input to Sensor fusion for orientation.

plain: How close a robot actually gets to the exact spot it was told to reach.
snappy: The closeness between a robot's achieved pose and its commanded target pose.
detail: Accuracy measures correctness against the commanded target, so it depends on good Calibration of the robot's kinematic model and on compensating for flex and Backlash. It differs from Repeatability, which only measures consistency: a robot can repeat a wrong Pose perfectly. Accuracy matters most when a robot works from CAD coordinates or a Vision-guided robotics frame rather than being hand-taught, and it is improved by Hand-eye calibration and careful Transform chains.

plain: Car-style steering where the two front wheels turn at slightly different angles so they roll cleanly around a curve.
snappy: A steering geometry in which the inner and outer front wheels turn at different angles so all wheels share a common turn center, eliminating tire scrub.
detail: Ackermann steering is the geometry of road cars and is used by larger field and Mobility robots and a Self-driving car, where the front wheels pivot about a single instantaneous turn center while the rear wheels drive. Like Differential drive it produces Nonholonomic motion, so planners use Reeds-Shepp curves or Dubins path solutions to respect a minimum turning radius. It contrasts with Skid steering, which turns by slipping its wheels.

plain: A method that teaches a robot to copy demonstrations by predicting short bursts of moves using a kind of neural network good at sequences.
snappy: A Transformer-based imitation policy that predicts chunked action sequences from demonstrations, popularized by low-cost bimanual teleoperation.
detail: ACT pairs Action chunking with a Transformer and a Variational autoencoder to learn smooth manipulation skills from a few dozen demonstrations, and became well known via the ALOHA Bimanual manipulation setup. It ingests Demonstration data collected by Teleoperation and outputs short action sequences, sidestepping the drift that breaks naive Behavioral cloning. ACT sits alongside Diffusion policy as a leading recipe for Contact-rich manipulation and learning from demonstration.

plain: A way to tell a robot to carry out a longer task while it keeps reporting progress and lets you cancel partway through.
snappy: A goal-oriented interface providing feedback and preemption for long-running robot tasks.
detail: An Action extends the basic Service idea for jobs that take seconds or minutes, like commanding Navigation to a Waypoint or asking MoveIt to execute a Trajectory; the client sends a goal, streams feedback, and can cancel before completion. In ROS this was the actionlib library, while ROS 2 builds actions on top of its Topic and Service primitives. They are heavily used by the Nav2 navigation stack and by motion-planning frameworks.

plain: Having a robot predict a short burst of moves at once instead of deciding each tiny step separately.
snappy: Predicting a short sequence of future actions per inference step rather than one action at a time.
detail: Action chunking reduces the compounding error and jittery, indecisive motion that plague step-by-step Imitation learning by committing to a coherent multi-step plan. It is central to ACT and to Diffusion policy approaches for Contact-rich manipulation and Bimanual manipulation, where smooth Trajectory execution matters. By cutting the number of decision points, it also improves Sample efficiency and robustness when learning from limited Demonstration data.

plain: When a robot deliberately moves its camera or other sensors to get a better look, rather than passively taking in whatever happens to be in view.
snappy: Purposefully controlling sensor placement and viewpoint to reduce uncertainty and gather the most informative observations.
detail: Active perception closes a loop between sensing and motion: a robot might rotate its head, reposition a Gimbal, or move its base to resolve an occlusion, treating viewpoint selection as part of the task. It is central to Next-best-view planning, robust Pose estimation, and Tactile servoing, and it complements the broader Perception-action loop. By choosing where to look, the system fights Uncertainty and Sensor noise far more effectively than a fixed Camera ever could.

plain: A learning setup with two parts working together: one part chooses actions and the other judges how good they were, so the chooser improves.
snappy: An RL architecture combining a policy (actor) with a value estimator (critic) that guides its updates.
detail: Actor-critic methods pair an actor, which is the Policy that selects actions, with a critic that learns a Value function to evaluate them and reduce the variance of the Policy gradient. This structure underpins many continuous-control algorithms used in robotics, including Proximal policy optimization and Soft actor-critic, which train controllers for Legged locomotion and Whole-body control. The critic accelerates learning over pure policy-gradient methods by providing low-variance feedback within a Markov decision process.

plain: Turning stored energy, such as electricity or compressed air, into the movement that makes a robot move.
snappy: The conversion of energy into the controlled motion or force that drives a robot's mechanism.
detail: Actuation is the output side of a robot, producing the motion that Sensing and computation call for. It is delivered by an Actuator, most commonly an Electric motor or Servomotor, but also a Hydraulic actuator, Pneumatic actuator, or Series elastic actuator. The choice shapes Torque density, Backdrivability, and Compliance, and it feeds through a Gearbox or Harmonic drive into each Joint to move the End-effector. Together with Sensing it completes the Perception-action loop.

plain: The part of a robot that actually creates movement or force, like a muscle in a body.
snappy: A component that converts an energy input into mechanical motion or force at a robot joint.
detail: The Actuator is what physically moves a Joint or End-effector in response to a command, turning electrical, hydraulic, or pneumatic energy into motion. Most robots use an Electric motor as the actuator, often paired with a Gearbox and a Motor controller that regulates current. Other forms include the Hydraulic actuator, the Pneumatic actuator, and compliant designs such as the Series elastic actuator used for force-controlled tasks.

plain: A controller that tunes its own settings on the fly as the machine or its load changes, so it keeps working well without a human re-tuning it.
snappy: Control that estimates and adjusts its own parameters online to track a plant whose dynamics are uncertain or time-varying.
detail: Adaptive control updates controller gains in real time using a parameter-estimation law, useful when a Manipulator picks up an unknown Payload that changes its Dynamics, or when a Quadruped robot crosses shifting terrain. Schemes include model-reference adaptive control and self-tuning regulators, and it is closely related to System identification and Gain scheduling. It contrasts with Robust control, which fixes one controller to tolerate uncertainty rather than learning it, and connects to Learning-based control at the data-driven end.

plain: Cruise control that not only holds a set speed but also automatically slows down to keep a safe gap behind the car in front.
snappy: A driver-assistance feature that maintains a set speed while automatically adjusting it to preserve a chosen following gap to the vehicle ahead.
detail: Adaptive cruise control (ACC) uses automotive radar, a camera, or 4D imaging radar to track the lead vehicle and modulate throttle and braking, often via drive-by-wire. As an SAE Level 1 advanced driver-assistance systems feature, it pairs naturally with lane keeping assist to form a hands-on highway pilot. It relies on time to collision and gap estimates and can hand off to automatic emergency braking when closing speed becomes dangerous.

plain: A control style where a robot senses the push from a person or object and responds by moving, making it feel like it gives way gently.
snappy: Interaction control that measures contact force and outputs a commanded motion, the force-in, motion-out dual of impedance control.
detail: Admittance control reads a Force/torque sensor and synthesizes a velocity or position command so the robot behaves like a virtual mass-spring-damper, then a stiff Position control inner loop executes it, making it well suited to position-controlled Industrial robot arm hardware. It is the dual of Impedance control (which outputs force from motion) and a way to achieve Compliance control. It powers Hand guiding on a Cobot and Compliant manipulation tasks like Peg-in-hole and surgical tool insertion.

plain: Electronic helpers in a car that warn or briefly act to keep the driver safe, while the human stays in charge.
snappy: Driver-supervised electronic systems that assist with safety and control but keep the human responsible for the driving task.
detail: Advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) span Automatic emergency braking, Lane keeping assist, Adaptive cruise control, Blind spot monitoring, and Forward collision warning, sitting at L1-L2 on the SAE levels of driving automation. They lean on Automotive radar, Camera, and increasingly a Bird's-eye-view representation for Perception, and suppliers like Mobileye build them at scale. Crucially the driver must still supervise, unlike an Automated driving system, and a Driver monitoring system enforces attention.

plain: Shooting film and video from a flying camera drone to get sweeping shots that would otherwise need a helicopter or crane.
snappy: Capturing professional film and video footage from a stabilized camera-equipped drone.
detail: Aerial cinematography mounts a high-end camera on a stabilized Gimbal beneath a Multirotor drone, using the Flight controller and smooth Trajectory tracking to fly cinematic moves like orbits and reveals. Operators rely on First-person view feeds, GPS hold, and increasingly on autonomous subject-tracking systems such as those from Skydio for hands-free follow shots. It is the most common Service & Consumer use of camera drones, governed by Visual line of sight rules unless a Beyond visual line of sight waiver is held.

plain: Building accurate 3D models and maps of the ground by combining many overlapping photos taken from the air.
snappy: Reconstructing 3D geometry and maps from sets of overlapping aerial images with known or recovered camera positions.
detail: Aerial photogrammetry flies a Drone in a grid so successive frames overlap, then uses Structure from motion and Bundle adjustment to recover Camera intrinsics, poses, and a dense Point cloud for 3D reconstruction. The processed output is typically an Orthomosaic or a textured Mesh, and image quality is governed by Ground sample distance set by altitude and lens. It is widely used in Agriculture, surveying, and construction monitoring, often paired with RTK positioning for survey-grade accuracy.

plain: What an object lets you do with it, like a handle that can be grasped or a button that can be pressed.
snappy: An action possibility an object or environment offers an agent, such as graspable, pushable, or sittable.
detail: An affordance describes the actionable opportunities a Robot can exploit on an object, for example that a mug handle is graspable or a drawer is pullable. Affordance reasoning links Perception to Manipulation: an Affordance detection model proposes where and how to act, feeding Grasp planning and selecting a Grasp pose. Affordances are increasingly predicted by a Vision-language-action model so a robot can act on novel objects via Generalization.

plain: A robot working out what it can actually do with an object it sees, such as whether a handle can be grasped or a surface can be pushed.
snappy: Perceiving the action possibilities an object offers — graspable, pushable, openable — and localizing where on the object each action applies.
detail: Affordance detection maps raw perception onto what an object permits, predicting, for example, which region of a mug is a graspable handle versus its rim, so the robot can plan accordingly. It bridges Perception and Manipulation: outputs feed Grasp planning, Grasp pose selection, and Pushing or Nonprehensile manipulation in tasks like Bin picking and Pick and place. Models are usually built on a Convolutional neural network or Transformer trained on labelled Demonstration data, and the predicted affordances ground a robot's choice of Skill primitive or Tool use. In Humanoid robot and Manufacturing settings it lets a system generalize to novel objects rather than relying on fixed, pre-programmed grasp points.

plain: Anything that senses its surroundings and takes actions to reach a goal.
snappy: An entity that perceives its environment and acts upon it to pursue objectives, the basic unit of autonomous behavior.
detail: In robotics an agent is the abstraction tying Perception to action: it observes the world through a Sensor, decides, and commands an Actuator, closing a Perception-action loop. A single mobile robot is one agent, while a warehouse Fleet is many agents forming a Multi-robot system. The concept overlaps with AI, but the embodied robotics view stresses that an Embodied agent must contend with noisy sensing, physical dynamics, and real-time deadlines that a purely software agent does not.

plain: A company that makes Digit, a two-legged robot that moves boxes and totes in warehouses.
snappy: Maker of Digit, a bipedal humanoid designed for warehouse logistics and tote handling.
detail: Agility Robotics builds Digit, a Bipedal robot optimized for Logistics & Warehouse tasks such as Goods-to-person tote moving and Material handling. Unlike many Humanoid robot projects chasing general dexterity, Agility narrows Digit to bin and conveyor work, integrating with Fleet management and warehouse Automation systems. Its Legged locomotion lets Digit navigate human-scale spaces with steps and uneven floors that block an Automated guided vehicle.

plain: A robot that helps grow crops by doing farm jobs like planting, pulling weeds, picking fruit, or checking on plants.
snappy: A field robot built for agricultural tasks such as seeding, mechanical or laser weeding, selective harvesting, and crop monitoring.
detail: An agricultural robot is a specialized Field robot that drives crop rows using RTK positioning and GPS for centimetre accuracy, then uses computer vision and object detection to tell crop from weed. Companies like John Deere deploy units for autonomous tillage and spraying, while harvesting bots add a soft gripper and grasp planning to handle delicate fruit without bruising. Aerial scouting is often done by a precision agriculture drone doing NDVI mapping, complementing the ground agbot in Agriculture workflows.

plain: A specialized chip built to run artificial-intelligence calculations far faster and more efficiently than a normal processor.
snappy: A dedicated chip optimized for neural-network inference, speeding onboard robot AI within a tight power envelope.
detail: An AI accelerator, also called a neural processing unit (NPU), offloads the matrix and tensor math of a Neural network from the CPU, delivering more inference per watt for a robot's Power budget. On a Humanoid robot it runs perception and a Vision-language-action model in real time; the Tensor processing unit and many a System on a chip block are examples. Throughput is commonly measured in TOPS, and accelerators complement the Graphics processing unit in modern Onboard compute and Edge computing setups.

plain: Amazon's in-house team that builds the fleets of robots which move shelves and packages around its warehouses.
snappy: Amazon's warehouse-automation division operating mobile fulfillment robots, including the Kiva-derived drive units and the Proteus AMR.
detail: Born from Amazon's acquisition of Kiva Systems, Amazon Robotics runs one of the world's largest fleets of warehouse robots, using a Goods-to-person model where squat drive units ferry mobile shelving to human pickers to raise Pick rate. Newer systems include Proteus, a fully Autonomous mobile robot that navigates open floor among workers, plus robotic arms for sortation. Coordinating tens of thousands of units demands sophisticated Fleet management and Multi-agent path finding.

plain: The widely used software that lets a wheeled robot continuously track its position on a known map by matching laser scans.
snappy: The adaptive particle-filter localizer that dynamically resizes its particle set and is the default 2D localization node in ROS navigation.
detail: AMCL is the standard implementation of Monte Carlo localization in ROS and Nav2: it runs a Particle filter against a static Occupancy grid map, using the KLD-sampling rule to shrink the particle count once the robot is confident and grow it again when it is lost (the kidnapped-robot case). It fuses Wheel odometry with Lidar scan matching to maintain the map-to-odom Transform that the rest of the Navigation stack consumes. AMCL handles Localization but not Mapping, so it pairs with a map built earlier by SLAM.

plain: A robot deliberately built to look and move like a human being.
snappy: A humanlike robot whose form, face, and motion are designed to closely resemble a person.
detail: An android is a styling and human-factors choice layered on top of a Humanoid robot platform: it adds lifelike skin, facial actuation, and gestures intended to read as human. The closer the resemblance, the more designers must navigate the Uncanny valley and manage Anthropomorphism in Human-robot interaction. Androids appear in reception, telepresence, and research settings; most working bipedal machines such as Atlas or Tesla Optimus are not androids because they prioritize Bipedal locomotion and payload over cosmetic human likeness.

plain: An American defence-technology company that builds autonomous military hardware and the software that ties it all together.
snappy: Defence-tech firm building autonomous air, ground, and undersea systems unified by its Lattice command-and-control software.
detail: Anduril develops Autonomous weapon-adjacent and surveillance platforms — counter-drone interceptors, Autonomous underwater vehicle systems, and sentry towers — coordinated through its Lattice software, which fuses sensor feeds into a shared picture and tasks assets, including Drone swarm operations and Counter-UAS engagements. Its products sit squarely in the Lethal autonomous weapons system policy debate around human-in-the-loop control. The company contrasts with traditional primes by emphasising autonomy, software updates, and self-funded product development.

plain: The spinning kind of motion a robot has, which it can shuffle around its body to keep from toppling.
snappy: The rotational momentum of a robot's bodies, managed about the center of mass for balance and agile motion.
detail: Angular momentum about the Center of mass changes only when an external torque acts, so a free-flying or single-support robot must regulate it through Contact dynamics and Ground reaction force. Humanoid robots deliberately swing arms and torso to dump or generate angular momentum during recovery, and it is the rotational half of Centroidal dynamics. Conserving it during flight phases lets a Quadruped robot or gymnastic Humanoid robot re-orient mid-air, as Boston Dynamics has demonstrated with Atlas.

plain: Noticing when something in the sensor data looks unusual or out of place compared with what is normal.
snappy: Flagging observations that deviate from learned normal patterns in sensor or perception data.
detail: Anomaly detection learns what 'normal' looks like and raises a flag when an observation departs from it, useful when defects or threats are too rare or varied to label in advance. On a Manufacturing line it drives Quality inspection by catching unfamiliar product defects, and in Defense & Security it spots out-of-place objects in a scene. It overlaps with Condition monitoring and Predictive maintenance for machine health, and is one way robots cope with the Open world and Long-tail scenario cases that closed classifiers miss.

plain: The American safety standard that tells factories how to install and run industrial robots safely.
snappy: The US national industrial-robot safety standard, the American adoption of ISO 10218 Parts 1 and 2.
detail: ANSI/RIA R15.06 is the United States robot-safety standard published by the Robotic Industries Association (now A3), and it adopts the international ISO 10218 Parts 1 and 2 essentially verbatim. It guides the Robot integrator through the Risk assessment, safeguarding selection (Machine guarding, Light curtain, Safety scanner), and Collaborative robot safety modes such as Speed and separation monitoring. OSHA references it as the recognized good practice for US robot installations.

plain: A robot hand shaped like a human hand, with fingers and a thumb that can pinch and grip.
snappy: A human-like robotic hand with fingers, an opposable thumb, and human-scale proportions.
detail: An Anthropomorphic hand is a Robotic hand deliberately patterned on human anatomy, with four fingers and an opposable thumb so it can use tools and objects designed for people. Its human-like kinematics support Precision grasp and Power grasp as well as Finger gaiting during In-hand manipulation. These hands are a hallmark of the Humanoid robot, appearing on platforms like Tesla Optimus and from companies such as Apptronik, and are usually built as a Tendon-driven hand to fit the actuators into a slim palm.

plain: Making robots look or act human-like, or people treating robots as if they were human.
snappy: The design or perception of robots with human-like form, expression, or behavior.
detail: Anthropomorphism has two sides: deliberately giving a robot a human-like body, such as an Android or Humanoid robot with an Anthropomorphic hand, and people's tendency to attribute feelings and intent to machines. Human-likeness can ease Human-robot interaction and build Trust in a Service robot, but overdoing it risks the Uncanny valley. Designers weigh it carefully, since the same face that makes a greeter robot friendly can make a near-human one unsettling.

plain: A safeguard that stops a controller from over-building a correction it cannot actually deliver, so it does not lurch when limits clear.
snappy: A technique that prevents a controller's integral term from accumulating during actuator saturation.
detail: When an Actuator hits Saturation, a PID controller's integral term keeps summing the unresolved Error signal, winding up to a huge value that then causes massive Overshoot once the actuator unclips. Anti-windup stops this by clamping or back-calculating the integrator while saturated, so the controller resumes cleanly. It is essential in robot joints and drone Flight controller loops that frequently run actuators to their limits during aggressive moves.

plain: Gripping an object by pinching two flat sides that face directly opposite each other.
snappy: A two-finger grasp made on opposing, roughly parallel surfaces of an object.
detail: An Antipodal grasp places two contacts on opposite, near-parallel faces of an object so their normals point toward each other, the natural grasp geometry for a Parallel-jaw gripper. When friction at the Contact points is sufficient (the line between them lies inside both Friction cone regions) the grasp achieves Force closure. Antipodal points are the dominant grasp representation in Bin picking and Learned grasping, because they are simple to detect from a Depth camera or Point cloud and easy to score with a Grasp quality metric.

plain: A Swiss company that makes a four-legged robot which walks around industrial sites taking readings and spotting problems.
snappy: Swiss developer of the ANYmal quadruped inspection robot for autonomous monitoring of industrial facilities.
detail: ANYbotics is a spin-off from ETH Zurich that builds ANYmal, a Quadruped robot designed for autonomous inspection of refineries, offshore platforms, and substations, where its Legged locomotion lets it climb stairs and traverse terrain a wheeled robot cannot. Equipped with thermal cameras, microphones, and lidar, it performs Condition monitoring and Predictive maintenance rounds, navigating via onboard SLAM and Foothold selection. It competes directly with the Spot platform from Boston Dynamics in the industrial inspection market.

plain: A company that makes Apollo, a human-shaped robot for warehouse and factory jobs.
snappy: Humanoid-robot maker of Apollo, targeting logistics and manufacturing material handling.
detail: Apptronik, spun out of the University of Texas Human Centered Robotics Lab, builds Apollo, a Humanoid robot for Manufacturing and Logistics & Warehouse tasks like case handling and Palletizing. Apollo uses force-controlled, mass-producible actuators emphasizing Compliance and safe Human-robot interaction on the factory floor. The company has partnered with automakers and logistics firms for Pilot deployment of its Bipedal locomotion platform.

plain: Free, open-source software that controls drones, planes, boats, and rovers automatically.
snappy: Open-source Autopilot firmware supporting many uncrewed vehicle types from a single project.
detail: ArduPilot, descended from the early APM project, runs on a Pixhawk and other flight controllers and provides flight modes including Loiter, Waypoint navigation, and Return-to-home for a Multirotor, Fixed-wing drone, Hybrid VTOL, rover, or boat. Like PX4 it uses the MAVLink protocol to talk to a Ground control station such as Mission Planner or QGroundControl. The two stacks compete for the same open-hardware ecosystem and both target Pixhawk-class boards.

plain: A robot arm built from rigid segments connected by rotating joints, usually six of them, so it can reach almost any angle.
snappy: A serial manipulator with multiple rotary (revolute) joints, typically six axes, giving full position and orientation freedom.
detail: An articulated robot is a Serial manipulator whose Revolute joint axes give it six Degrees of freedom, letting its End-effector reach any Pose within the Workspace, which is why it is often called a Six-axis robot. Control depends on Forward kinematics and Inverse kinematics, with care taken near a Kinematic singularity. It is the workhorse of Manufacturing for Robotic welding, Assembly, and machine tending, built by FANUC, KUKA, and ABB Robotics.

plain: A grade from A to D showing how serious a car's electronic safety function is, with D being the most critical, like the brakes.
snappy: The ISO 26262 risk classification (ASIL A-D, plus QM) assigned to automotive functions based on severity, exposure, and controllability.
detail: ASIL is the risk-rating scheme of ISO 26262, derived from a hazard analysis that combines severity, exposure, and controllability; ASIL D is the most stringent (e.g., steering and braking in an Autonomous vehicle). It dictates the rigor of the development process and the diagnostic coverage needed for a function in an Automated driving system. ASIL is the automotive counterpart of the Safety Integrity Level scale from IEC 61508.

plain: Putting separate parts together into a finished product, done by a robot instead of by hand.
snappy: Joining parts via robotic insertion, fastening, mating, or stacking operations.
detail: Robotic Assembly covers screwing, snapping, press-fitting, and mating tasks on a Production line, and most of it is Contact-rich manipulation where parts touch and slide under force. The hard sub-steps are insertion problems like Peg-in-hole, which demand a Force/torque sensor and Hybrid position/force control rather than pure Position control. Tight-tolerance work often relies on Fixturing, a Remote center of compliance, or Compliant manipulation, while complex products may need Bimanual manipulation to hold and join at once.

plain: A human-shaped robot that can walk, lift things, and balance on two legs, made by Boston Dynamics.
snappy: Boston Dynamics' bipedal humanoid robot, now an all-electric commercial platform aimed at industrial tasks.
detail: Atlas is the flagship Humanoid robot from Boston Dynamics, originally hydraulic and famous for parkour and backflip demos that showcased aggressive Dynamic walking and Whole-body control. The platform was relaunched as an all-electric robot positioned for manufacturing and Material handling rather than research stunts. Its control stack relies on Model predictive control, Zero moment point reasoning, and online Trajectory optimization to stay balanced under disturbance.

plain: A device that continuously tells a robot which way it is tilted and which direction it is facing.
snappy: A system that fuses IMU and magnetometer data to output 3D orientation in real time.
detail: An attitude and heading reference system (AHRS) extends a raw Inertial measurement unit by adding a Magnetometer and running an onboard fusion filter, such as a Kalman filter, to produce stable roll, pitch, and yaw. Unlike a bare IMU, it outputs corrected orientation rather than raw rates, countering Sensor drift. A Drone Flight controller and a Humanoid robot both rely on an AHRS for Balance control and stabilizing a Gimbal.

plain: A company building the self-driving system for big freight trucks on highways.
snappy: Autonomous-driving company focused on self-driving trucks via the Aurora Driver.
detail: Aurora Innovation develops the Aurora Driver, a Self-driving stack initially targeting the Self-driving truck market for highway freight in Logistics & Warehouse supply chains. It uses LiDAR (including long-range FMCW LiDAR), Radar, and Camera sensing for Level 4 automation along defined trucking lanes as its Operational design domain. Long-haul trucking is attractive because highway driving is more structured than the urban Robotaxi problem.

plain: The combined hardware and software that can drive a vehicle by itself across an entire trip.
snappy: The hardware and software collectively capable of performing the entire dynamic driving task on a sustained basis.
detail: An Automated driving system (ADS) is the L3-L5 brain of an Autonomous vehicle: it runs the full Self-driving stack, performing the entire Dynamic driving task within an Operational design domain rather than just assisting like Advanced driver-assistance systems. It must manage its own Fallback to a Minimal risk condition and is built to Functional safety standards such as ISO 26262. The ADS behind a Waymo or Aurora vehicle integrates Perception, prediction, Behavior planning, and control into one certified system.

plain: A driverless cart that hauls loads around a factory by following a fixed route, like a magnetic strip or wire taped to the floor.
snappy: A mobile transport robot that follows predefined guide paths (wire, magnetic tape, or fiducial markers) rather than planning its own routes.
detail: An AGV is the older, infrastructure-dependent cousin of the Autonomous mobile robot: it tracks a fixed guidepath and stops when something blocks it, rather than replanning around obstacles. AGVs are common in Manufacturing and Logistics & Warehouse Material handling, governed by the safety standard ISO 3691-4. Compared with an AMR, an AGV is cheaper and more deterministic but far less Flexible automation when the layout changes.

plain: A system that steers the car into a parking space for you, sometimes while you watch from outside with your phone.
snappy: A feature that autonomously maneuvers the vehicle into or out of a parking space, controlling steering and often throttle and braking.
detail: Automated parking uses ultrasonic sensors, a camera, and sometimes LiDAR to detect a free space and plan a parking maneuver, executing it through drive-by-wire. It applies path planning and trajectory tracking in a tight, low-speed envelope, leaning on Ackermann steering geometry and Reeds-Shepp curves for the forward-and-reverse arcs. It is the supervised precursor to automated valet parking, where the driver leaves the vehicle entirely.

plain: A warehouse system of computer-controlled cranes or shuttles that automatically put goods away into racks and fetch them back without people walking the aisles.
snappy: A computer-controlled arrangement of cranes, shuttles, and racking that stores and retrieves loads at fixed locations on command.
detail: An Automated storage and retrieval system (AS/RS) uses cranes or rail-guided shuttles moving in dense high-bay racking, directed by control software tied into a Warehouse management or Manufacturing execution system. It is a core piece of warehouse Material handling and often pairs with a Goods-to-person station and an Autonomous mobile robot for the last leg of transport. Because the storage map is fixed and deterministic, an AS/RS achieves high Throughput and density compared with manual picking, and vendors like Symbotic and Amazon Robotics build large-scale versions.

plain: Where you get out at the entrance and the car drives itself off to find a parking space and park, with no one inside.
snappy: Driverless parking in which the vehicle navigates and parks itself within a designated facility after the occupants have left.
detail: Automated valet parking (AVP) is an SAE Level 4 feature confined to a structured environment such as a parking garage, often using vehicle-to-infrastructure communication and fiducial markers or an HD map for localization. The car performs its own path planning, obstacle avoidance, and trajectory tracking with no safety driver aboard, treating the garage as its operational design domain. It is more autonomous than automated parking because the human is fully out of the loop within that domain.

plain: A safety feature that slams on the brakes by itself when it senses a crash is about to happen and the driver has not reacted.
snappy: A system that autonomously applies braking to prevent or reduce the severity of an imminent collision.
detail: Automatic emergency braking (AEB) fuses automotive radar, a camera, and pedestrian detection to estimate time to collision, then commands maximum braking through brake-by-wire when impact is imminent. It is usually preceded by forward collision warning, which alerts the driver first, and is a core advanced driver-assistance systems function regulated under standards like ISO 26262. AEB extends to vulnerable road user protection, braking for cyclists and pedestrians who enter the path.

plain: Using machines to do tasks on their own so that little or no human effort is needed.
snappy: The use of machines and control systems to perform tasks with minimal human intervention.
detail: Automation spans from a single self-running machine to a whole automated plant, and robotics is one of its most flexible forms. Industrial automation organizes equipment along the Automation pyramid, from a Programmable logic controller on the floor up to a Manufacturing execution system. The field divides into Fixed automation for rigid high-volume lines and Flexible automation for changeable production, with an Industrial robot arm and Cobot deployments sitting in between.

plain: A diagram showing factory control as a stack of layers, from sensors at the bottom up to company-wide planning at the top.
snappy: A layered reference model of plant control, from field devices up through control, MES, and enterprise planning.
detail: The classic pyramid runs field devices and sensors at the base, then control via the Programmable logic controller and SCADA, then the Manufacturing execution system, and finally Enterprise resource planning at the apex, mirroring the ISA-95 hierarchy. Each layer abstracts and aggregates data from the one below, with cycle times getting slower toward the top. Industry 4.0 and the Industrial Internet of Things are flattening this strict pyramid as data flows directly between layers in a Smart factory.

plain: A self-operating machine built to move or perform actions on its own, often a historical mechanical figure that predates modern robots.
snappy: A self-acting mechanical device that follows a fixed sequence without sensing or adapting, the pre-electronic ancestor of the robot.
detail: Classic automata, like 18th-century clockwork writing figures, executed predetermined motions through cams and gears with no Feedback or Perception. They contrast sharply with a modern Robot, which closes a Perception-action loop and exhibits Autonomy and Automation under software control. The term survives in computer science (finite automata) and is echoed by the Finite state machine that still governs much robot Behavior planning today.

plain: A car sensor that bounces radio waves off objects to measure how far away they are and how fast they move.
snappy: A millimeter-wave radio sensor that measures range and relative velocity of road objects, robust in rain, fog, and darkness.
detail: Automotive radar uses mmWave signals (typically 77 GHz) and the Doppler effect to read closing speed directly, making it the backbone of Adaptive cruise control and Automatic emergency braking in Advanced driver-assistance systems. It complements Camera and LiDAR through Sensor fusion because it sees through weather that blinds vision, though classic radar has coarse angular resolution. Higher-resolution variants are sold as 4D imaging radar, and it feeds the AV's Perception layer.

plain: A robot driving itself back to a charging station and plugging in without a person's help.
snappy: A robot autonomously navigating to and aligning with a charging station to recharge unattended.
detail: Autonomous docking lets an Autonomous mobile robot or robot vacuum return to its charger when State of charge runs low, using Localization, a Fiducial marker, and fine Visual servoing to align contacts precisely. It closes the loop on unattended operation, and Fleet management schedules docking across a Fleet to keep enough robots working. The dock may use physical contacts or Wireless charging, and it is an alternative to a Hot-swappable battery swap when continuous human handling is undesirable.

plain: A wheeled robot that drives itself around a building, figuring out its own path instead of following a painted line or buried wire.
snappy: A self-navigating mobile robot that builds a map, localizes within it, and plans collision-free routes on the fly.
detail: An AMR uses onboard Localization and Mapping (often SLAM with a LiDAR or cameras) plus a Navigation stack to reach goals while avoiding people and changing obstacles, unlike an Automated guided vehicle that needs fixed infrastructure. AMRs dominate Logistics & Warehouse Goods-to-person picking, with vendors like Locus Robotics and Amazon Robotics deploying large fleets coordinated by Fleet management software. Most run ROS 2 with Nav2 for Path planning and Obstacle avoidance.

plain: A small, slow, driverless bus that ferries passengers along set routes.
snappy: A low-speed, driverless passenger vehicle operating fixed or semi-flexible routes, typically in geofenced campuses or city zones.
detail: An Autonomous shuttle is a boxy, often bidirectional Level 4 automation vehicle running under 25 mph within a tightly bounded Operational design domain, using LiDAR and Camera Perception plus Map-relative localization against an HD map. Because routes are fixed and speeds low, it is a relatively tractable deployment compared with a general Robotaxi, and it falls back to a Minimal risk condition by stopping in lane. Operators frequently keep a Remote operation center for Teleoperation oversight.

plain: An untethered robot submarine that navigates and runs its mission underwater on its own, with no cable to the surface.
snappy: A self-navigating, untethered submersible robot that executes preprogrammed or autonomous underwater missions.
detail: An AUV carries its own power and runs missions without a tether, unlike the cable-connected Remotely operated vehicle, navigating by Dead reckoning, an Inertial measurement unit, and acoustic positioning since GPS does not penetrate water (GPS-denied navigation). It is used in Research/Frontier oceanography, seabed mapping, and Defense & Security mine countermeasures. AUVs require careful State estimation and Sensor fusion because surfacing to fix position is costly.

plain: A car or vehicle that drives itself by sensing the world around it, without a person steering.
snappy: A vehicle that perceives its environment and performs the driving task itself without continuous human control.
detail: An Autonomous vehicle (AV) runs a Self-driving stack that fuses LiDAR, Camera, and Automotive radar through Perception, then Behavior planning and control, often localizing against an HD map. Degree of capability is graded by the SAE levels of driving automation, with a true driverless Robotaxi like those from Waymo or Zoox sitting at Level 4 automation within a fixed Operational design domain. The car must always be able to fall back to a Minimal risk condition when automation fails.

plain: A weapon system that can choose and attack targets on its own, without a person directly controlling each engagement.
snappy: A weapon system that can select and engage targets without direct human control of each engagement.
detail: An autonomous weapon, often termed a lethal autonomous weapon system (LAWS), uses onboard Perception and decision-making to find and engage targets without a human approving each shot. The category overlaps with a Loitering munition and armed Drone swarm concepts, and it sits at the center of Robot ethics debates over meaningful human control. Policy discussion stresses keeping a Human-in-the-loop and applying strict Verification and validation before any field use.

plain: A robot's ability to do its job by itself, without a person controlling it the whole time.
snappy: The capacity of a robot to sense, decide, and act toward a goal without continuous human control.
detail: Autonomy ranges from none, where a person drives every motion via Teleoperation, up to a fully self-directed Autonomous mobile robot or Autonomous vehicle. Achieving it requires Perception, Localization, Navigation, and decision-making that close the loop without an operator. Because full independence is rare in practice, designers describe systems along Levels of autonomy and often deploy intermediate schemes such as Shared autonomy and Supervised autonomy.

plain: The system that flies a drone or aircraft automatically along a set route, without the operator steering by hand.
snappy: The hardware-and-software stack that stabilizes a vehicle and flies programmed routes autonomously.
detail: A drone autopilot runs on a Flight controller such as a Pixhawk and fuses an Inertial measurement unit with GPS to hold attitude and execute Waypoint navigation, Loiter, and Return-to-home. The two dominant open-source autopilot stacks are PX4 and ArduPilot, both of which speak MAVLink to a Ground control station. The term is used identically for ground and marine vehicles, where the same Sense-plan-act loop applies.

plain: Describing how a body is turned by naming a single line to spin around and how far to spin it.
snappy: Orientation expressed as a rotation angle about a single unit axis.
detail: By Euler's rotation theorem any 3D orientation equals one rotation by some angle about one fixed axis, and the axis-angle form states exactly that pair. Scaling the axis by the angle gives the rotation vector used in Screw theory and in the exponential map onto the Special orthogonal group SO(3). It converts directly to a Quaternion or Rotation matrix and avoids the Gimbal lock that troubles Euler angles.

plain: How easily you can push or move a robot's joint by hand from the outside, without the robot resisting you.
snappy: The ease with which a joint can be moved by an external force applied at its output.
detail: A backdrivable joint transmits force smoothly in both directions, so a person pushing on the limb feels little resistance and the motor itself can sense the contact. High backdrivability is central to safe physical interaction and underpins approaches like Series elastic actuator and Quasi-direct drive designs in a Humanoid robot or Legged robot. It is the opposite of a high-ratio Harmonic drive or Cycloidal drive, whose large Gear reduction makes the output very hard to backdrive.

plain: The tiny bit of slack or play between gears or parts, so when you reverse direction nothing moves for a moment until the gap closes.
snappy: Lost motion caused by clearance between mating parts such as gear teeth, felt as dead motion when the drive reverses direction.
detail: Backlash is the small free play between meshing teeth in a Gearbox or Gear reduction; on direction reversal the input moves before the output responds, hurting Repeatability and Accuracy. It is a key reason a Harmonic drive or Cycloidal drive is favored in an Industrial robot arm, since both offer near-zero backlash, and why Direct drive and Quasi-direct drive joints avoid geartrains entirely. Backlash shows up as Deadband in a Servo control loop and is often confused with mechanical Hysteresis.

plain: The system that keeps a walking robot from tipping over by constantly adjusting how it stands and steps.
snappy: Control that keeps a legged or wheeled-inverted robot upright by regulating its center of mass and foot forces.
detail: Balance control regulates the Center of mass relative to the Support polygon, keeping the Zero moment point inside it, often using the Linear inverted pendulum model and the Capture point to decide where to step. It is implemented with Model predictive control or Whole-body control commanding ground forces through Torque control, and it draws on Center of pressure and Ground reaction force feedback. It is what lets a Humanoid robot like Atlas recover from a shove via Disturbance rejection.

plain: A threaded rod that uses tiny rolling balls to convert spinning into smooth straight-line motion with very little friction.
snappy: A low-friction power screw that recirculates ball bearings between screw and nut to convert rotation to linear motion.
detail: A Ball screw replaces the sliding contact of a Lead screw with recirculating balls, slashing friction and enabling high efficiency, speed, and back-driving precision for a Prismatic joint or Linear actuator. It is standard on CNC machine tools and high-accuracy Cartesian robot axes, usually riding a Linear guide and driven by a Servomotor. The low friction improves positioning Accuracy and Repeatability over a lead screw.

plain: How fast a control system can keep up with changing demands before it starts lagging behind.
snappy: The frequency range over which a control system responds effectively to commands or disturbances.
detail: Bandwidth measures how quickly a controller can react: a high-bandwidth joint can track fast, jerky Trajectory commands, while a low-bandwidth one smooths them out and falls behind. It is limited by the Control rate, actuator dynamics, Sensor latency, and the need to avoid Overshoot or instability. In Force control and Impedance control, bandwidth determines how crisply a robot can respond to contact before the loop becomes sluggish or unstable.

plain: Control that only ever turns the actuator fully on or fully off, with nothing in between, like a basic thermostat.
snappy: A control scheme that switches the actuator between full-on and full-off rather than proportioning the command.
detail: Bang-bang control applies maximum effort in one direction until the Error signal flips sign, then maximum effort the other way, producing a limit-cycle oscillation around the Setpoint. It is simple and time-optimal for some systems but causes chatter, so practical versions add Hysteresis or a Deadband to slow switching. Robotics uses it for simple gripper opening, cooling fans, and as the bang-bang phase of time-optimal Trajectory optimization where actuators run at Saturation.

plain: Electronics that watch over a robot's battery to keep it safe and working well.
snappy: Electronics that monitor, balance, and protect a battery pack while estimating its charge and health.
detail: A Battery management system (BMS) measures cell voltages, current, and temperature, balances cells, and enforces safe limits to protect a Lithium-ion battery or Lithium iron phosphate battery from over-charge, over-discharge, and thermal runaway. It computes State of charge and state of health, feeding the robot's Power budget decisions and Thermal management, and is itself an Embedded system on a Microcontroller. On a Humanoid robot or AMR the BMS also coordinates a Hot-swappable battery swap and reports status during Autonomous docking.

plain: A component that lets parts move smoothly against each other while reducing friction.
snappy: A machine element that constrains relative motion to a desired type while minimizing friction.
detail: A Bearing supports a Joint or shaft so it rotates or slides cleanly, carrying radial and axial loads while keeping a Link rigidly located; its quality directly affects a robot's Backlash, Accuracy, and Repeatability. Robotics uses specialized types such as the Crossed roller bearing in compact joints and the Slew bearing under a rotating base. Bearings pair with Gearbox elements and Linear guide rails throughout a manipulator's drivetrain.

plain: The part of a self-driving car's brain that makes the everyday driving choices, like whether to change lanes, yield, or wait at a junction.
snappy: The decision-making layer that selects high-level maneuvers such as lane change, yield, or proceed before detailed trajectory generation.
detail: Behavior planning sits above the local planner and motion planning in a self-driving stack, turning the outputs of behavior prediction and the route from route planning into discrete tactical decisions. It commonly uses a finite state machine, behavior tree, or learned policy to resolve situations like an unprotected left turn or a cut-in. Its chosen maneuver is then handed to trajectory optimization and trajectory tracking for execution within the safety envelope.

plain: Guessing what the cars, cyclists, and pedestrians around a self-driving vehicle are about to do next, so it can plan ahead safely.
snappy: Forecasting the future trajectories and intentions of surrounding road agents so the planner can react in advance.
detail: Behavior prediction takes tracked objects from multi-object tracking and an HD map and outputs likely future paths for each road agent, often as multiple weighted trajectories. In a self-driving stack it sits between perception and behavior planning, letting the car anticipate a cut-in or an unprotected left turn rather than merely reacting. Modern systems use a transformer or other neural network trained on datasets like nuScenes and the Waymo Open Dataset, and feed the resulting forecasts into time to collision and safety envelope checks.

plain: A diagram, shaped like a branching tree, that lays out the if-this-then-that logic a robot follows to decide what to do next.
snappy: A modular, hierarchical structure that sequences and selects a robot's tasks by ticking nodes in priority order.
detail: A Behavior tree organizes decision logic into reusable nodes such as sequences, fallbacks, and condition checks, evaluated by a periodic tick that flows down from the root. It has largely replaced the flat Finite state machine for complex robot autonomy because subtrees compose and reorder cleanly, which is why the Nav2 navigation stack uses BehaviorTree.CPP to orchestrate recovery behaviors like backing up and clearing the Cost map. Behavior trees pair naturally with Task planning and a Behavior planning layer that supplies high-level goals to the underlying Motion planning system.

plain: Building a robot's smarts out of many small, simple behaviors that all run at once instead of one big planning program.
snappy: A control paradigm that composes intelligence from a set of parallel, reactive behaviors rather than a single deliberative reasoner.
detail: Behavior-based robotics, pioneered by Rodney Brooks, rejects the slow Sense-plan-act pipeline in favor of many tightly-coupled sensing-to-action modules running concurrently. Each behavior, such as avoid-obstacle or follow-wall, maps stimuli to motor commands, so the robot stays responsive without maintaining a heavy world model. The best-known instance is the Subsumption architecture, and the style sits firmly in the Reactive control tradition, often blended with planning in a Hybrid architecture for tasks needing foresight.

plain: The simplest way to copy a demonstration: train the robot to output the same move the expert made in each situation it saw.
snappy: Supervised imitation that directly maps observations to demonstrated actions.
detail: Behavioral cloning treats Imitation learning as plain supervised learning, fitting a Policy that reproduces the Action an expert took for each observed state. It is fast and simple but suffers from compounding errors when the Robot drifts into states absent from the Demonstration data, a problem DAgger addresses by querying the expert on visited states. In manipulation, behavioral cloning is often improved with a Diffusion policy and Action chunking to handle multimodal, long-horizon behavior.

plain: A way to send power between two spinning shafts using a flexible loop of belt over pulleys.
snappy: A power-transmission element using a flexible belt over pulleys to couple rotating shafts.
detail: A Belt drive (often a toothed timing belt) transmits torque and motion between pulleys, letting a Servomotor sit away from the Joint it drives, much like a Cable-driven mechanism but for rotary transmission. SCARA robot and Cartesian robot axes commonly use timing belts, sometimes with a Gearbox or Gear reduction, while the belt's slight stretch can add compliance and Backlash. Belts are quiet, low-cost, and tolerant of misalignment compared with a rigid geartrain.

plain: A standard test and scoring rule used so that different robot systems can be compared fairly on the same task.
snappy: A standardized task and metric used to compare the performance of robot systems.
detail: A benchmark fixes the task, the data, and the metric so results from different teams are comparable rather than anecdotal. In autonomous driving, the Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes serve as benchmarks for 3D object detection and tracking, scored against Ground truth labels. In manipulation, Open X-Embodiment provides shared data and tasks so a Generalist policy can be compared across labs, and simulators like Isaac Lab host standardized Gym environment benchmarks.

plain: Flying a drone so far away that the operator can no longer see it with their own eyes.
snappy: Drone operation conducted beyond the operator's direct unaided sight, requiring extra safety systems and approvals.
detail: BVLOS unlocks long-range Drone delivery, pipeline inspection, and Agriculture surveys, but because the pilot cannot see traffic the operation must add Detect and avoid, reliable command links over MAVLink, Remote ID, and often participation in Unmanned traffic management. Regulators like the FAA grant BVLOS approvals as waivers or under emerging rules beyond standard Part 107. It is the operational opposite of Visual line of sight flight.

plain: Using two robot arms or hands together to handle something neither could manage alone.
snappy: Coordinating two arms or hands to manipulate an object cooperatively.
detail: Bimanual manipulation lets a robot hold a part with one arm while working on it with the other, as when folding cloth, threading a cable, or stabilizing a box during Assembly. Coordinating two arms creates a Closed kinematic chain and tight constraints, so it needs Whole-body control and careful Collision avoidance between the limbs. It is central to the Humanoid robot agenda and to Dual-arm robot platforms, and is a common testbed for Imitation learning and Teleoperation data collection.

plain: A robot reaching into a box of jumbled-up parts and pulling out one item at a time.
snappy: Grasping individual parts from a cluttered, randomly piled bin or container.
detail: Bin picking is a classic warehouse and factory challenge because parts overlap at unpredictable angles, so the robot must run Pose estimation on each item before computing a Grasp pose. A 3D vision system such as a Depth camera or Structured light scanner feeds an Object detection and Grasp planning pipeline, often paired with a Suction gripper or Parallel-jaw gripper on an Industrial robot arm. Modern systems increasingly use Learned grasping and Synthetic data to handle the long tail of part shapes and lighting conditions.

plain: A robot designed to copy how a real animal or living thing is built and moves.
snappy: A robot whose morphology, materials, or control are modeled on a biological organism to gain its mechanical or behavioral advantages.
detail: A bio-inspired robot borrows a solution that evolution already refined, such as a Snake robot using snake locomotion to slither through rubble or a Legged robot copying animal gaits for terrain adaptation. The approach leans on bio-inspired robotics and morphological computation, where bio-inspired structure offloads work from the controller to the body itself, often built with soft robotics or a tensegrity structure. It overlaps with swarm robotics for collective insect-like behavior and is a major Research/Frontier theme distinct from rigid factory machinery.

plain: Designing robots by copying clever ideas from animals and plants.
snappy: Designing robot structure, materials, and behavior by drawing on principles observed in biological organisms.
detail: Bio-inspired robotics borrows solutions evolution already found: gecko-foot adhesion, fish undulation, or insect Hexapod locomotion, often realized with a Bio-inspired structure. It overlaps heavily with Soft robotics for compliant bodies and with Morphological computation, where the body's mechanics do part of the control job. Examples include a Snake robot for confined spaces and the collective coordination of Swarm robotics modeled on ant colonies and bird flocks.

plain: A robot body designed by copying how living things are built, like legs based on insects or a spine based on a fish.
snappy: A robot structure whose form and mechanics are modeled on biological organisms to capture their efficiency, agility, or robustness.
detail: A bio-inspired structure borrows morphology from nature, such as a tendon-and-muscle layout, a segmented spine, or a gecko-like foot, and pairs with Bio-inspired robotics design methods. Examples include a Hexapod robot patterned on insects, a Snake robot mimicking serpentine motion, and a Tendon-driven hand copying human anatomy; many lean on Morphological computation so the body itself simplifies control. Such structures frequently use Soft robotics structure materials and Tensegrity structure principles, and are a staple of Research/Frontier robotics.

plain: Walking or running on two legs the way humans do.
snappy: Legged locomotion on two legs, the dominant mode for humanoid robots that must operate in human-built spaces.
detail: Bipedal locomotion is the hardest common locomotion problem because two contacts give a small Support polygon, so the robot relies heavily on Dynamic stability, the Zero moment point, and the Capture point to avoid falling. It is the defining capability of a Humanoid robot such as Atlas or Tesla Optimus, and underpins Running and stair climbing. Controllers often build on the Linear inverted pendulum model and Whole-body control.

plain: A robot that stands and walks on two legs, balancing like a person does.
snappy: A legged robot that locomotes on two limbs, requiring active balance because its support area is small.
detail: Bipedal robots are statically unstable while walking, so they rely on Balance control schemes built around the Zero moment point, Capture point, and the Linear inverted pendulum model to stay upright. They underpin every Humanoid robot and are studied for Dynamic walking and Passive dynamic walking. Compared with a Quadruped robot, a Bipedal robot trades stability for a smaller footprint and human-like Bipedal locomotion.

plain: A flattened, looking-straight-down map of everything around the robot, as if seen from a drone overhead.
snappy: A top-down, ego-centric spatial representation of the surrounding scene, widely used in driving perception.
detail: Bird's-eye view, or BEV, projects camera and lidar observations into a common top-down grid centered on the Ego vehicle, which is far easier for planning than raw perspective images. Modern self-driving stacks learn to lift surround-view cameras into a BEV representation where 3D object detection, Lane detection, and an Occupancy grid all live in one consistent frame. It pairs naturally with Camera-lidar fusion and feeds Behavior prediction and motion planning.

plain: A system that watches the areas beside and behind your car that you cannot easily see, and warns you when another vehicle is hiding there.
snappy: A driver-assistance feature that detects vehicles in the side and rear blind zones and alerts the driver, especially during lane changes.
detail: Blind spot monitoring (BSM) uses rear-facing automotive radar or a camera to detect vehicles in the adjacent-lane blind zones, lighting an indicator or sounding an alert during a lane change. As an advanced driver-assistance systems feature it complements lane keeping assist and forward collision warning to cover the areas a driver cannot see directly. Many systems escalate the warning if the driver signals a lane change into an occupied blind spot.

plain: A well-known robot company famous for building machines that walk and run like animals and people.
snappy: Hyundai-owned robotics company known for the Atlas humanoid, Spot quadruped, and Stretch warehouse robot.
detail: Founded out of MIT and now owned by Hyundai, Boston Dynamics built its reputation on dynamically balancing Legged robot designs, pioneering Dynamic walking and agile locomotion years before competitors. Its commercial lineup spans the Spot quadruped for inspection, the Atlas humanoid robot, and the Stretch box-moving arm for Logistics & Warehouse work. The company's research heavily influenced modern Whole-body control and Model predictive control on legged platforms.

plain: A simple rectangle drawn around an object in an image to mark where it is.
snappy: A rectangular region enclosing a detected object, used as the standard output of detection.
detail: A bounding box (bbox) is the axis-aligned or oriented rectangle that an Object detection model places around each target, defined by its corners or center, width, and height. It is the lightweight handle that downstream Multi-object tracking and Behavior prediction follow over time. Its 3D counterpart, the 3D bounding box, adds depth and orientation for an Autonomous vehicle, and the same idea underlies a Fiducial marker corner detection.

plain: An efficient, long-lasting motor that uses electronics instead of physical contacts to keep spinning.
snappy: An electronically commutated DC motor offering high efficiency and reliability for robot joints and drones.
detail: A Brushless DC motor replaces the worn-prone brushes of a DC motor with a Motor controller that switches current through the windings electronically, a process called Commutation. Its high Torque density and reliability make it the standard choice for a robot Joint, a Quadcopter rotor (driven by an Electronic speed controller), and Quasi-direct drive legged actuators. Closely related to the Permanent magnet synchronous motor, it is often run with Field-oriented control for smooth torque.

plain: Fine-tuning where the cameras were and where points in the world are so that everything lines up across all the photos at once.
snappy: Jointly optimizing camera poses and 3D point positions to minimize reprojection error across multiple views.
detail: Bundle adjustment (BA) is the large nonlinear least-squares step that simultaneously refines all camera Pose estimates and 3D landmark coordinates so projected points best match their image observations. It is the accuracy-critical back end of Visual SLAM and Structure from motion, and it can be cast as a sparse Factor graph problem. Reprojection relies on accurate Camera intrinsics from Camera calibration, and the result is a globally consistent reconstruction.

plain: A way of moving a robot's far parts by pulling on cables, so the heavy motors can sit further back.
snappy: A transmission that routes motion through cables, enabling remote, lightweight, low-inertia actuation.
detail: A cable drive (tendon drive) routes force from a motor to a distant joint through tensioned cables and pulleys, letting designers place heavy motors at the base and keep moving links light, with low inertia and good Backdrivability. This makes it common in a Surgical robot from companies like Intuitive Surgical, a Continuum robot, and dexterous wrists. The same principle scales up into Tendon-driven actuation for a Robotic hand.

plain: Adjusting a robot's settings so its internal model matches how the real hardware actually behaves.
snappy: Tuning sensor and model parameters so software predictions match the physical robot.
detail: Calibration corrects systematic errors between assumed and actual geometry, scaling, or offsets, improving Accuracy and Repeatability. Examples include Camera calibration to recover Camera intrinsics and Camera extrinsics, Hand-eye calibration linking an arm to its Camera, and Extrinsic calibration aligning a LiDAR with an Inertial measurement unit. In Manufacturing, periodic calibration keeps an Industrial robot arm placing parts within tolerance.

plain: A sensor that captures color images, giving a robot something like eyesight.
snappy: An imaging sensor that captures visible-light pixels for robot vision.
detail: A camera converts incoming light into a grid of pixels, the primary input for Computer vision and Perception tasks like Object detection and Semantic segmentation. Robots calibrate it with Camera calibration to recover Camera intrinsics, and may pick a Global shutter or Rolling shutter readout depending on motion. Specialized variants include the Stereo camera, Depth camera, Event camera, and Thermal camera.

plain: Measuring a camera's exact lens and viewing properties so its images can be used for accurate distance and angle measurements.
snappy: Estimating a camera's intrinsic parameters and lens distortion so image pixels map correctly to rays.
detail: Camera calibration determines focal length, optical center, and lens distortion, the Camera intrinsics that define the camera's Projection model. Without it, measured angles and reconstructed depths are wrong, so it is done before Stereo matching, Visual odometry, or 3D reconstruction, often by photographing a Fiducial marker or checkerboard. It is distinct from Camera extrinsics (where the camera sits) and from Hand-eye calibration, which relates a Manufacturing arm's gripper to its camera.

plain: Where a camera is and which way it points relative to the robot or the world, expressed as its position and orientation.
snappy: The rigid pose (rotation and translation) of a camera relative to a robot or world reference frame.
detail: Camera extrinsics give the Camera's Pose — its rotation and translation — within a chosen Coordinate frame, as opposed to the lens geometry captured by Camera intrinsics. They are found through Extrinsic calibration and stored in the robot's Transform tree so that Perception data can be expressed in a common Reference frame. Accurate extrinsics are vital for Sensor fusion, Camera-lidar fusion, and projecting detections onto a map.

plain: The fixed internal settings of a camera, like its zoom and the exact center of its image, needed to turn pixels into real-world angles.
snappy: The internal optical parameters of a camera (focal length, principal point, distortion) mapping 3D rays to pixels.
detail: Camera intrinsics describe a single Camera's internal geometry — focal length, principal point, and lens distortion — captured in a projection matrix during Camera calibration. They are required to back-project pixels into 3D rays for Visual odometry, Depth estimation, Stereo matching, and Image rectification. Intrinsics are distinct from Camera extrinsics, which describe where the camera sits in the world.

plain: Blending what a camera sees with what a laser scanner measures to get one richer picture of the surroundings.
snappy: Combining camera imagery and lidar point clouds into a single, complementary perception output.
detail: Camera-lidar fusion pairs the rich color and texture of a Camera with the accurate range of LiDAR so each covers the other's weakness, the camera classifying objects and the lidar pinning down their distance. It requires careful Extrinsic calibration so a Point cloud aligns with image pixels, and it is a form of Sensor fusion central to a Mobility self-driving stack. Results often feed 3D object detection and a Bird's-eye view representation for downstream planning.

plain: A networking standard built on the CAN bus from cars, adapted to connect small industrial and motion devices.
snappy: A CAN-bus-based higher-layer protocol for embedded industrial, motion, and motor-control devices.
detail: CANopen layers a standardized object dictionary and device profiles on top of the automotive CAN bus, making it popular for compact Motion control, a Motion controller, drives, and sensors in machinery and a Mobile robot. It defines profiles for devices like a servo or a Variable frequency drive so components from different vendors interoperate. As a Fieldbus it suits modest data rates and short distances, complementing faster Industrial Ethernet options like EtherCAT in cost-sensitive subsystems.

plain: A sensor that detects a nearby object or touch by sensing the tiny change it causes in an electric field.
snappy: A proximity/touch sensor that detects objects via changes in capacitance of an electric field.
detail: A capacitive sensor registers an approaching or touching object — even a human hand — through the change it induces in a sensed capacitance, making it a common Proximity sensor and touch modality. In robotics it appears in safety-edge skins, Tactile sensor surfaces, and Robotic skin that enables safe Human-robot interaction and Collision detection on a Collaborative robot. Unlike an Ultrasonic sensor or Photoelectric sensor, it needs no emitted beam and works at very short range.

plain: The spot where a stumbling robot should plant its next foot to come safely to a stop.
snappy: The ground location where stepping would bring a walking robot's center of mass to rest.
detail: The capture point (also instantaneous capture point or divergent component of motion) is derived from the Linear inverted pendulum model and combines Center of mass position and velocity into a single point to step toward. Stepping so the foot covers the capture point cancels the robot's forward momentum and re-centers it over a new Support polygon. It is a workhorse criterion for push recovery and Dynamic walking on Bipedal robots and Humanoid robots, complementing the Zero moment point for balance control.

plain: A super-light, super-stiff material made of woven carbon threads set in plastic, used to build strong robot parts that weigh very little.
snappy: A polymer-matrix material reinforced with carbon fibers, offering very high stiffness-to-weight for low-mass robot structures.
detail: Carbon fiber composite (CFRP) embeds high-strength carbon fibers in a resin, delivering exceptional Stiffness at a fraction of aluminum's mass, which raises a structure's natural frequency and lowers arm inertia. Roboticists use it for Drone airframes, Quadcopter propellers, Exoskeleton frames, and lightweight Link members where reducing the Inertia tensor improves control Bandwidth and Payload-to-weight ratio. It is especially valued in Space robotics, where launch mass is costly, though its low Mechanical compliance and brittleness must be weighed against metal.

plain: A free, realistic driving simulator used to test self-driving car software in virtual cities.
snappy: An open-source simulator for autonomous-driving research with realistic urban scenes and sensor modeling.
detail: CARLA renders virtual towns with traffic, pedestrians, and weather, emitting simulated Camera, LiDAR, and Radar streams so a Self-driving stack can be tested safely, supporting Scenario-based testing and Synthetic data generation. It is the autonomous-driving counterpart to general robotics simulators like Gazebo and Isaac Sim. Researchers use it to probe Edge case and Long-tail scenario events before on-road testing of an Autonomous vehicle.

plain: A robot that moves a tool along three straight rails set at right angles, like a 3D printer's overhead frame.
