Use cases include warehouse Goods-to-person picking, a Humanoid robot doing household tasks, and an Autonomous mobile robot servicing factory machines.

plain: A robot that combines a driving base with a robot arm, so it can move to a spot and then pick things up there.
snappy: A mobile base carrying a manipulator arm, combining navigation with grasping for navigate-and-fetch tasks.
detail: A mobile manipulator fuses an Autonomous mobile robot base with an Industrial robot arm or Cobot, enabling Mobile manipulation: the robot navigates to a workstation, then performs Grasping and Pick and place there. Coordinating the base and arm together is a Whole-body control problem, often planned with MoveIt and Nav2. It is used in Logistics & Warehouse order fulfillment and flexible Manufacturing where fixed cells are too rigid.

plain: A company that makes the camera-and-chip systems many cars use to see the road and assist the driver.
snappy: Intel-affiliated maker of ADAS and self-driving vision chips (the EyeQ family).
detail: Mobileye supplies the EyeQ system-on-chip and Computer vision software behind much of the world's Advanced driver-assistance systems, from Lane keeping assist to Automatic emergency braking. It is also building a full Self-driving stack and championed the Responsibility-sensitive safety formal model for Autonomous vehicle decision-making. Its camera-centric Object detection and Pedestrian detection pipelines ship in millions of production cars.

plain: A simple, decades-old way for industrial devices to talk to each other over a wire, still common because it is easy and cheap.
snappy: A simple, openly published legacy serial and TCP protocol for industrial device communication.
detail: Modbus is one of the oldest and most ubiquitous Fieldbus protocols, prized for its simplicity: a master polls registers and coils on slave devices over RS-485 (Modbus RTU) or Ethernet (Modbus TCP). It is common between a Programmable logic controller, a Remote terminal unit, sensors, a Variable frequency drive, and SCADA systems, especially in older or cost-sensitive installations. It lacks the speed and Determinism of EtherCAT or PROFINET, but its openness keeps it in wide use across Industrial automation.

plain: A controller that looks a few seconds into the future, plans the best sequence of moves, does only the first one, then re-plans on the next step.
snappy: Control that solves a constrained optimization over a rolling prediction horizon each cycle and applies only the first command.
detail: MPC repeatedly solves a Trajectory optimization problem using a model of the Dynamics, naturally respecting limits like joint torque or Collision avoidance, which is why it is also called receding horizon control. It is central to modern Balance control and Whole-body control on a Humanoid robot, and to path-following on an Autonomous vehicle via Trajectory tracking. It demands fast Real-time control because the optimization must finish inside the Control rate, and it shares the cost-minimizing spirit of the Linear quadratic regulator and Optimal control.

plain: A learning approach where the robot first builds an internal model of how the world works, then uses it to plan good actions.
snappy: RL that learns a predictive world model and uses it to plan or generate training data.
detail: Model-based reinforcement learning learns a World model of environment dynamics and exploits it to plan, imagine rollouts, or generate synthetic experience, typically boosting Sample efficiency over Model-free reinforcement learning. This matters in robotics where real-world trials are slow and risky, so an accurate dynamics model lets a Robot rehearse internally before acting. Its quality hinges on the learned model, and errors there echo the Reality gap seen in Sim-to-real transfer.

plain: A learning approach where the robot improves purely from trial-and-error reward, without ever building a model of how the world works.
snappy: RL that learns a policy or value function directly from experience without modeling environment dynamics.
detail: Model-free reinforcement learning skips learning a World model and instead optimizes a Policy or Value function straight from observed Reward, as in Q-learning, Soft actor-critic, and Proximal policy optimization. It is simpler and avoids model-bias, but generally needs far more interaction, hurting Sample efficiency compared with Model-based reinforcement learning. In robotics it dominates learned Legged locomotion, where Massively parallel simulation supplies the enormous sample counts it requires.

plain: Building a self-driving system as separate stages, each handling one job like seeing, predicting, or planning.
snappy: An autonomy architecture decomposed into distinct perception, prediction, planning, and control modules with defined interfaces.
detail: The Modular pipeline is the dominant Self-driving stack design: Perception and Sensor fusion feed an explicit object list and Occupancy grid, prediction forecasts agents, then Behavior planning and Motion planning hand a trajectory to control. Each stage is separately testable and traceable, which suits Functional safety and ISO 26262, the key advantage over an End-to-end driving model. Waymo and Aurora favor this approach for its interpretability when diagnosing a Disengagement.

plain: A robot built from many small, interchangeable building blocks that can be rearranged into different shapes.
snappy: A robot composed of standardized modules that can be connected, swapped, or reconfigured to change its capabilities or form.
detail: Modular robots trade a fixed body for a kit of repeated units, each carrying its own actuator, sensor, and computer. Self-reconfigurable variants can rearrange their own modules to switch between a Snake robot, a Legged robot, or a rolling Wheeled robot for different terrain. Research platforms emphasize morphological computation and exploit changing morphology and degrees of freedom, and they are common testbeds for swarm robotics and emergent behavior, distinguishing them from a monolithic Industrial robot arm.

plain: A structure where the outer shell itself carries the loads instead of an internal frame.
snappy: A construction in which the external skin bears primary structural loads rather than a separate frame.
detail: In a Monocoque the outer skin is the structure, eliminating a separate internal frame to save weight, a strategy borrowed from aerospace and motorsport and valued where mass matters, as in a Space robot or a racing-style Chassis. It contrasts with the Endoskeleton approach and frequently uses Carbon fiber composite to maximize stiffness-to-weight, improving the Payload-to-weight ratio. Skin damage in a monocoque is structurally significant, unlike a cosmetic cover.

plain: A way for a robot to guess where it is by scattering many candidate positions and keeping the ones that best match what its sensors see.
snappy: A particle-filter localization method that represents the robot's pose belief as a cloud of weighted samples updated by motion and sensing.
detail: Monte Carlo localization (MCL) applies a Particle filter to the Localization problem: each particle is a hypothesized Pose, motion commands push the cloud forward (akin to Dead reckoning), and each new Lidar scan reweights particles by how well they match the Occupancy grid map. Resampling concentrates particles on likely poses. MCL is robust to the multi-modal uncertainty that trips up a plain Kalman filter, which is why its adaptive variant AMCL is the default localizer in the ROS Navigation stack.

plain: The surprising observation that things any toddler does easily, like walking or picking up a toy, are extremely hard for robots, while abstract reasoning like chess is comparatively easy.
snappy: The principle that high-level reasoning needs little computation but low-level sensorimotor skills require enormous computation, making perception and motion the hard part of robotics.
detail: Named for Hans Moravec, the paradox explains why Manipulation and Locomotion lagged behind symbolic AI for decades: tasks like Grasping a soft object or Bipedal locomotion over rough ground demand exquisite Perception and control. It motivates today's emphasis on Imitation learning, Reinforcement learning, and large-scale Simulation to acquire the Dexterity humans take for granted. The paradox is often cited to temper expectations for a Generalist robot and to explain why a Contact-rich manipulation task remains a frontier problem.

plain: Letting a robot's body shape do some of the 'thinking', so the control software has to do less.
snappy: Offloading part of a robot's control and computation onto its physical body design, so mechanics handle work the controller otherwise would.
detail: Morphological computation says intelligence is partly embodied: clever Morphology can stabilize motion or simplify grasping with little active control. The classic example is Passive dynamic walking, where a well-tuned leg geometry produces a natural gait downhill with no motors, improving Energy efficiency. It is a guiding principle of Soft robotics and Bio-inspired robotics, where a Compliant mechanism or Series elastic actuator absorbs disturbances that a rigid robot would have to compute away.

plain: A robot's physical shape and how its parts are put together.
snappy: The physical form of a robot, the number, type, and arrangement of its links, joints, and limbs.
detail: Morphology covers whether a robot is a Quadruped robot, a Humanoid robot, or a wheeled platform, and how its Link and Joint elements connect, captured formally in a URDF or by Denavit-Hartenberg parameters. Form shapes function: morphology fixes the Workspace, the Degrees of freedom, and which gaits or grasps are possible. The idea that body design can do computational work for the controller is Morphological computation, and choosing morphology to match a task is central to Bio-inspired robotics.

plain: The system that coordinates several motors at once so a machine's many axes move together smoothly and in sync.
snappy: Coordinated regulation of position, velocity, and acceleration across multiple motorized axes.
detail: Motion control sits above per-axis Servo control, generating coordinated, jerk-limited profiles so a Cartesian robot, SCARA robot, or CNC machine moves its axes in concert, often over a Fieldbus like EtherCAT. It handles Time parameterization and synchronization of Trajectory tracking, run by a Motion controller and ultimately the Robot controller. It overlaps with Computer numerical control in machine tools and is the practical glue between Motion planning and the motors.

plain: A device that coordinates the precise, synchronized movement of several motors in a machine or robot.
snappy: A controller that plans and coordinates multi-axis servo and stepper motion in machinery.
detail: A motion controller generates coordinated position, velocity, and acceleration commands for multiple axes, handling tasks like interpolation, cam profiles, and electronic gearing that a generic Programmable logic controller may not. It drives a Servomotor or stepper through amplifiers, closing the loop with feedback from an Encoder, and underpins Motion control on machine tools, packaging lines, and an Industrial robot arm. Tight synchronization across axes typically demands a deterministic Industrial Ethernet link such as EtherCAT.

plain: Working out how a robot should move from where it is to where it needs to be without bumping into anything.
snappy: Computing a feasible, collision-free trajectory through Configuration space from a start state to a goal.
detail: Motion planning generalizes Path planning by accounting for the robot's geometry, joint limits, and often its Dynamics, producing a sequence of configurations a manipulator or mobile base can actually execute. A typical pipeline uses a Global planner to find a coarse route and a Local planner to refine it against nearby obstacles, with Collision checking validating each candidate. Frameworks such as MoveIt and OMPL implement Sampling-based planning algorithms like Rapidly-exploring random tree and Probabilistic roadmap, while Trajectory optimization smooths the result before Time parameterization assigns speeds.

plain: A small, ready-made piece of movement that can be strung together with others to build up complicated actions.
snappy: A reusable parameterized action segment that serves as a building block for composing longer motions.
detail: A Motion primitive is a precomputed or learned chunk of movement, such as a short arc, a grasp approach, or a stepping motion, that a planner concatenates rather than solving every move from scratch. Driving robots build a State lattice from a library of kinematically feasible motion primitives so that Path planning becomes a graph search over drivable segments. In manipulation, a manipulation primitive like pushing or inserting is composed by a Task and motion planning layer, and learned motion primitives also underpin a Skill primitive in many imitation-learning systems.

plain: The electronics that decide how much power to send a motor and when, so it moves the way the robot wants.
snappy: Electronics that regulate motor current and commutation to execute a commanded motion.
detail: A motor controller (motor driver, or ESC for a drone) sits between the robot's computer and the motor, switching power transistors to set current, voltage, and Commutation so the motor produces the demanded torque or speed. It typically uses Pulse-width modulation to vary power and, for a Brushless DC motor, runs Field-oriented control with feedback from an Encoder or Hall effect sensor. It is the electronic half of the Servomotor and the Servo control loop closed by a PID controller.

plain: A widely used free software package that figures out how to move a robot arm without hitting anything.
snappy: The de facto ROS motion-planning framework for manipulator arms, bundling planning, kinematics, and collision checking.
detail: MoveIt is the standard manipulation stack in the ROS ecosystem (now MoveIt 2 on ROS 2), wiring together Inverse kinematics solvers, Collision checking, and Trajectory optimization. It delegates the actual planning to sampling-based algorithms from OMPL and executes the result through ros2_control. A typical use is an Industrial robot arm doing Pick and place: MoveIt plans a collision-free Trajectory from the current Pose to a Grasp pose.

plain: A fast physics simulator that is especially good at modeling robots touching and gripping things, widely used in research.
snappy: A fast physics engine specializing in contact-rich rigid-body dynamics for robotics and learning research.
detail: MuJoCo's solver computes Contact dynamics and Rigid body dynamics efficiently enough to run many simulations in parallel, making it a favorite for Reinforcement learning and Sim-to-real research. Robots are described in MJCF, analogous to URDF or SDF, and the engine now ships free and open-source. It competes with PyBullet, Drake, and the Physics engine inside Gazebo, and underlies much Learned locomotion work.

plain: Working out routes for a whole fleet of robots in the same building so they all reach their destinations without bumping into each other.
snappy: Planning collision-free paths for many robots that share one workspace so that none collide in space or time while reaching their goals.
detail: Multi-agent path finding (MAPF) assigns each robot a goal and computes time-indexed paths over a shared graph or Occupancy grid map such that no two agents occupy the same cell at the same step. Algorithms like Conflict-Based Search and prioritized planning scale to the hundreds of Autonomous mobile robot units in a goods-to-person Logistics & Warehouse, and tie directly into Fleet management and Multi-robot system coordination. It contrasts with reactive schemes like Optimal Reciprocal Collision Avoidance, which avoid collisions locally without a global joint plan.

plain: Following many moving things at the same time while never mixing up which is which.
snappy: Tracking multiple objects simultaneously while preserving a consistent identity for each.
detail: Multi-object tracking, often abbreviated MOT, extends Object tracking to crowded scenes where cars, cyclists, and pedestrians all move at once and must keep stable IDs frame to frame. The dominant tracking-by-detection approach runs Object detection each frame and then solves Data association to stitch detections into tracks, frequently using a Kalman filter to predict where each track will move. In a self-driving stack it produces the labeled, persistent obstacles that Behavior prediction and motion planning rely on, and it is benchmarked on datasets like nuScenes.

plain: A group of robots that work together as a team to get a job done.
snappy: A collection of two or more robots that coordinate their actions toward shared or complementary goals.
detail: A multi-robot system pools sensing, computation, and physical reach across many machines so the team can cover more ground or lift more than any single unit. In a warehouse a Fleet of Autonomous mobile robots split picking routes under a Fleet management layer, often communicating over a Publish-subscribe network and resolving conflicting paths with Multi-agent path finding. The approach spans from tightly choreographed Swarm robotics to loosely coupled cooperatives, and the resulting team can show Emergent behavior that no individual robot was programmed to perform.

plain: A drone held up by several spinning propellers, usually four, that can hover in place and take off straight up.
snappy: A drone lifted and controlled by several fixed-pitch rotors (commonly four), enabling hover and vertical takeoff.
detail: A multirotor controls attitude and position by varying the speeds of its rotors, typically arranged as a Quadcopter, Hexacopter, or Octocopter, with each motor driven by an Electronic speed controller. It hovers precisely but has limited Endurance compared with a Fixed-wing drone, so it suits Aerial cinematography, inspection, and Last-mile delivery. A Flight controller stabilizes it using an Inertial measurement unit, and vendors like DJI and Skydio dominate the consumer and prosumer market.

plain: Training one robot model to do many different jobs at once so it shares what it learns between them.
snappy: Training a single model jointly on multiple tasks so shared structure improves performance and data efficiency on each.
detail: In robotics, multitask learning lets one network learn picking, inserting, and wiping together, so features useful for one task help another and overall Sample efficiency improves. It underpins any Generalist policy and large systems like RT-1 and RT-X trained across diverse Demonstration data. It is closely tied to Transfer learning and Representation learning, and must guard against negative transfer where unrelated tasks interfere.

plain: The standard free software, built on the popular ROS robot platform, that gives a wheeled robot a complete sense-where-am-I-and-drive-there ability.
snappy: The ROS 2 navigation framework that orchestrates planners, controllers, costmaps, and recovery behaviors through a behavior tree.
detail: Nav2 is the production-grade Navigation stack for ROS 2, replacing the original move_base. It uses a Behavior tree to sequence a Global planner (for example Dijkstra's algorithm or A* search), a Local planner / controller such as the Dynamic Window Approach or Timed Elastic Band, a Cost map with an Inflation layer, and AMCL for Localization, plus recovery actions when the robot gets stuck. It is the default autonomy brain for countless Autonomous mobile robot and Service robot deployments built on ros2_control.

plain: Working out a route from where a robot is to where it needs to go, and then following it.
snappy: Deciding and following a collision-free path from a start to a goal in an environment.
detail: Navigation combines Localization (knowing where you are), Mapping, Path planning, and obstacle handling so a robot can travel safely. In practice it is delivered by a Navigation stack such as Nav2, which fuses a Global planner, a Local planner, a Cost map, and Collision avoidance. It is the core competence of an Autonomous mobile robot, a Delivery robot, and a Self-driving car alike, and depends on continuous Obstacle detection.

plain: The full bundle of software that lets a robot figure out where it is, decide a route, and actually drive there without hitting things.
snappy: The integrated software pipeline that maps, localizes, plans, and drives a mobile robot from point A to point B.
detail: A navigation stack ties together Mapping, Localization (often AMCL), a Global planner and Local planner, a Cost map with its Inflation layer, and recovery behaviors into one autonomy pipeline. It is the backbone of Logistics & Warehouse and Service & Consumer robots: a Differential drive Autonomous mobile robot uses it to follow Waypoint navigation goals while doing live Obstacle avoidance. The canonical modern implementation is Nav2, the ROS 2 successor to the original ROS Navigation stack.

plain: Imaging fields from the air to color-code how healthy and green the plants are, using light the human eye cannot see.
snappy: Producing crop-health maps from a vegetation index computed from red and near-infrared bands of drone multispectral imagery.
detail: NDVI mapping flies a Precision agriculture drone carrying a multispectral Camera, then computes the vegetation index per pixel to highlight stressed or vigorous crop zones. The index layer is georeferenced onto an Orthomosaic built by Aerial photogrammetry, with detail set by Ground sample distance, so agronomists can target irrigation or spraying. It is a staple Agriculture workflow, often flown the same mission that gathers the 3D reconstruction of the field.

plain: A way of capturing a real scene with a few photos so a computer can then generate a realistic image of it from any angle you choose.
snappy: A neural network that encodes a scene's color and density as a continuous volume, letting you render photorealistic novel views from arbitrary camera poses.
detail: A NeRF trains a small neural network to predict color and opacity at every point in space, so a robot can render the scene from viewpoints it never directly photographed. In robotics it is used for dense 3D reconstruction and Photorealistic rendering of cluttered environments, feeding Sensor simulation pipelines and closing the Reality gap for Sim-to-real transfer. Capture requires accurate Camera intrinsics and poses, often recovered by Structure from motion or Visual SLAM, and the result complements Point cloud maps where smooth, view-dependent appearance matters. Rendering is slower than Gaussian splatting, which is why many embodied systems now prefer the latter for real-time use.

plain: A brain-inspired computer model that lets a robot learn skills from examples instead of being hand-programmed, by adjusting many internal numbers.
snappy: A trainable model that maps a robot's sensor inputs to actions or predictions, with its internal weights learned from data.
detail: A neural network is the workhorse function approximator behind nearly every learned robot Policy, used to represent a Value function in Reinforcement learning, a perception model in Computer vision, or a control law in Learning-based control. Specialized variants dominate different jobs: a Convolutional neural network for images, a Transformer for sequences and a Robot foundation model. On robots it typically runs on Onboard compute such as an NVIDIA Jetson, where size constraints motivate Policy distillation.

plain: A fast, step-by-step way to compute the forces in a robot by sweeping out along the links and then back again.
snappy: A recursive force-and-torque-balance method that computes robot dynamics link by link.
detail: The recursive Newton-Euler algorithm (RNEA) computes Inverse dynamics in two passes along the Kinematic chain: an outward sweep propagates velocity and acceleration, then an inward sweep balances forces and torques link by link, applying Newton's and Euler's laws to each Link. It produces the same Equations of motion as Lagrangian dynamics but is far faster, which is why dynamics libraries such as Pinocchio and physics engines like MuJoCo use it for Real-time control and Computed torque control.

plain: A single self-contained program that does one job inside a robot's larger collection of cooperating programs.
snappy: An individual executable process that performs computation and communicates within a robot's software graph.
detail: A robot's software is built from many nodes, each handling a focused task such as reading a Camera, running Localization, or driving a motor, all connected into a graph by Middleware. Nodes exchange data over a Topic via Publish-subscribe, call each other through a Service, or coordinate long jobs with an Action. ROS and ROS 2 organize software this way, and tools like RViz can inspect the running node graph.

plain: A rule built into how something moves: a car or a normal wheel can't slide straight sideways, even though it can still get anywhere by driving and turning.
snappy: A motion restriction that limits which directions a robot can move instantaneously without limiting where it can eventually reach, as when a rolling wheel cannot slide sideways.
detail: Formally, the limit applies to velocities rather than positions, so a robot under a nonholonomic constraint still has full reach but must maneuver to get there, the way a car parallel-parks instead of sliding into a space. A Differential-drive robot and any Ackermann steering vehicle are the classic cases, which is why their Path planning relies on curved primitives like Dubins path and Reeds-Shepp curves rather than straight-line moves. Removing the constraint, for example with an Omni wheel or Mecanum wheel base, yields Holonomic motion; the distinction is central to Motion planning and Kinematics.

plain: Methods for steering machines whose behavior does not scale up neatly, where doubling the command does not simply double the response.
snappy: Control of systems whose dynamics violate superposition, requiring techniques beyond linear State feedback.
detail: Most real robots are nonlinear because of gravity, Coriolis and centrifugal forces, friction, and Contact dynamics, so a Legged robot or Manipulator cannot be fully captured by linear theory. Techniques include Computed torque control (feedback linearization), Sliding mode control, backstepping, and Lyapunov-based design, and stability is shown via Lyapunov stability rather than poles. It generalizes the linear methods like Pole placement and the Linear quadratic regulator that only hold near an operating point.

plain: Moving an object around without actually grabbing it, by pushing, tipping, sliding, or even tossing it.
snappy: Manipulating objects without grasping, e.g. pushing, tilting, rolling, or throwing.
detail: Nonprehensile manipulation exploits Contact dynamics, friction, and momentum to control objects a Gripper cannot or need not hold, such as Pushing a flat part across a table or tilting a box to reorient it. It is harder to plan than grasping because the object is underactuated and slips according to the Friction cone, making it a rich Research/Frontier topic often tackled with learned policies and accurate Physics engine models. Practical payoffs include singulating parts in Bin picking and repositioning items too large or fragile for Force closure.

plain: The set of joint movements that reshuffle a robot arm internally without moving its hand at all.
snappy: Joint motions that leave the end-effector pose unchanged.
detail: The null space of the Jacobian matrix collects every joint velocity that produces zero End-effector Twist, so a Kinematic redundancy arm can shift its elbow, dodge an obstacle, or stay away from a Kinematic singularity while the gripper holds its Pose. Null-space projection adds these self-motions as a lower-priority task on top of the primary Inverse kinematics goal, a core trick in Whole-body control and Operational space control.

plain: A company that makes small driverless pods designed to carry groceries and packages, not people.
snappy: Autonomous-vehicle company building driverless last-mile delivery pods.
detail: Nuro builds compact, occupant-free vehicles purpose-built for Last-mile delivery, carrying goods rather than passengers across a defined Operational design domain. Because no human rides inside, the design can prioritize pedestrian Safety and a lighter Chassis, using LiDAR, Radar, and Camera sensing for Level 4 automation. Nuro sits at the intersection of the Autonomous vehicle and Logistics & Warehouse worlds, competing with sidewalk Delivery robot approaches at larger scale.

plain: A large public collection of real driving data, with sensor recordings and labels, used to train and test self-driving software.
snappy: A widely used multimodal autonomous-driving dataset providing synchronized camera, LiDAR, and radar with rich 3D annotations.
detail: Released by Motional, nuScenes spans 1000 scenes across Boston and Singapore and is a standard benchmark for 3D object detection, multi-object tracking, and prediction. Its annotations heavily cover the vulnerable road user classes that pedestrian detection must handle, and it provides a lane graph-style map layer. Alongside the Waymo Open Dataset, it is one of the most cited datasets in autonomy research and a common testbed for bird's-eye view perception.

plain: NVIDIA's collection of robotics tools, covering realistic simulators for training robots and AI models for controlling them.
snappy: NVIDIA's robotics platform spanning simulation, perception acceleration, and humanoid foundation models, including Isaac Sim, Isaac Lab, and Isaac GR00T.
detail: NVIDIA Isaac bundles Isaac Sim, a photorealistic Robot simulator built on USD, and Isaac Lab for large-scale reinforcement learning, enabling Sim-to-real workflows with Domain randomization and Massively parallel simulation on GPUs. Its GR00T effort develops a Robot foundation model for the Humanoid robot, alongside perception libraries that run on NVIDIA Jetson edge hardware. The platform competes with open tooling such as Gazebo and MuJoCo while integrating with ROS 2.

plain: A line of small, powerful computer modules from NVIDIA that act as the brain for many robots.
snappy: A family of embedded GPU compute modules widely used as the onboard brain for AI-driven robots.
detail: NVIDIA Jetson modules (Orin, Thor) pack a Graphics processing unit, CPU, and AI accelerator onto a single System on a chip, delivering high TOPS within a modest Power budget for Onboard compute. They are a default choice for a Humanoid robot, a drone Flight controller, and an Autonomous mobile robot, and pair with the NVIDIA Isaac software stack and Isaac Sim for development. Running ROS 2 on Jetson lets developers move perception and a Vision-language-action model from the cloud to Edge computing on the robot.

plain: Spotting things in an image and drawing a box around each one with a label saying what it is.
snappy: Locating and classifying objects in an image, typically by predicting labeled bounding boxes.
detail: Object detection finds each object's position and class, outputting a Bounding box and a label, usually via a Convolutional neural network. In robotics it lets an Autonomous vehicle find vehicles and Pedestrian detection targets, and lets an arm locate parts for Bin picking. It is the 2D foundation that extends to 3D object detection for depth-aware perception and contrasts with the pixel-level Semantic segmentation.

plain: Working out what a thing the robot is looking at actually is, such as a cup, a box, or a person.
snappy: Assigning a category label to an object detected in an image or sensor scan.
detail: Object recognition takes a region of an image and answers 'what is this?', whereas Object detection answers 'where is it?' and the two are usually run together in a perception pipeline. In a Logistics & Warehouse robot it lets a Bin picking system tell a screwdriver from a wrench before planning a grasp, typically using a Convolutional neural network. It is a core building block of Scene understanding and of Vision-guided robotics on a Manufacturing line.

plain: Keeping tabs on a single moving thing as it travels across the frames of a video.
snappy: Maintaining the position and identity of one detected object over successive video frames.
detail: Object tracking links a detection in one frame to the same object in the next so the robot perceives continuous motion rather than disconnected snapshots. In Mobility it follows a single lead vehicle for Adaptive cruise control, and in Defense & Security it keeps a camera Gimbal locked on a target. It usually starts from Object detection, can be sped up with Optical flow, and scales up to Multi-object tracking when many targets must be followed at once.

plain: Keeping a moving robot from running into people, furniture, or anything else in its way.
snappy: The capability of steering a robot clear of detected obstacles, usually as a reactive layer atop a planned route.
detail: Obstacle avoidance combines Obstacle detection from a LiDAR or Depth camera with short-horizon planning that adjusts the robot's motion in real time. On an Autonomous mobile robot it is usually the job of the Local planner, using methods like the Dynamic Window Approach, Timed Elastic Band, or the Potential field method to deviate around a person while a Global planner keeps tracking the original goal. The Nav2 navigation stack maintains a Cost map and Inflation layer so the planner naturally keeps clearance from detected obstacles.

plain: Finding the things in front of a robot that it must not run into.
snappy: Identifying objects and surfaces the robot must avoid, from sensor data, to support safe motion.
detail: Obstacle detection turns raw sensor data into a list of things to avoid, the perception half of Obstacle avoidance and Collision avoidance. A Mobility robot may detect obstacles from a LiDAR Point cloud after Ground segmentation, from Stereo matching, or from a fused Depth map, then mark them in a Cost map or Occupancy grid for the planner. In Logistics & Warehouse settings it stops an Autonomous mobile robot before it strikes a pallet or a worker.

plain: A map made of small squares where each square is marked as free, blocked, or unknown.
snappy: A grid representation dividing space into cells, each storing the probability that it is occupied by an obstacle.
detail: An occupancy grid (or Occupancy grid map) discretizes the environment into cells whose values encode the chance an obstacle is present, built up from LiDAR or Depth camera returns. It is the workhorse map for 2D navigation and the basis of the Cost map used by planners. Closely related are the 3D Voxel grid and the memory-efficient OctoMap, and the same data supports detecting Free space for path planning.

plain: A learned system that predicts which chunks of 3D space around a vehicle are solid, including things it has never seen labeled before.
snappy: A neural network that predicts dense 3D occupancy of the space surrounding an autonomous vehicle from sensor inputs.
detail: Occupancy networks (occ nets) learn to output a 3D Voxel grid of occupancy directly from cameras or LiDAR, capturing arbitrary geometry rather than fixed Bounding box categories. They have become central to the modern Self-driving stack because they represent unexpected obstacles and the Free space a planner needs, often paired with a Bird's-eye-view representation. Unlike a hand-built Occupancy grid, the geometry and semantics are learned end-to-end, complementing 3D object detection.

plain: A drone with eight propellers, built to carry heavy loads and keep flying even if a couple of motors quit.
snappy: An eight-rotor Multirotor used for heavy-lift Payload and high-redundancy missions.
detail: An Octocopter can often survive multiple motor failures because the Flight controller uses Control allocation across eight rotors, making it favored for cinema cameras, lidar survey rigs, and Defense applications where a controlled descent is mandatory. The configuration may be a flat octo or a coaxial X8 where motors are stacked in pairs to keep the frame compact. Its high Payload comes at the cost of weight and reduced Endurance compared with a Quadcopter or Hexacopter.

plain: A compact 3D map that saves memory by using big blocks for empty areas and small blocks only where detail is needed.
snappy: An octree-based probabilistic 3D occupancy map that adapts cell resolution for memory efficiency.
detail: OctoMap stores 3D occupancy in an octree, recursively splitting space so that large empty or uniformly occupied regions use a single coarse node while detailed areas subdivide. It is a popular open-source choice for 3D navigation and collision checking on drones and manipulators, fusing repeated Depth camera or LiDAR observations probabilistically. It is far more compact than a dense Voxel grid while serving the same role as a 3D Occupancy grid.

plain: A robot's way of estimating how far and which way it has moved by tracking its own wheels or camera.
snappy: Estimating a robot's change in position over time by integrating sensed motion, such as wheel rotation or visual displacement.
detail: Odometry gives a continuous Pose estimate by accumulating small motion increments, but because it integrates, small errors compound into Drift over distance. Wheel odometry counts encoder ticks on the drive wheels, while Visual odometry and Visual-inertial odometry track image features and inertial data instead. It is a core input to Localization and SLAM, where Sensor fusion corrects its drift against landmarks or a Map. Closely related to Dead reckoning.

plain: A learning style where the robot can learn from old experiences, even ones gathered while behaving differently.
snappy: Reinforcement learning that improves the current policy using data generated by other or older policies.
detail: Off-policy methods like Q-learning and Soft actor-critic store experience in a replay buffer and reuse it many times, giving far better Sample efficiency than On-policy learning, which matters when real-robot data is scarce. This reuse underpins Offline reinforcement learning and lets a robot learn from teleoperation logs or another robot's runs. The trade-off is instability from learning about actions the current Policy would not take, so techniques like Actor-critic value estimation are used to stabilize it.

plain: Teaching a robot from a fixed pile of recorded experience without letting it try anything new during training.
snappy: Learning a control policy purely from a static logged dataset, with no further interaction with the environment.
detail: Offline RL is attractive in robotics because it can reuse logs from teleoperation, prior deployments, or human Demonstration data without risking hardware on fresh exploration. The core challenge is distribution shift: the learned Policy may favor actions absent from the data, so algorithms add conservative constraints. It is a flavor of Off-policy learning, complements Sim-to-real transfer, and improves Sample efficiency by squeezing value from data already collected by a Fleet.

plain: A special wheel with small rollers around its rim, so the robot it carries can scoot sideways and spin in place instead of only driving forwards and backwards.
snappy: A wheel ringed with free-spinning perimeter rollers that let it roll forward normally while sliding sideways with little resistance, enabling omnidirectional movement.
detail: Each omni wheel drives forward under motor power but offers almost no resistance to sideways slip, so a set of three or four mounted at angles can produce true Holonomic motion. This makes them popular on warehouse Omnidirectional robot platforms and on an Autonomous mobile robot that must strafe between tight aisles without turning first. The closely related Mecanum wheel uses angled rollers to achieve a similar effect on a four-wheel chassis, and both stand in contrast to the Nonholonomic constraint that limits a normal Differential drive base.

plain: A wheel system that lets a robot scoot in any direction instantly without having to turn first.
snappy: A holonomic drive system that lets a robot translate in any direction and rotate independently, without reorienting first.
detail: An omnidirectional drive gives a robot Holonomic motion, decoupling translation from rotation so it can strafe sideways or move diagonally on the spot, which is invaluable for an Omnidirectional robot maneuvering in tight Logistics and warehouse aisles. It is usually built from a Mecanum wheel or an Omni wheel set, whose roller geometry converts wheel spin into arbitrary motion. This contrasts sharply with the Nonholonomic Differential drive and Ackermann steering.

plain: A robot that can move straight in any direction, including sideways, without having to turn its body first.
snappy: A holonomic mobile base that can translate in any direction and rotate independently, without reorienting first.
detail: An omnidirectional robot achieves Holonomic motion using special wheels such as the Mecanum wheel or Omni wheel that allow Omnidirectional drive, so it can strafe sideways or spin in place. This contrasts with the Nonholonomic Differential-drive robot, which must turn before driving in a new heading. The freedom is valued in tight Logistics & Warehouse aisles and Service & Consumer settings where maneuverability beats efficiency.

plain: A free collection of well-tested algorithms for finding a clear path for a robot to follow.
snappy: An open library of sampling-based motion-planning algorithms, used as the planning backend inside MoveIt.
detail: OMPL packages randomized planners such as Rapidly-exploring random tree, RRT*, and Probabilistic roadmap into a single interface that searches a robot's Configuration space for a collision-free route. It deliberately stays abstract about geometry, relying on the caller to supply Collision checking, which is why MoveIt embeds it as its default Motion planning engine for manipulator arms. Practitioners pick a planner based on whether they need Completeness, optimality, or speed for a given Sampling-based planning problem.

plain: A learning style where the robot only learns from experiences it gathers using its current way of behaving.
snappy: Reinforcement learning that updates the policy using data generated by that same, current policy.
detail: On-policy methods such as Proximal policy optimization and Policy gradient discard old experience whenever the Policy changes, which makes them stable but data-hungry and thus weaker on Sample efficiency. In robotics they shine inside Massively parallel simulation, where Isaac Lab or MuJoCo can generate fresh rollouts cheaply for Learned locomotion. They contrast with Off-policy learning and Offline reinforcement learning, which reuse data from earlier policies.

plain: The computer the robot carries with it to run its software.
snappy: The processing hardware mounted on a robot that runs its perception, planning, and control software.
detail: Onboard compute is the robot's brain, typically combining a System on a chip, a Graphics processing unit, and sometimes an AI accelerator or FPGA to handle the Perception-action loop locally via Edge computing. A Humanoid robot like Tesla Optimus or a quadruped like Spot packs this into a compact, power- and heat-constrained module governed by the Power budget and Thermal management. Popular off-the-shelf choices include the NVIDIA Jetson family, and the stack usually runs ROS 2 on a Real-time operating system.

plain: Letting a robot tweak its own behavior on the fly as conditions change, like carrying a heavier load or walking on ice, without being retrained offline.
snappy: Adjusting a deployed policy or its parameters at runtime to cope with changing dynamics, payloads, or environments.
detail: Online adaptation lets a fielded Policy update itself at test time, for example inferring a latent 'context' vector that captures new Payload, friction, or Terrain adaptation and conditioning the controller on it. It is a practical answer to the Reality gap when System identification cannot be done offline, and shows up in rapid-adaptation Learned locomotion and in Adaptive control. It overlaps with Meta-learning and Lifelong learning, and must guard against Catastrophic forgetting when conditions shift back.

plain: A vendor-neutral standard that lets different brands of factory machines and software securely share data with each other.
snappy: A platform-independent, secure standard for industrial data exchange and interoperability across vendors.
detail: OPC UA provides a common, secure information model so a Programmable logic controller, SCADA, a Manufacturing execution system, and enterprise software can interoperate regardless of vendor. It sits high in the Automation pyramid as the connective tissue of Industry 4.0 and the Industrial Internet of Things, carrying both data and rich semantics. Unlike a raw Fieldbus such as Modbus, OPC UA adds authentication, encryption, and self-describing models, and a pub/sub mode lets it ride on Time-Sensitive Networking for real-time exchange.

plain: A robot structure where parts connect end-to-end in a single line, like a human arm.
snappy: A mechanism with links connected in one open serial sequence from base to end-effector.
detail: An Open kinematic chain is the architecture of every Serial manipulator and Articulated robot: a base, a sequence of Link members and Joint connections, and a free End-effector at the tip. It offers a large Workspace and easy closed-form Forward kinematics, but accumulates compliance and positioning error along the chain, unlike a stiffer Closed kinematic chain. Most six-axis Industrial robot arm designs are open chains.

plain: A setting where the robot constantly meets things it was never specifically programmed or trained to expect.
snappy: An operating regime with open-ended novelty, where objects, situations, and goals fall outside any fixed, enumerated list.
detail: Open-world operation breaks the closed-set assumptions of classic Object recognition, demanding Generalization, Anomaly detection, and Zero-shot generalization to cope with the unexpected. A Delivery robot on a public sidewalk or an Agricultural robot in a field faces an Unstructured environment full of edge cases no Benchmark fully captures. This is why a Foundation model and a Generalist policy are attractive: they aim to transfer broad priors into novel scenes rather than relying on a hand-built Long-tail scenario list.

plain: A giant shared collection of robot demonstrations gathered from many different labs and robot types.
snappy: A community-pooled, cross-robot dataset aggregating demonstrations from dozens of labs to train policies that span embodiments.
detail: Open X-Embodiment combines Demonstration data from many distinct robots, grippers, and tasks so a single model can learn skills that transfer across hardware, an instance of Cross-embodiment learning. It is the training corpus behind RT-X and a key resource for building any Generalist policy or Robot foundation model. By spanning embodiments it pushes Transfer learning and Multitask learning toward robots that are not tied to one arm or one lab.

plain: A way of telling a machine what to do where it follows the instructions blindly, never checking whether the result actually happened.
snappy: Control that issues commands on a fixed schedule without using sensor feedback to verify or correct the outcome.
detail: Open-loop control sends a predetermined command to an Actuator and assumes it executes faithfully, with no Error signal to close the gap. A Stepper motor driven by counting pulses is the classic robotics example: it moves an assumed distance with no Encoder confirming it. It is cheap and simple but fails silently under load, backlash, or Saturation, which is why most robots use Feedback control or Closed-loop control instead.

plain: A freely available robot brain that takes a camera view and a spoken instruction and produces the moves to carry it out.
snappy: An open-source vision-language-action model for generalist manipulation, trained on large cross-embodiment demonstration data.
detail: OpenVLA is an open-weight Vision-language-action model trained on Open X-Embodiment-scale Demonstration data, offering a publicly available alternative to closed systems like RT-2. It maps camera images plus a natural-language instruction to robot actions, enabling Language-conditioned manipulation and serving as a fine-tunable Generalist policy and Robot foundation model. Its openness makes it a common baseline for research on Few-shot learning and Transfer learning to new robots.

plain: The specific conditions, places, and weather a self-driving system is designed to handle.
snappy: The defined set of conditions (roads, speeds, weather, time of day) within which an automated driving system is engineered to operate.
detail: An Operational design domain (ODD) might be 'daytime, dry weather, geofenced downtown surface streets under 45 mph', and an Automated driving system is only certified to perform the Dynamic driving task inside it. ODD is the dividing line between Level 4 automation (works within an ODD) and Level 5 automation (no ODD limits) in the SAE levels of driving automation. Leaving the ODD must trigger a Fallback to a Minimal risk condition, and Geofencing is the common technical enforcement.

plain: Controlling where a robot's hand goes in real-world space directly, instead of telling each joint separately what to do.
snappy: Control formulated in the end-effector's Cartesian task space rather than in joint space.
detail: Operational space (task-space) control writes the dynamics and control law in the frame of the End-effector, using the Jacobian matrix to map task forces to joint torques via Torque control, so a Manipulator can regulate Cartesian position and contact force together. It naturally handles Redundancy by adding Null space tasks (like avoiding a Kinematic singularity) and is the basis for Whole-body control on a Humanoid robot. It contrasts with joint-space Computed torque control and underpins Hybrid position/force control.

plain: The hardware and software that directly run physical machinery in a plant, as opposed to the office computers that handle email and spreadsheets.
snappy: Hardware and software that directly monitor and control physical industrial equipment and processes, distinct from IT business systems.
detail: Operational technology (OT) is the layer of a plant that touches the real world: a Programmable logic controller, a Distributed control system, SCADA, a Remote terminal unit, drives, and sensors that close control loops in Real-time. It sits at the lower tiers of the Automation pyramid and increasingly connects upward to IT systems and the Industrial Internet of Things under Industry 4.0, which raises cybersecurity concerns because OT was historically air-gapped. OT spans both Process automation and Discrete automation, and standards like ISA-95 define how it integrates with a Manufacturing execution system and Enterprise resource planning.

plain: A measurement of how every point in a video appears to move from one frame to the next.
snappy: The dense per-pixel field of apparent motion between consecutive image frames.
detail: Optical flow estimates a small motion vector for each pixel, capturing how the image shifts as the camera or the scene moves. A robot uses it to sense its own Ego-motion estimation, to drive Visual odometry, and to spot moving objects against a static background for Obstacle detection. In a Service & Consumer drone it helps hold position indoors, and it speeds up frame-to-frame Object tracking; an Event camera offers a low-latency alternative for capturing fast motion.

plain: Working out the very best way to move a machine from where it is to where it should be, according to some measure of cost like time or energy.
snappy: Choosing control inputs that minimize (or maximize) a defined cost functional over the system's motion.
detail: Optimal control formalizes 'best' as minimizing a cost over a Trajectory, solved via Pontryagin's principle, dynamic programming, or numerical Trajectory optimization. The Linear quadratic regulator is its closed-form special case for linear systems and quadratic cost, while Model predictive control applies it repeatedly online. It minimizes things like Cost of transport for a Legged robot or fuel for a Drone, and overlaps with Reinforcement learning, which learns optimal policies from data instead of a model.

plain: A way for a crowd of robots to avoid each other smoothly, where each one takes responsibility for half of the dodging so no two collide.
snappy: A decentralized multi-agent collision-avoidance method where each agent assumes half the reciprocal avoidance burden.
detail: Optimal Reciprocal Collision Avoidance, or ORCA, refines the reciprocal velocity obstacle, RVO, idea by having each agent select the velocity closest to its preferred one while staying outside a shared half-plane that guarantees collision-free motion if every agent does the same. Because it is decentralized and needs no explicit communication, it scales to large groups, making it a staple of Swarm robotics and multi-robot warehouse Fleet coordination, as well as crowd simulation. It builds directly on the Velocity obstacle concept and complements global Multi-agent path finding by handling the close-range Obstacle avoidance layer.

plain: A quick, lightweight way to mark and describe distinctive points in an image so a robot can recognize them again in real time.
snappy: Fast, rotation-aware binary image features combining a FAST detector with a BRIEF descriptor.
detail: ORB stands for Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF: it detects corners with FAST, adds an orientation, and describes each point with a compact binary string that is extremely fast to match. Because it is free and efficient, it powers many Visual SLAM systems on embedded robots where the heavier SIFT descriptor would be too slow. It is used inside Feature extraction and Feature matching to drive Visual odometry and Loop closure.

plain: A single large map-like image stitched from many aerial photos and geometrically corrected so distances on it are true to scale.
snappy: A seamless, geometrically rectified aerial image map assembled from many overlapping photos with perspective and terrain distortion removed.
detail: An orthomosaic is the flat, to-scale image product of Aerial photogrammetry, created after Structure from motion recovers camera poses and a terrain model removes lean and perspective distortion. Unlike a raw aerial snapshot, every pixel maps to a real ground coordinate, so its resolution is described by Ground sample distance. Farmers overlay an orthomosaic with NDVI mapping for crop-health analysis, and surveyors use it alongside the 3D reconstruction and Point cloud from the same flight.

plain: The US government agency that writes and enforces the rules keeping workers safe on the job, including around robots.
snappy: The US federal agency that sets and enforces workplace safety regulations, applying its general and machine-safety rules to robot installations.
detail: OSHA is the US workplace-safety regulator; while it has no robot-specific standard, it enforces robot safety through its machine-guarding rules, the General Duty Clause, and by referencing consensus standards like ANSI/RIA R15.06. Employers must protect workers from robot hazards identified in a Risk assessment, using measures such as Machine guarding, an Interlock, or an Emergency stop. It is the US analogue to Europe's Machinery Directive regime.

plain: A single percentage score that measures how well a machine actually runs, combining how often it's up, how fast it runs, and how many good parts it makes.
snappy: A composite metric multiplying availability, performance, and quality to score equipment productivity, abbreviated OEE.
detail: OEE multiplies three factors, availability (uptime versus planned time), performance (actual versus ideal speed), and quality (good parts versus total), into one figure where 100% means flawless production with zero downtime, full speed, and no defects. It is the headline efficiency metric tracked by a Manufacturing execution system, and improving it is the goal behind Predictive maintenance, Statistical process control, and faster Takt time. A Smart factory uses Industrial Internet of Things data to compute OEE live across every Production line.

plain: When a system shoots past its target before swinging back, like a door that slams past closed before settling.
snappy: The amount by which a response exceeds its setpoint before settling.
detail: Overshoot is the peak excursion past the Setpoint, usually expressed as a percentage of the step size, and it trades off against speed: aggressive Gain gives fast response but more overshoot. It is governed by the system's Damping, with too little damping causing oscillatory ringing and longer Settling time. In robotics, overshoot in a joint can cause collisions or scrap parts, so Gain tuning aims to minimize it while keeping Bandwidth adequate.

plain: Robots stacking boxes or products neatly onto a shipping pallet, the way a worker would load a delivery skid.
snappy: Automated stacking of cases, bags, or cartons onto pallets in a programmed pattern for shipping.
detail: A palletizing robot, often a high-payload Six-axis robot or a dedicated gantry, builds stable multi-layer stacks following a defined pattern, then a new empty pallet rotates in. Throughput depends on Cycle time and End-of-arm tooling such as a vacuum Suction gripper or fork-style tool, and the cell frequently uses Conveyor tracking to grab cases off a moving line. Palletizing is common in both Manufacturing shipping bays and Logistics & Warehouse operations, and is a flagship application for Material handling automation alongside Pick and place.

plain: Labeling every pixel in an image while also telling apart each distinct object, covering both countable things and background stuff at once.
snappy: A unified per-pixel labeling that combines semantic background classes with distinct object instances.
detail: Panoptic segmentation merges Semantic segmentation (for uncountable 'stuff' like road and sky) with Instance segmentation (for countable 'things' like cars and people) into one coherent per-pixel map. This single complete scene parse is attractive for an Autonomous vehicle because nothing in the image is left unlabeled, supporting Scene understanding and Free space detection together. It builds directly on Object detection and dense pixel prediction.

plain: A robot whose moving platform is held and driven by several arms working together.
snappy: A robot whose end-effector is connected to its base by multiple independent kinematic limbs.
detail: A Parallel manipulator forms a Closed kinematic chain in which several legs share the load on a single moving platform, giving high stiffness, speed, and Payload capacity at the cost of a smaller Workspace. The Stewart platform and the Delta robot are the best-known examples, used in motion simulators and high-speed Pick and place. Its Forward kinematics is usually harder to solve than its Inverse kinematics, the reverse of a Serial manipulator.

plain: Running thousands of copies of a simulated robot at the same time on one graphics chip to gather experience fast.
snappy: Simulating many robot instances simultaneously, typically vectorized on a GPU, to accelerate data collection and training.
detail: Parallel (or vectorized) simulation steps thousands of independent environments in lockstep on a GPU, turning weeks of Reinforcement learning into hours by feeding a learner massive batches of experience. It is usually run in Headless simulation mode and exposed through a vectorized Gym environment. Massively parallel simulation in NVIDIA Isaac and Isaac Lab is the workhorse behind modern Learned locomotion on quadrupeds and humanoids, followed by Sim-to-real transfer.

plain: A simple robot hand with two flat fingers that squeeze together to pinch an object.
snappy: A gripper with two flat fingers that close toward each other along a single linear axis.
detail: The Parallel-jaw gripper is the workhorse of industrial Manipulation: two parallel fingers driven open and closed along one axis, typically by a Pneumatic actuator or electric motor. Because it makes two opposing Contact points, it naturally produces an Antipodal grasp and can achieve Force closure on box-like parts. It is the default end effector for Pick and place and Bin picking, and most Grasp planning systems output a Grasp pose tailored to its two-finger geometry.

plain: The US rulebook that says what commercial drone pilots are allowed to do and how to get certified.
snappy: The US FAA regulation governing routine commercial small uncrewed aircraft operations.
detail: FAA Part 107 sets the framework for commercial drones under 55 pounds, covering pilot certification, daylight Visual line of sight operation, altitude limits, and airspace authorization, with waivers available for night, over-people, or Beyond visual line of sight flight. Compliance increasingly assumes Remote ID equipage and may interact with Unmanned traffic management. It is the certification most commercial Drone delivery and inspection operators build their procedures around.

plain: Estimating where a robot is by scattering many guesses, then keeping the ones that best match what the sensors see.
snappy: A nonparametric estimator representing the state distribution as many weighted sampled hypotheses.
detail: A particle filter approximates the belief over a robot's state with a swarm of weighted samples, reweighting and resampling them as measurements arrive, which lets it represent multimodal and non-Gaussian Uncertainty. Its best-known robotics form is Monte Carlo localization (MCL), implemented as AMCL in the ROS navigation stack to localize against an Occupancy grid. It handles the kidnapped-robot and global Localization problems better than a Kalman filter but costs more compute.

plain: A walking machine that strolls down a gentle slope using only gravity, with no motors at all.
snappy: Walking driven purely by gravity and the natural swinging dynamics of the legs, requiring no actuators.
detail: Passive dynamic walking, pioneered by Tad McGeer, shows that a well-tuned mechanism can walk down a shallow incline with a remarkably low Cost of transport and a strikingly human-like Gait, purely from pendulum-like leg motion. It is the conceptual seed of Dynamic walking and of Morphological computation, where mechanical design does work that would otherwise need control. Adding minimal actuation turns a passive walker into an efficient powered Bipedal robot.

plain: Finding a route from a start point to a goal, treating the robot as a shape that must not hit anything, without yet worrying about speed or timing.
snappy: Computing a geometric, collision-free route from start to goal while ignoring velocity and dynamics.
detail: Path planning answers where the robot should go, leaving when and how fast to a later stage; the resulting geometric path is fed to Time parameterization or Trajectory optimization to become an executable trajectory. Graph-based methods like A* search and Dijkstra's algorithm operate on an Occupancy grid or Cost map, while Sampling-based planning handles high-dimensional arm problems. In a mobile robot, a Global planner does map-wide path planning and a Local planner reconciles that path with live Obstacle avoidance.

plain: Taking the zig-zag route a planner spits out and rounding off the corners so the robot can actually drive it smoothly.
snappy: Refining a coarse, jagged planned path into a continuous, curvature-bounded curve that a real robot can drive comfortably.
detail: Grid- and graph-based planners like A* search produce paths with sharp 45 or 90 degree turns that violate a vehicle's dynamics; path smoothing post-processes them into gentle curves using gradient descent, splines, or conjugate-gradient optimizers (as in CHOMP and STOMP). It respects the Nonholonomic constraint of the platform and keeps clear of the Inflation layer cost gradient. The smoothed geometry is then handed to Time parameterization and a Local planner so the Trajectory tracking controller sees feasible commands.

plain: The useful cargo or equipment a robot or drone carries to do its job, separate from the machine itself.
snappy: The maximum useful load a robot can carry or manipulate, excluding the vehicle's own structure and power.
detail: On a Multirotor or Hybrid VTOL the payload might be a Gimbal-stabilized camera, a delivery box, or a sensor pod, and it trades directly against flight Endurance because lifting more mass burns more battery. Payload limits are set by the airframe's Thrust-to-weight ratio and motor sizing, so a Hexacopter or Octocopter is chosen when heavier payloads or redundancy are needed. The related metric Payload capacity quantifies this for industrial arms and Automated guided vehicles as well as aircraft.

plain: The heaviest load a robot is rated to carry or handle.
snappy: The maximum load mass a robot can carry or manipulate within its rated specifications.
detail: Payload capacity is a headline spec for any manipulator or mobile platform, set by Actuator torque, Gearbox limits, Bearing ratings, and structural stiffness, and it must include the mass of the End-effector and any End-of-arm tooling. Quoting it correctly matters because exceeding it degrades Accuracy and Repeatability and can trip a Protective stop. A Parallel manipulator typically offers higher payload capacity than a comparable Serial manipulator, and it directly bounds the Payload-to-weight ratio.

plain: How much a robot can carry compared with how much the robot itself weighs.
snappy: The ratio of a robot's rated payload to its own mass, a key efficiency metric.
detail: Payload-to-weight ratio captures structural and actuation efficiency: a high ratio means a robot lifts a lot for its own mass, which is critical for a Humanoid robot that must also carry its own limbs and a Lithium-ion battery. It is improved by light Carbon fiber composite structures, a Monocoque shell, high Torque density actuators, and a Quasi-direct drive. Humans sit near 1:1, a target frontier humanoids aim to match while bounded by Payload capacity.

plain: A standard way of writing down, in a fixed format, what actions a robot can take and what goal it should reach, so an automatic planner can solve it.
snappy: The standard formal language for describing symbolic task-planning domains and problems in terms of predicates, actions, preconditions, and effects.
detail: PDDL cleanly separates a domain file (the available Action operators with their preconditions and effects) from a problem file (the initial state and goal), letting general-purpose solvers tackle any encoded Task planning problem. In robotics it specifies the discrete layer of a Task and motion planning system, where each symbolic action must be grounded into feasible Motion planning. It is the lingua franca of the planning research community and increasingly the structured output target for a Foundation model or large language model driving an Embodied agent.

plain: The strongest burst of turning force a motor can produce for a short moment before it overheats.
snappy: The maximum short-duration torque an actuator can deliver before thermal or current limits force a derate.
detail: Peak torque is the brief overload an Actuator musters for transients like a Humanoid robot catching a stumble or a robot arm accelerating a heavy Payload, typically a few times its continuous rating. It is bounded by drive current from the Motor controller and by winding heat, so it cannot be sustained the way Holding torque can. Engineers weigh peak torque against Torque density and Peak torque rating curves when selecting a Permanent magnet synchronous motor for dynamic Trajectory tracking.

plain: A car's ability to spot people on or near the road so it can avoid hitting them.
snappy: The perception task of identifying and localizing people in a vehicle's environment to enable safe planning and collision avoidance.
detail: Pedestrian detection typically runs object detection and 3D object detection over camera and LiDAR data, often producing a bounding box and track via multi-object tracking so motion planning can react. It is a core competency for protecting any vulnerable road user and feeds automatic emergency braking and behavior prediction. Datasets like nuScenes and the Waymo Open Dataset are used to train and benchmark it, with heavy attention to occlusion, night scenes, and avoiding phantom braking from false positives.

plain: The textbook test of fitting a peg snugly into a hole that is barely bigger than it is.
snappy: Benchmark assembly task of inserting a peg into a tight-clearance hole.
detail: Peg-in-hole is the canonical Contact-rich manipulation benchmark: clearances are small, so even tiny misalignment jams the part and generates large contact forces. Robots solve it with Hybrid position/force control or Impedance control, sometimes with a passive Remote center of compliance device to absorb lateral error, and increasingly with learned policies trained in Sim-to-real loops. It stands in for real Assembly steps such as seating bearings, connectors, and shafts on a Production line.

plain: How a robot turns raw sensor signals into a useful picture of the world around it.
snappy: The process of interpreting sensor data into a structured, usable understanding of the robot's surroundings.
detail: Perception sits between raw Sensor streams and decision-making, transforming images, LiDAR, and Radar into objects, free space, and maps the robot can act on. It spans Computer vision, Sensor fusion, Object detection, and Semantic segmentation, and feeds the planning stages of the Sense-plan-act and Perception-action loop pipelines. In a self-driving stack, perception produces the scene model that Behavior planning and Motion planning consume.

plain: The constant back-and-forth in which a robot senses what is happening and immediately uses that to decide its next move.
snappy: The continuous cycle linking a robot's Sensing to its action, repeated fast enough to operate in a changing world.
detail: The perception-action loop is the core organizing principle of an embodied Robot: Sensing feeds Perception, which informs a decision, which drives Actuation, which changes the world and the next sensor reading. It is the conceptual root of Closed-loop control and of architectures like Sense-plan-act, Reactive control, and Subsumption architecture. Running it fast and predictably is a Real-time problem, and tightening it with Feedback is what lets a robot correct errors instead of executing blindly.

plain: A letter grade, from a up to e, showing how reliably a machine's safety control will do its job.
snappy: An ISO 13849 rating (PL a-e) of the reliability of a machine's safety-related control function, based on architecture, failure rates, and diagnostics.
detail: Performance Level (PL) is the output of an ISO 13849 evaluation, with PLd and PLe being the levels most required for robot safety functions such as Speed and separation monitoring or a Safety-rated monitored stop. It is determined from the safety circuit's category, mean time to dangerous failure, and diagnostic coverage, and is typically realized on a Safety PLC. PL is the machinery-sector counterpart to the Safety Integrity Level scale of IEC 61508.

plain: A highly efficient motor that uses magnets on its spinning part to produce strong, smooth motion.
snappy: A synchronous AC motor with rotor-mounted permanent magnets, prized for high efficiency and torque density.
detail: A Permanent magnet synchronous motor (PMSM) embeds magnets in the rotor so it locks to the rotating magnetic field set up by the stator windings, giving excellent efficiency and Torque density. It is mechanically nearly identical to the Brushless DC motor and is almost always run with Field-oriented control to deliver smooth, ripple-free torque. PMSMs power high-performance robot joints, a Frameless motor integrated into a Humanoid robot, and electric-vehicle traction drives.

plain: When a car brakes hard for no real reason because its sensors thought they saw an obstacle that wasn't there.
snappy: Unwarranted automatic braking triggered by a false-positive detection or misclassification.
detail: Phantom braking is a notorious failure mode in adaptive cruise control and automatic emergency braking, where a shadow, overpass, or stationary object is misread as a hazard. It stems from perception errors in object detection or sensor fusion, and is dangerous because it invites rear-end collisions and erodes trust. Reducing it is a key motivation for camera-lidar fusion, better 3D object detection, and careful tuning against the long tail of confusing scenes.

plain: A sensor that shines a beam of light and detects when something blocks or reflects it, used to spot objects passing by.
snappy: A sensor that detects object presence, absence, or distance by emitting and sensing a light beam.
detail: A photoelectric sensor (photo eye) emits light, often infrared, and registers a part when the beam is broken (through-beam), reflected back (retroreflective), or bounced off the object itself (diffuse). On a Production line it counts parts, confirms presence before a robot picks, and triggers Conveyor tracking or indexing, complementing a Proximity sensor for metal detection. Its on/off output wires into a Programmable logic controller, and a safety-rated array of beams forms the Light curtain that guards a Robot cell.

plain: Drawing computer images so lifelike they look like real photographs.
snappy: High-fidelity image synthesis, often ray-traced, that produces camera frames indistinguishable from real photos in simulation.
detail: Photorealistic rendering models light transport, often via ray tracing, so a virtual Camera in simulation sees shadows, reflections, and materials that match reality. It is the visual half of Sensor simulation and is what makes simulator-generated Synthetic data usable for training perception. Engines such as NVIDIA Isaac and Isaac Sim use it to narrow the Reality gap, and modern techniques like Gaussian splatting and NeRF push it toward capturing real scenes for Sim-to-real transfer.

plain: A research company teaching robots general skills with a single large AI model, much like a chatbot but for physical actions.
snappy: Embodied-AI lab building general robot foundation models such as pi0 for cross-platform manipulation.
detail: Physical Intelligence (Pi) develops a Robot foundation model line, most notably pi0, a Vision-language-action model that maps camera images and language instructions to robot actions across many embodiments. Its approach centers on Cross-embodiment learning and large-scale Imitation learning so one Generalist policy can control different arms and grippers. pi0 uses a Diffusion policy-style action head to generate smooth Manipulation trajectories, building on datasets like Open X-Embodiment.

plain: The math core of a simulator that calculates how objects move, collide, and push on each other.
snappy: Software that computes rigid-body dynamics, collisions, contacts, and friction to advance a simulated world.
detail: A physics engine integrates the equations of motion each timestep, resolving Contact dynamics, Rigid body dynamics, and collisions so a simulated robot behaves plausibly. Different engines trade speed for fidelity, which is why simulators expose them as choices: MuJoCo, Bullet (in PyBullet), and the engines inside Gazebo and Isaac Sim. Its accuracy directly governs the Reality gap a Policy faces during Sim-to-real transfer.

plain: A robot grabbing an object from one spot and putting it down somewhere else.
snappy: Picking an object up from one location and setting it down at another, the most common manipulation task.
detail: Pick and place is the bread-and-butter Manipulation task: a Manipulator grasps an object at a source Pose and releases it at a target, repeated at high speed on a Production line or in a warehouse. It chains Grasp planning, Motion planning, and a Gripper such as a Parallel-jaw gripper or Suction gripper, often with Conveyor tracking to grab moving parts. It is the basis of Palletizing, Machine tending, and warehouse Bin picking, and a benchmark task for Learned grasping policies.

plain: How many items a picking robot can grab and move in an hour, used to judge how fast and useful it is.
snappy: A throughput metric measuring items a picking robot retrieves per hour, often quoted as picks per hour.
detail: Pick rate (picks per hour, or PPH) is the headline number for warehouse automation: a Bin picking or Pick and place robot is judged against a human picker's rate and against its own Return on investment target. It depends on Grasp planning speed, gripper reliability, and how quickly a Goods-to-person system presents inventory. Pick rate is one component of overall Throughput, and a high but unreliable rate is worthless if it tanks Uptime or damages goods.

plain: The most common automatic controller, which corrects errors based on how big they are now, how long they have lasted, and how fast they are changing.
snappy: A feedback controller that sums proportional, integral, and derivative terms of the error to drive a system to its setpoint.
detail: A PID controller combines three responses to the Error signal: proportional (react to present error), integral (eliminate Steady-state error), and derivative (anticipate by reacting to error rate, adding Damping). Each term has a Gain set during Gain tuning, often with the Ziegler-Nichols method. PID drives countless robot joints, motor Servo control loops, and Manufacturing process loops; practical implementations add Anti-windup to handle actuator Saturation.

plain: A part that bends or pushes by a tiny, extremely precise amount when you apply voltage to a special crystal inside it.
snappy: An actuator that converts voltage-induced strain in a piezoelectric crystal into sub-micron, high-bandwidth motion.
detail: A piezoelectric actuator (piezo motor) expands a stack of ceramic crystals under voltage to produce nanometer-scale displacement at high Bandwidth, with enormous force over a tiny stroke. It drives focus stages, fine positioners, and a Surgical robot end stage where an Electric motor is too coarse, and stick-slip piezo motors achieve long travel by repeated micro-steps. Its precision rivals a Voice coil actuator for fine motion, and it complements the Shape memory alloy actuator and Dielectric elastomer actuator among nonconventional actuators feeding a high-resolution Encoder loop.

plain: A small, limited trial of a robot system to see if it works before committing to use it everywhere.
snappy: A limited-scope trial of a robot system used to validate value before full deployment.
detail: A pilot runs a robot system in a constrained real setting to test value, reliability, and integration before a wider rollout.
