detail: State estimation combines a motion model with sensor data to recover quantities the robot cannot measure directly, such as its Pose, velocity, or orientation. Classic tools include the Kalman filter and Particle filter, and the estimate usually carries an explicit Uncertainty. It underpins Localization, Odometry, and the feedback loops that make Closed-loop control possible.

plain: A way of steering a machine where the controller looks at the machine's complete internal condition and uses all of it to decide what to do next.
snappy: A control law that computes commands as a function of the full system state rather than just the measured output.
detail: State feedback multiplies the system's state vector by a gain matrix to produce a control command, the foundation of State-space control. Because the true state is often not directly measured, it is usually paired with State estimation from a Kalman filter, and the gains are chosen by Pole placement or by solving a Linear quadratic regulator. It underlies controllers from balancing a Bipedal robot to regulating a Servomotor.

plain: A grid of pre-built movement snippets that a car-like robot can search through, where every snippet is a motion the vehicle can really perform.
snappy: A search graph whose edges are precomputed, dynamically feasible motion primitives connecting discretized states.
detail: A State lattice discretizes the robot's state, including heading and sometimes velocity, and connects states only with a precomputed library of feasible Motion primitive segments, so any path found by Graph search is guaranteed drivable. This is a popular Global planner for Autonomous vehicle and rover navigation because it captures the Nonholonomic constraint of the platform up front, much like Hybrid A* but with an explicitly enumerated edge set. The lattice planner pairs with A* search or Dijkstra's algorithm over the lattice and was central to several DARPA Challenge vehicles.

plain: How much energy is left in a robot's battery, shown as a percentage like a phone's battery icon.
snappy: The remaining charge in a battery pack relative to its full capacity, expressed as a percentage.
detail: State of charge (SOC) is the battery's fuel gauge, estimated by the Battery management system from voltage, current integration, and cell models since it cannot be measured directly. A robot uses SOC against its Power budget to decide when to trigger Autonomous docking or a Hot-swappable battery swap before Endurance runs out. Accurate SOC is harder near the flat discharge curve of a Lithium iron phosphate battery, so the BMS fuses multiple signals.

plain: Describing a system by tracking a set of internal numbers that capture its condition, and the rules for how they change over time.
snappy: Modeling and controlling a system through its internal state variables and their first-order evolution equations.
detail: State-space control represents a system as a vector of state variables, like positions and velocities, evolving by first-order differential equations, enabling multi-input multi-output design beyond single-loop methods. It is the foundation for State feedback, Pole placement, Optimal control like the Linear quadratic regulator, and estimators such as the Kalman filter that recover unmeasured states. Robotics uses it for State estimation and to control coupled multi-joint Dynamics that classical Control theory handles awkwardly.

plain: Being balanced even when standing completely still, like a table that will not tip over.
snappy: Balance that holds without any motion, achieved by keeping the projected center of mass inside the support polygon at all times.
detail: A statically stable robot will not topple if you stop it at any instant, because its Center of mass always projects inside the Support polygon formed by its ground contacts. This is the principle behind a Crawl gait, where a Quadruped robot keeps at least three feet down so the body stays supported. Static stability is simpler and safer than Dynamic stability but inherently slower, since the robot must always preserve a valid base of support.

plain: Using statistics and charts to watch a manufacturing process so you can spot it drifting toward defects before bad parts are made.
snappy: Monitoring process measurements with control charts to detect and correct variation before defects occur, abbreviated SPC.
detail: SPC plots measurements, dimensions, weights, temperatures, on control charts with statistically derived limits, distinguishing normal random variation from a genuine shift that signals the process is going out of control. Data often comes from automated Quality inspection and Machine vision gauging, and acting on SPC signals keeps the quality term of Overall equipment effectiveness high. It is a cornerstone of lean and Six Sigma practice and increasingly runs live on Industrial Internet of Things data inside a Smart factory.

plain: A leftover gap between where a system ends up and where it was supposed to be, even after it stops moving.
snappy: The residual offset between setpoint and actual value remaining after the response has fully settled.
detail: Steady-state error is the persistent component of the Error signal once all transients decay, caused by friction, gravity, or constant disturbances that a proportional Gain alone cannot fully cancel. The integral term of a PID controller exists precisely to drive it to zero by accumulating error over time, though that integral can suffer windup during Saturation, requiring Anti-windup. Feedforward control also reduces it by preempting known loads like gravity in a robot arm.

plain: A motor that moves in small, fixed steps, letting a machine position itself precisely without needing to check where it is.
snappy: A motor that rotates in discrete steps, enabling open-loop positioning without feedback.
detail: A stepper divides each rotation into many equal steps, so a Motor controller can command an exact angle simply by counting pulses, giving repeatable positioning in Open-loop control without an Encoder. This makes it popular in 3D printers, CNC machines, and Manufacturing automation where loads are predictable. Its weaknesses are limited high-speed torque and the risk of silently losing steps under overload, which a true Servomotor with feedback avoids.

plain: A pair of side-by-side cameras that judge how far away things are, the way two eyes give people depth perception.
snappy: A two-lens camera that infers depth by measuring left-right disparity between matched image points.
detail: A stereo camera uses two lenses a known distance apart and computes Depth estimation from the horizontal shift, or disparity, between matching features in the left and right images via Stereo matching. Unlike a Depth camera using Structured light, it is passive and works outdoors in sunlight, making it popular for Mobility and Visual SLAM. Its output is typically a Depth map or Point cloud used for Obstacle detection.

plain: Working out distance by comparing the slightly different views from two side-by-side cameras, the way two eyes judge depth.
snappy: Finding corresponding points across a calibrated camera pair to compute per-pixel disparity and hence depth.
detail: Stereo matching searches for the same scene point in the left and right images of a Stereo camera; the horizontal shift between them, called disparity, is inversely proportional to distance and yields a Depth map. It depends on accurate Camera calibration and on Image rectification so corresponding points lie on the same image row. It is a standard source of Depth estimation for Mobility robots and a building block of 3D reconstruction.

plain: A moving platform supported by six adjustable legs that can tilt and shift it in any direction.
snappy: A six-actuator parallel mechanism providing full six-degree-of-freedom platform motion.
detail: The Stewart platform connects a base and a top plate with six length-adjustable legs, each ending in a Spherical joint, making it a stiff Closed kinematic chain with six Degrees of freedom. It is the archetypal Parallel manipulator, used in flight and driving simulators, precision positioning, and machine tools. Its Inverse kinematics is simple (per-leg length) while its Forward kinematics requires numerical solving.

plain: How strongly a part resists bending or stretching when force is applied; a stiff thing barely moves, a flexible thing gives easily.
snappy: The ratio of applied load to resulting elastic deflection in a structure, member, or joint.
detail: Stiffness is the inverse of Mechanical compliance: high stiffness means a Link, Joint, or Robot wrist deflects little under load, preserving Accuracy and Repeatability at the End-effector. A robot built from Carbon fiber composite achieves high stiffness at low mass, raising structural Bandwidth and the natural frequency of the arm. Controllers can also command apparent stiffness electronically through Impedance control, and a Variable stiffness actuator lets a robot switch between rigid and springy behavior for safe Human-robot interaction.

full: Stochastic Trajectory Optimization for Motion Planning
plain: A planning method that improves a robot's path by trying many small random tweaks and blending the ones that work out best, no calculus required.
snappy: A sampling-based stochastic optimizer that improves a trajectory by averaging noisy rollouts weighted by cost.
detail: STOMP perturbs the current trajectory with many noisy variations, evaluates each against a cost combining smoothness and obstacle clearance, and updates toward the lower-cost samples, so it needs no gradient and can handle non-differentiable costs. This gradient-free trait lets it escape local minima that can trap the gradient-based CHOMP, making the two complementary Trajectory optimization planners in MoveIt for robot arms. Like CHOMP it typically refines an initial guess from a Sampling-based planning method and respects joint limits before Time parameterization.

plain: A thin element that changes its electrical resistance when it is stretched or squeezed, letting a robot measure force.
snappy: A sensing element whose electrical resistance changes with mechanical deformation, used to measure force or strain.
detail: A strain gauge bonds to a structure and changes resistance as the material stretches under load; arranging several into a bridge circuit yields a sensitive force signal. It is the underlying transduction element inside a Load cell and most of a Force/torque sensor. Robots use strain gauges for Force control, Compliance sensing, and Condition monitoring, often paired with Calibration to convert resistance to engineering units.

plain: Building a 3D model of a place by combining many photos taken from different positions as the camera moves around.
snappy: Jointly recovering 3D scene geometry and camera poses from a set of 2D images taken from different viewpoints.
detail: Structure from motion, or SfM, takes overlapping images and simultaneously solves for where each photo was taken and where the 3D points lie, usually refined by Bundle adjustment. It relies on Feature extraction and Feature matching to find common points across views and on RANSAC to reject bad matches. It underpins 3D reconstruction and Aerial photogrammetry, and is the offline, multi-image cousin of online Visual odometry used in Space and Mobility surveying.

plain: A workspace engineered to be neat and predictable so a robot's job is much easier.
snappy: A controlled, well-known workspace where object positions, lighting, and layout are engineered to be predictable.
detail: In a structured environment such as a fixtured assembly station, parts arrive in known poses on a Conveyor tracking line, so a robot can rely on Open-loop control or simple Programming by teaching rather than rich Perception. This predictability underpins classic Industrial robotics and high Repeatability. Removing that structure forces the move toward Computer vision, Bin picking, and adaptive policies needed in an Unstructured environment.

plain: A way to measure 3D shape by shining a known pattern of light onto an object and watching how the pattern bends over its surface.
snappy: A depth-sensing method that projects a known light pattern and computes distance from its observed distortion.
detail: Structured light projects a precise pattern, such as stripes or a dot grid, and a Camera observes how the pattern deforms across surfaces to triangulate depth. It is one of the main technologies inside a Depth camera and supports detailed Pose estimation for Bin picking and Grasp planning. Because it relies on seeing its own projection, it works best indoors and is challenged outdoors where a Stereo camera or Time-of-flight sensor may be preferred.

plain: A text-based way of programming factory controllers that looks like a regular computer programming language with if-statements and loops.
snappy: A high-level, Pascal-like textual PLC programming language defined by IEC 61131-3.
detail: Structured text (the ST language) is one of the five languages in IEC 61131-3, favored for math, loops, and complex algorithms that would be cumbersome to draw as Ladder logic. It runs on a Programmable logic controller or a Programmable automation controller and is often mixed with a Function block diagram in the same project, with computation in ST and machine sequencing in ladder. Motion calculations, recipe handling, and data manipulation on an Industrial PC frequently use structured text for its readability and power.

plain: A way of layering a robot's behaviors so that more important ones can take over from less important ones.
snappy: A layered reactive control architecture in which higher-priority behavior layers can suppress or override the outputs of lower ones.
detail: Introduced by Rodney Brooks in 1986, the subsumption architecture stacks competence layers, with each layer a complete sensing-to-action loop; higher layers like wander or explore subsume lower ones like avoid-collision when they need control. Crucially there is no shared world model, making it the flagship of Behavior-based robotics and a pure form of Reactive control. Its limits in long-horizon tasks led designers toward the Hybrid architecture that bolts a planner on top of reactive layers.

plain: A robot tool that grabs things by sucking onto them like a sink plunger.
snappy: An end effector that holds objects by pulling a vacuum through one or more suction cups.
detail: A Suction gripper uses vacuum, generated by a pump or venturi, to hold objects against rubber suction cups, requiring only one flat, sealable surface rather than two opposing faces. This makes it the dominant choice for Bin picking and Goods-to-person logistics work, where a single cup can pick a box, bag, or book. Compared with a Parallel-jaw gripper it grasps faster and handles flat items, but struggles with porous or curved objects; Grasp planning for suction predicts where a cup can form a reliable seal.

plain: A device that stores a little energy but can charge and release it extremely fast.
snappy: A high-power-density energy store that charges and discharges rapidly to buffer peak loads on robots.
detail: A supercapacitor (ultracapacitor) bridges battery and capacitor, offering very high Power density and millions of cycles but modest Energy density, so it buffers bursts rather than providing long Endurance. On a robot it smooths the current spikes a Lithium-ion battery dislikes, for instance absorbing regenerative braking energy or handling a peak motor load to ease the Power budget. It is often paired with a battery and managed alongside the Battery management system; pure-supercap robots are rare due to limited storage.

plain: A setup where the robot does the work on its own while a person watches and can take over if needed.
snappy: An operating mode where a robot acts autonomously while a human monitors and retains authority to intervene.
detail: Under supervised autonomy the machine executes tasks by itself, but a human supervisor stays in the loop to monitor, approve, or override, the Human-in-the-loop model used for an Autonomous weapon, a Self-driving truck with a Safety driver, or an inspection Drone. It is a midpoint on the Levels of autonomy between full Teleoperation and full Autonomy, and differs from Shared autonomy, where human and robot act simultaneously rather than the human supervising. Intervention is triggered by a Takeover request, a Disengagement, or a detected anomaly.

plain: The area on the ground enclosed by everything a robot is standing on, like the patch between its two feet.
snappy: The convex hull of a robot's ground contact points, defining the region for static balance.
detail: The support polygon (or base of support) is the convex region spanned by all current Contact point locations, such as the outlines of both feet plus the gap between them. For Static stability the Center of mass projection must stay inside it; for Dynamic walking the Zero moment point and Center of pressure must stay inside it instead. It shrinks to a line or point during single-support stance, which is why a Humanoid robot relies on the Capture point to plan recovery steps that re-establish a valid polygon.

plain: A robot a surgeon controls to perform operations through very small incisions with great precision.
snappy: A teleoperated or assistive robotic system that lets a surgeon perform minimally invasive procedures with enhanced precision, dexterity, and tremor filtering.
detail: A surgical robot maps a surgeon's hand motions, captured at a console, onto small instruments inside the patient through teleoperation, scaling motion and removing tremor for fine dexterous manipulation. Systems such as those from Intuitive Surgical use a continuum robot or cable-driven mechanism wrist for tight workspaces and rely on haptics and force/torque sensor feedback. Newer work explores shared autonomy and visual servoing for sub-tasks, but the human surgeon stays in the loop under strict functional safety requirements.

plain: One of many simple robots that work together as a group, like a colony of ants, with no single robot in charge.
snappy: An agent in a multi-robot system where many simple, locally-interacting units produce coordinated collective behavior without central control.
detail: Swarm robots follow simple local rules so that useful group patterns appear as emergent behavior rather than from a master controller, a core idea in swarm robotics and bio-inspired robotics. Each unit senses only its neighbors, making the system robust to losing members, which suits a Drone swarm for area coverage or distributed search. The field overlaps with multi-agent path finding and multi-robot system coordination, and is studied for Defense & Security and exploration tasks where many cheap units beat one expensive Field robot.

plain: Using lots of cheap, simple robots that together behave like one smart group, without a boss telling each one what to do.
snappy: A field that builds collective capability from many simple robots following local rules, with no central controller.
detail: Swarm robotics takes inspiration from ants and bees: each robot senses only its neighbors and follows simple local rules, yet the group produces useful Emergent behavior such as coverage, foraging, or formation keeping. Because there is no single point of failure, a swarm degrades gracefully and scales well, which is why a Drone swarm is attractive for Defense & Security mapping. It is a decentralized special case of a Multi-robot system, and it leans heavily on Bio-inspired robotics for its coordination strategies.

plain: How an underwater robot moves through water, whether by spinning propellers, flapping fins, or wriggling its body like a fish.
snappy: Propelling a robot through water using fins, body undulation, propellers, or thrusters to generate thrust against the surrounding fluid.
detail: Swimming robots either use a Propeller and thrusters for efficient cruising or mimic fish with undulating bodies and fins for quiet, agile maneuvering in tight or sensitive habitats, a recurring Research/Frontier and Bio-inspired robotics theme. The platform is typically an Autonomous underwater vehicle or a Remotely operated vehicle, and control must contend with buoyancy, currents, and drag rather than ground contact, putting weight on Attitude and heading reference system data and Sensor fusion. Like Snake locomotion, fin-based swimming relies on propagating body waves, and station-keeping demands fine Thrust-to-weight ratio and Control allocation.

plain: The part of a step when a foot is lifted off the ground and moving forward to its next position.
snappy: The portion of the gait cycle during which a foot is off the ground and swinging forward to its next placement.
detail: In swing phase the leg carries no load and is free to reposition, so this is when Foothold selection chooses where the foot will next land. The shorter the swing relative to the Stance phase, the higher the Duty factor and the more statically stable the Gait. Coordinating swing and stance across legs through the Gait cycle is what produces a Trot, Crawl gait, or Gallop.

plain: A company that builds high-speed robot systems to store and retrieve boxes of goods inside large warehouses.
snappy: Warehouse-automation firm whose autonomous case-handling robots travel a dense storage structure at high speed to build mixed pallets.
detail: Symbotic replaces conventional racking with a dense grid through which fast Autonomous mobile robot units retrieve and sequence individual cases, functioning as a software-driven Automated storage and retrieval system. The robots coordinate via Fleet management and Multi-agent path finding to feed automated Palletizing, raising warehouse Throughput and density. Major retailers such as Walmart deploy its systems to reconfigure distribution-centre Material handling.

plain: Fake-but-labeled training examples created by a computer instead of collected in the real world.
snappy: Simulator-generated, automatically labeled data used to train robot perception models and policies at scale.
detail: Because a Robot simulator already knows the exact position and identity of every object, it can emit perfectly labeled images, depth maps, and Point cloud data for free, sidestepping costly manual annotation and giving cheap Ground truth. Synthetic data is generated with Photorealistic rendering and Sensor simulation, then combined with Domain randomization to survive the Reality gap during Sim-to-real transfer. Pipelines built on NVIDIA Isaac and Isaac Sim produce millions of frames to pretrain Object detection and grasping networks.

plain: Measuring how a real robot actually behaves, like its true weight, friction, and motor strength, so the simulator can be made to match it.
snappy: Estimating a system's true dynamics parameters from data so models and simulators match real-world behavior.
detail: System identification fits parameters of a robot's Dynamics, such as link masses in the Inertia tensor, joint friction, motor constants, and Backlash, by exciting the hardware and observing its response. Accurate sys-ID shrinks the Reality gap so that a Policy trained in a Physics engine transfers cleanly, complementing Domain randomization rather than replacing it. It feeds Model predictive control and Computed torque control, and is a prerequisite for trustworthy Sim-to-real transfer of Learned locomotion.

plain: A specialist company that takes robots and other parts and assembles them into a complete working setup tailored to a customer's factory or warehouse.
snappy: A firm that designs, builds, installs, and commissions complete robotic cells and lines for end customers.
detail: A system integrator (often just 'integrator') is the bridge between a robot vendor and the factory floor: it selects the arm, designs the End-of-arm tooling, programs the Robot controller, and ensures the installation meets safety standards like ISO 10218 before handover. Integrators build the Robot cell around a process, wiring it to the plant's Programmable logic controller and Manufacturing execution system. They are a large share of any Total cost of ownership, and the same role for mobile fleets is sometimes called a Robot integrator.

plain: A single chip that packs a robot's whole computer onto one piece of silicon.
snappy: An integrated chip combining CPU, GPU, memory controllers, and accelerators on one die for compact robot compute.
detail: A System on a chip (SoC) lets a robot's Onboard compute fit in a small, low-power package by merging a CPU with a Graphics processing unit and often an AI accelerator or DSP. The NVIDIA Jetson modules are SoC-based and serve as the compute core for many a Humanoid robot, drone Flight controller, and Autonomous mobile robot. Choosing an SoC trades raw performance against the robot's Power budget and Thermal management constraints.

plain: A robot's ability to feel physical contact, pressure, and surface texture through touch, much like a human fingertip.
snappy: Sensing contact, pressure, slip, and texture at a robot's surfaces through touch.
detail: Tactile sensing gives a robot local contact information that Vision cannot see, such as how hard it is gripping or whether an object is slipping. A Robotic hand uses a Tactile sensor array on its fingertips to enable Grip force control and Slip detection during Dexterous manipulation. Newer approaches use a Vision-based tactile sensor that watches a soft pad deform, feeding Contact-rich manipulation and Tactile servoing controllers.

plain: A sensor that lets a robot feel touch, pressure, or texture where it contacts an object.
snappy: A sensor that detects contact, pressure distribution, or texture on a robot's surface.
detail: A tactile sensor gives a robot a sense of touch at the contact interface, reporting where, how hard, and sometimes how an object presses. It is central to Dexterous manipulation and In-hand manipulation, supporting Slip detection, Grip force control, and Tactile servoing. Implementations range from a Capacitive sensor array to a Vision-based tactile sensor, and large coverings form a Robotic skin on a Humanoid robot.

plain: Letting a robot adjust its grip moment-by-moment based on what its fingertip sensors feel touching the object.
snappy: Closing the control loop on tactile (often vision-based) sensor feedback for in-hand control.
detail: Tactile servoing makes the touch signal the feedback in a Control loop, the touch analogue of Visual servoing, so a robot continuously regulates contact location, force, or slip to keep an object correctly seated in the hand. It typically reads a Vision-based tactile sensor or other Tactile sensor and is the workhorse for In-hand manipulation, Slip detection, and Dexterous manipulation. By complementing Grip force control and Compliant manipulation, it lets a Robotic hand handle delicate or unmodeled objects that pure vision and Pose estimation cannot fully resolve.

plain: A clear prompt telling the human driver to put their hands back on the wheel and take over driving from the automated system.
snappy: A multimodal prompt issued by a conditional-automation system asking the human to resume manual control within a time budget.
detail: A takeover request (TOR) is central to SAE Level 3 driving: when a highway pilot reaches the edge of its operational design domain, it alerts the driver via audio, visual, and haptic cues to resume control. The driver monitoring system verifies the driver is ready, and if no handover occurs within the time budget the vehicle executes a fallback to a minimal risk condition. TOR timing and clarity are key safety case arguments for any Level 3 system.

plain: The rhythm a production line must hit to exactly meet customer demand, like a metronome pace for making things.
snappy: The available production time divided by customer demand, setting the required pace per unit.
detail: Takt time is computed as available working time divided by units demanded, so if customers need 480 units in an 8-hour shift, each unit must finish every minute. It sets the target rhythm that each station on a Production line and every Robot cell must meet, and the actual Cycle time of each operation must stay below takt to keep up. Balancing stations to takt is central to lean manufacturing and to hitting the performance term in Overall equipment effectiveness.

plain: A specific job you want a robot to do, like move a box from here to there.
snappy: A defined objective or job a robot is meant to accomplish, often decomposed into sub-goals and primitive actions.
detail: A task is the unit of work a robot is assigned, from a single Pick and place to a multi-step assembly; it is what Task planning sequences and what a Skill or Motion primitive executes. Tasks set the success criteria against which a Benchmark or Reward is judged. In Task and motion planning a symbolic task plan (what to do and in what order) is interleaved with geometric Motion planning (how to move there) so the abstract goal becomes a feasible Trajectory.

plain: Planning both the big sequence of steps a robot should do and the exact arm-and-body movements for each step, at the same time, so the plan actually works.
snappy: Jointly solving the discrete what-to-do (symbolic task) and the continuous how-to-move (collision-free geometry) so that each action is physically executable.
detail: Task and motion planning (TAMP) closes the gap between Task planning (often in PDDL) and Motion planning: a symbolic step like 'put cup in cupboard' is only valid if a collision-free Inverse kinematics and Grasp planning solution exists, so TAMP interleaves the two layers and backtracks when geometry fails. It is essential for Manipulation by a Humanoid robot or Manufacturing arm rearranging cluttered objects, where Collision checking constrains which symbolic plans are even reachable. TAMP solvers couple a Sampling-based planning motion layer with a symbolic search.

plain: Deciding the ordered list of big steps a robot should take, like 'open door, then pick up box, then carry it out', to reach its objective.
snappy: High-level sequencing of discrete, symbolic actions whose preconditions and effects chain together to achieve a stated goal.
detail: Task planning (symbolic planning) reasons over discrete states and Action operators with preconditions and effects, searching for a sequence that transforms the start state into the goal, often specified in PDDL. For a Humanoid robot or Manufacturing arm, a planner might output 'grasp tool, move to fixture, insert part' before any geometry is considered. Because a symbolic step like 'place the cup' may have no collision-free Motion planning solution, task planning is increasingly fused with low-level motion in Task and motion planning. Modern systems also pair it with a Behavior tree or Foundation model for execution.

plain: The everyday description of where a robot's hand is and how it is angled, rather than the settings of its individual joints.
snappy: The Cartesian space of end-effector position and orientation, as opposed to joint angles.
detail: Task space (or operational space) describes a goal in terms a person cares about, such as 'move the gripper to this Pose above the part,' rather than in terms of individual joint values. It is the natural setting for Operational space control and for Inverse kinematics, which converts a task-space target back into Joint space. The Jacobian matrix is the bridge that relates velocities in task space to velocities in joint space.

plain: A handheld controller with buttons and a screen used to move an industrial robot by hand and write its program.
snappy: A handheld terminal for jogging, teaching points, and editing programs on an industrial robot.
detail: An operator uses the Teach pendant to jog the arm to physical positions, record those waypoints, and step through a program before running it at speed, a workflow known as Programming by teaching. It connects to the Robot controller and includes a deadman switch plus an Emergency stop button required by ISO 10218. On a Six-axis robot doing Robotic welding or Machine tending, the technician teaches each path point on the pendant rather than coding coordinates by hand.

plain: A Taiwanese maker of robot arms that come with a built-in camera so they can see what they're doing.
snappy: Taiwanese cobot maker with integrated vision, owned by electronics giant Quanta.
detail: Techman Robot (the TM Robot) distinguishes its Collaborative robot arms with a built-in Smart camera, so Vision-guided robotics tasks like Pick and place and Quality inspection need no separate vision system. Owned by Quanta, it leverages electronics-manufacturing scale and integrates Machine vision directly into its programming flow. Like other cobots it supports Hand guiding and safe Human-robot interaction under ISO/TS 15066.

plain: Controlling a robot from a distance, with a person moving the controls while the machine does the physical work somewhere else.
snappy: Human-driven remote control of a robot, where an operator's inputs map to the robot's motion in real time.
detail: Teleoperation puts a human directly in command of a robot over a link, used heavily by the Surgical robot (the operator drives a manipulator from a console) and by a Remote operation center supervising a Robotaxi. It is also the workhorse for collecting Demonstration data: an operator teleoperates an arm and the recorded trajectories feed Imitation learning and Behavioral cloning. Latency and feedback quality are critical, which connects teleoperation closely to Haptics and Human-in-the-loop control.

plain: Technology that lets a person feel as if they are somewhere else by seeing, hearing, and acting through a remote machine.
snappy: Remote embodiment that gives an operator a sense of being present at the robot's location.
detail: Telepresence extends Teleoperation by adding rich sensory feedback, including video, audio, and Haptics, so the operator feels present rather than just issuing commands. A Telepresence robot lets someone attend a meeting or inspect a site remotely, and the same idea underlies remote surgery and a Remote operation center for vehicles. It sits within Telerobotics and complements Shared autonomy, where remote control blends with onboard Autonomy to cope with Latency.

plain: The field of operating a robot from a distance while getting feedback, such as video or touch sensations, that lets the operator feel almost present at the robot's location.
snappy: The study and practice of remotely controlling robots with sensory feedback to the operator, spanning teleoperation, telepresence, and time-delayed control.
detail: Telerobotics encompasses Teleoperation and Telepresence but emphasizes the feedback channel, including Haptics that render contact forces back to the operator's hand. NASA uses it to drive planetary rovers despite long Latency, and a Surgical robot like those from Intuitive Surgical lets a surgeon operate through a console. When delay grows large, telerobotics blends into Supervised autonomy and Shared autonomy, where the robot handles fine motion locally while the human sets intent.

plain: Moving a robot's fingers or limbs by pulling cables that act like the tendons in a human hand.
snappy: Actuation that transmits force through tendon-like cables, common in dexterous robotic hands.
detail: Tendon-driven actuation mimics biology by running cables from remote motors to joints, so a compact Robotic hand or Anthropomorphic hand can have many fingers without bulky motors in each digit. Routing the actuators away from the moving parts lowers inertia and improves Backdrivability, but cable stretch, friction, and routing complicate control. It is a scaled-up form of Cable drive and is central to a Tendon-driven hand and Underactuation strategies for grasping.

plain: A robot hand whose fingers are pulled by cables connected to motors tucked away in the forearm.
snappy: A robotic hand actuated by cables routed like tendons from finger joints to motors placed remotely.
detail: A Tendon-driven hand moves its fingers with cables that run over pulleys to motors located in the palm or forearm, keeping the fingers themselves light and slender, an example of Tendon-driven actuation. This Cable-driven mechanism lets engineers pack many Degrees of freedom into an Anthropomorphic hand, but introduces friction, Backlash, and stretch that complicate Grip force control. It is the standard construction for dexterous Robotic hand designs used in research on In-hand manipulation and the Underactuated gripper.

plain: A structure where stiff rods seem to float, held in place only by a web of tensioned cables so none of the rods actually touch each other.
snappy: A self-stabilizing structure of rigid compression struts held in equilibrium by a continuous network of tensioned cables.
detail: A tensegrity structure balances rigid struts in islands of compression suspended within a continuous net of cables in tension, giving a lightweight, deployable form that distributes loads and absorbs impact. A Tensegrity robot uses a Cable-driven mechanism to change cable lengths and roll or deform its whole frame, exhibiting strong Mechanical compliance and impact tolerance. NASA has studied tensegrity for Space landers that survive hard touchdowns and self-deploy, and the concept connects to Soft robotics and Bio-inspired structure research.

plain: A specialized chip that lets a robot run its AI brain quickly, doing the heavy number-crunching behind tasks like recognizing objects and deciding how to move.
snappy: A specialized accelerator built for the tensor and matrix math of neural-network inference, used as onboard compute to run a robot's perception and control models.
detail: A Tensor processing unit (TPU) is a class of AI accelerator optimized for the dense linear algebra of a Neural network, offering high throughput per watt that suits a robot's tight Power budget. On a humanoid robot it accelerates Computer vision and Vision-language-action model inference on Onboard compute, often integrated as a block within a System on a chip. Like other accelerators its capability is quoted in TOPS, and it competes with or complements the Graphics processing unit for Edge computing inference.

plain: A robot changing how it walks or drives to suit the ground it's on, picking careful footing on rocks or shifting its stance on a slope, instead of using one fixed motion.
snappy: Adjusting gait, foothold choice, stiffness, and posture in response to the ground underfoot so a robot can traverse uneven, soft, or unstructured surfaces.
detail: A Legged robot adapts by sensing the surface through Exteroception and Proprioception, then revising Foothold selection, Gait, and limb stiffness to stay stable on rubble, stairs, mud, or loose scree. Modern systems learn this behavior with Reinforcement learning and Sim-to-real transfer, training across many surfaces via Domain randomization so a Quadruped robot generalizes to ground it never saw. Crucial in Defense & Security and field deployments, terrain adaptation works alongside Balance control, Self-righting, and Tracked locomotion to keep a robot upright and moving on broken ground.

plain: Tesla's human-shaped robot designed to do everyday physical jobs in factories and eventually homes.
snappy: Tesla's general-purpose Humanoid robot intended for factory and consumer tasks, sharing its self-driving AI stack.
detail: Tesla Optimus (the Tesla Bot) is a Bipedal robot Tesla is developing to handle repetitive Manufacturing work, leveraging the company's Computer vision and Vision-only autonomy expertise from its cars. It depends on Imitation learning from human demonstrations plus Sim-to-real transfer to learn Manipulation skills like Pick and place. Tesla frames it as a Generalist robot whose perception and learning pipeline overlaps heavily with its Autonomous vehicle program.

plain: A drone connected to the ground by a cable that supplies it with power so it can hover in one spot for hours or days.
snappy: A drone held aloft and powered through a physical ground tether, trading mobility for near-unlimited hover time.
detail: A tethered drone runs a thin cable to a ground power supply, so Tethered power removes the battery Endurance limit and lets a Multirotor drone hover persistently as an elevated sensor or relay mast. The tether also carries a secure data link, which helps in GPS-denied or jamming environments where wireless control is risky. It is used for Defense & Security overwatch, border surveillance, and communications, filling the gap between a free-flying Drone and a fixed tower; station-keeping still relies on the Flight controller and Inertial measurement unit.

plain: Running a robot off electricity sent through a cable instead of carrying its own batteries.
snappy: Powering a robot through a physical cable rather than from an onboard battery, trading mobility range for unlimited runtime.
detail: Tethered power eliminates the Runtime ceiling imposed by a Lithium-ion battery, letting a robot operate indefinitely as long as the cable is connected, at the cost of restricted reach and an entangling cable to manage. It is common on a Tethered drone used for persistent surveillance, on a Remotely operated vehicle exploring deep water, and on bomb-disposal Unmanned ground vehicle platforms in Defense & Security. The tether often carries data alongside current, and a DC-DC converter or Power distribution board at the robot end conditions the incoming voltage for its motors and Onboard compute.

plain: A bookkeeper that keeps track of where every part of a robot is relative to every other part, moment by moment.
snappy: A ROS library that maintains a time-stamped tree of coordinate-frame transforms across a robot.
detail: tf (and its successor tf2) stores the relationships between every Coordinate frame on a robot as a Transform tree, letting code ask where a sensor reading sits in the base or world frame at a given time. It applies Homogeneous transformation matrix math under the hood and is consumed by RViz, MoveIt, and Nav2. Correct tf is essential for Sensor fusion and Localization, since a bad transform silently corrupts every downstream Pose.

plain: A camera that sees heat instead of visible light, so it can spot warm objects and people in total darkness.
snappy: A camera that images infrared heat radiation to see in darkness or detect temperature differences.
detail: A thermal camera, or infrared camera, forms an image from the heat radiated by objects rather than reflected visible light, letting a robot operate in darkness, smoke, or fog. In Defense & Security it supports Pedestrian detection and surveillance, and it is combined with a normal Camera through Sensor fusion to add warmth cues to Perception. It also drives Condition monitoring and Predictive maintenance by spotting overheating components.

plain: Keeping a robot from overheating by carrying its heat away from motors and chips.
snappy: The design of cooling and heat-dissipation paths that keep a robot's motors and compute within safe temperatures.
detail: Motors, a Graphics processing unit, and battery packs all generate heat, and without thermal management a robot will throttle its Onboard compute or shut down to protect itself. A Humanoid robot running high-torque actuators continuously must shed heat through fins, fans, or liquid cooling, which competes for mass within the Power budget. Thermal limits cap sustained Power density and effective Duty cycle, and a Battery management system monitors pack temperature to prevent thermal runaway.

plain: A famous set of fictional rules from science-fiction author Isaac Asimov meant to keep robots from harming people.
snappy: Isaac Asimov's fictional safety hierarchy (don't harm humans, obey orders, protect yourself) that popularized the idea of designed-in robot ethics.
detail: First stated in Asimov's 1942 story, the Three Laws are literary, not engineering, standards: they cannot be coded directly because terms like harm resist formal specification. Real safeguards instead come from standards such as ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066, mechanisms like an Emergency stop and Safe Torque Off, and broader Robot ethics debate around an Autonomous weapon. The laws remain a useful cultural touchstone when discussing Trust, Safety, and the limits of Autonomy.

plain: How much work a machine or system actually gets done in a given period, such as the number of items finished per hour.
snappy: The rate at which an automated system completes useful work, usually counted in units per hour.
detail: Throughput is the bottom-line output rate of an automation cell or warehouse, often quoted as units per hour (UPH) or a Pick rate in fulfillment. It depends on Cycle time, uptime, and how well stations are balanced; a single slow Industrial robot arm or a misfeeding Conveyor tracking station caps the whole line. In Logistics & Warehouse settings, fleets of Autonomous mobile robot units and Goods-to-person stations are sized to hit a target throughput, and the metric rolls up into Overall equipment effectiveness.

plain: A number comparing how hard a drone's motors can push against how heavy the drone is, which decides how punchy it feels.
snappy: The ratio of maximum available thrust to total vehicle weight, governing agility and climb.
detail: A ratio near 1 means a drone can barely hover, while First-person view racing quads target 4:1 or more for aggressive climbs and flips, set by Propeller and Brushless motor choice. Adequate headroom is also what gives a Hexacopter or Octocopter the ability to keep flying after a motor failure. The same concept governs Payload limits, since lifting cargo eats into the thrust margin the Flight controller needs for control authority.

plain: An aircraft whose propellers swivel from pointing up for takeoff to pointing forward for fast flight.
snappy: A VTOL aircraft that rotates its rotors (or whole wing) between vertical lift and horizontal cruise.
detail: Unlike a Hybrid VTOL that carries separate lift and cruise motors, a Tiltrotor reuses the same rotors, tilting them forward once airborne so the wing produces lift, which improves efficiency at the cost of complex transition control in the Flight controller. The full-scale V-22 and several eVTOL air-taxi designs use this layout for Urban air mobility. A tiltwing variant rotates the entire wing rather than just the nacelles.

plain: Deciding how fast a robot travels along an already-chosen path so it stays within its speed and force limits.
snappy: Assigning a time profile to a geometric path subject to velocity, acceleration, and torque limits.
detail: Time parameterization is the stage that converts a purely geometric path, such as the output of Path planning, into a timed Trajectory by choosing how quickly to traverse each segment without exceeding joint velocity or actuator torque bounds. Time-optimal path parameterization, or TOPP, computes the fastest legal traversal, which matters for industrial cycle-time on a manipulator and is provided in MoveIt. It decouples the planning problem cleanly: a Sampling-based planning method finds the shape, and time parameterization makes it executable for Trajectory tracking.

plain: An estimate of how many seconds are left before two things would crash if nothing changes about how they are moving.
snappy: The estimated time until impact between the ego vehicle and an object given their current relative position and closing speed.
detail: Time to collision (TTC) divides the gap to an object by the closing speed, giving a seconds-to-impact figure used as a risk threshold across advanced driver-assistance systems. Forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking fire when TTC drops below set limits, and TTC informs the safety envelope and behavior planning. It is computed from tracked objects produced by multi-object tracking and is a standard metric in scenario-based testing.

plain: A sensor that measures distance by clocking exactly how long a flash of light takes to bounce back from an object.
snappy: A depth sensor that measures distance from the round-trip travel time of emitted light.
detail: A time-of-flight sensor (ToF) illuminates a scene and times how long light takes to return, computing distance from the speed of light; this gives every pixel a depth value with one shot. It is a core technology inside many a Depth camera and is related in principle to LiDAR, which scans ToF ranging across a wider field. Robots use ToF for compact Obstacle detection, Proximity sensor replacement, and short-range Mapping.

plain: A set of upgrades to standard Ethernet that guarantee critical messages arrive exactly on time, so control and ordinary traffic can share one network.
snappy: A suite of IEEE Ethernet standards adding deterministic, scheduled timing to standard networks.
detail: TSN is a family of IEEE 802.1 standards that bring bounded latency and time synchronization to standard Ethernet, enabling Determinism without proprietary hardware. It lets time-critical Motion control traffic coexist with best-effort data on a single converged network, a key enabler for Industry 4.0 and the Industrial Internet of Things. Major Industrial Ethernet protocols including PROFINET, EtherNet/IP, and EtherCAT are adopting TSN, and OPC UA pub/sub uses it for real-time, vendor-neutral exchange.

plain: A local planning method that treats the robot's path like a stretchy band, continuously reshaping it to dodge obstacles while keeping the trip quick.
snappy: A local planner that optimizes a time-parameterized trajectory online, trading off travel time, clearance, and kinematic feasibility.
detail: The Timed Elastic Band models the trajectory as a series of poses connected by time intervals and deforms it like an elastic band pulled by competing objectives: short travel time, obstacle clearance, and respect for the robot's kinematics including the Nonholonomic constraint of a car-like base. As a Local planner in the ROS navigation stack, it produces smoother and faster motion than the Dynamic Window Approach by optimizing the whole local horizon at once. It performs continuous Obstacle avoidance against the live Cost map while tracking the Global planner route.

plain: A coupling that lets a robot drop one attachment and pick up another by itself, so the same arm can switch between a gripper, a welder, or a screwdriver.
snappy: A mechanism that automatically connects and disconnects different end-effectors on a robot, passing power and signals through the coupling.
detail: A tool changer is a two-part coupler, a master on the arm and a tool side on each attachment, that locks mechanically and passes electrical, pneumatic, and data connections so a single Industrial robot arm can swap its End-of-arm tooling mid-cycle. Mounted on the Tool flange, it lets one cell run a Parallel-jaw gripper for Pick and place, then exchange it for a Robotic welding torch, multiplying flexibility in Manufacturing. Changers are common in Machine tending and Assembly cells where Cycle time and uptime depend on fast, repeatable End-effector swaps.

plain: The flat metal face at the very tip of a robot arm with a standard bolt pattern where you attach whatever tool the robot needs to use.
snappy: The standardized mounting face at the end of a robot arm to which end-effectors and tooling are bolted.
detail: The tool flange is the machined plate at the wrist tip, usually following an ISO bolt-circle standard, where a Gripper, sensor, Tool changer, or other End-of-arm tooling attaches. It defines the mechanical origin of the End-effector and is the reference for Tool Center Point calibration and Hand-eye calibration. Sitting just past the Robot wrist and Spherical wrist axes, the tool flange is where a Force/torque sensor is often sandwiched to measure contact during Force control.

plain: When a robot picks up and uses an outside object, like a key or a screwdriver, to do something its bare body could not.
snappy: A robot extending its capabilities by grasping and operating an external object as an instrument.
detail: Tool use turns a fixed End-effector into an open-ended one: a Humanoid robot might grab a drill, a Gripper might wield a spatula, requiring Affordance reasoning about what the object is for and Grasp planning to hold it correctly. It is a benchmark of embodied intelligence because it combines Dexterous manipulation, perception, and planning, and is increasingly tackled with a Vision-language-action model that maps instructions to multi-step Skill primitive sequences. Robust tool use also leans on a Tool changer concept borrowed from Industrial robotics, where an arm swaps end-of-arm tooling automatically.

plain: A named channel that robot programs use to stream a particular kind of data to whoever is listening.
snappy: A named, typed, asynchronous message channel connecting publishing and subscribing nodes.
detail: A topic carries one message type, such as a Pose, a LiDAR point cloud, or a velocity command, flowing continuously from publishers to subscribers under the Publish-subscribe model. In ROS and ROS 2 every Node can publish or subscribe to any number of topics, and tools like RViz and rosbag tap topics to visualize or record them. For one-shot request-response a Service is used; for goal-driven jobs an Action.

plain: A number that says how many trillions of basic calculations a chip can do every second.
snappy: A throughput metric (trillions of operations per second) quantifying an accelerator's peak neural-inference capacity.
detail: TOPS rates how fast a Graphics processing unit, AI accelerator, or Tensor processing unit can push the operations behind a Neural network, helping engineers size Onboard compute to a perception workload. A robot vendor might advertise that an NVIDIA Jetson Thor delivers hundreds of TOPS to run a Vision-language-action model on the robot via Edge computing. The headline figure is peak and precision-dependent, so real Latency and the Power budget matter more than the raw number alone.

plain: Telling a motor exactly how hard to push or twist, rather than where to go or how fast.
snappy: Control that commands the force or torque an actuator delivers directly, typically via its current.
detail: Because motor torque is proportional to current, torque control is implemented as current control, often through Field-oriented control of a Brushless DC motor. It is essential for safe contact and for Compliance control, Impedance control, and Whole-body control on a Humanoid robot, where a Series elastic actuator or Quasi-direct drive joint makes torque cheap to sense and command. It is the third basic Servo control mode beside Position control and Velocity control, and it underlies Computed torque control.

plain: How much turning force a motor can produce for its size or weight, a measure of how punchy and compact it is.
snappy: The torque an actuator delivers per unit mass or volume, a defining figure of merit for actuator design.
detail: Torque density (torque-to-weight) decides whether a Humanoid robot can carry its own limbs, since every gram of Actuator adds mass the rest of the joints must lift. Designers raise it with strong magnets, a tight Harmonic drive or Cycloidal drive gearbox, or a Quasi-direct drive layout that trades a little Backdrivability for output force. It trades against Peak torque, Holding torque, and thermal limits, and is closely watched alongside Power density in legged-robot and Tesla Optimus actuator development.

plain: The complete amount of money a robot costs over its whole working life, not just the price you pay to buy it.
snappy: The full lifetime cost of a robot, summing purchase price plus installation, integration, energy, maintenance, downtime, and decommissioning.
detail: Total cost of ownership (TCO) is the number a buyer actually compares against labor when deciding to automate, and the hardware sticker price is often a minority of it. Big hidden line items include fees paid to a System integrator to design and commission the Robot cell, spare parts, software updates, energy, and the productivity lost whenever Uptime dips. Vendors increasingly bundle these into a Robotics-as-a-service subscription so customers pay a predictable monthly fee, and TCO is the denominator behind any Return on investment calculation.

plain: Moving on the kind of continuous rubber-or-metal belts you see on a tank or bulldozer, which grip loose ground far better than ordinary wheels.
snappy: Driving on continuous belts (tracks) wrapped around wheels, spreading the robot's weight over a large contact area for traction on soft, loose, or broken ground.
detail: By distributing load across the full belt footprint, a Tracked robot keeps ground pressure low and grip high on mud, sand, gravel, or rubble where Wheeled locomotion would dig in and bog down. Tracks turn by Skid steering, driving the two belts at different speeds, which gives strong Terrain adaptation but high friction and energy cost during turns. The approach is common on bomb-disposal and reconnaissance platforms in Defense & Security work and competes with Legged locomotion when the priority is rough-ground traction over agility; it also helps with Self-righting on shallow flips.

plain: A robot that moves on continuous belt-like tracks, like a tank, to grip loose or rough ground.
snappy: A mobile robot using continuous tracks for high traction and ground contact over loose, soft, or rough terrain.
detail: Tracked robots spread their weight over a long contact patch and steer by Skid steering (driving the two tracks at different speeds), giving traction on sand, mud, and rubble where a Wheeled robot would sink or spin. They are favored in Defense & Security (bomb-disposal Unmanned ground vehicle platforms) and Agriculture for Tracked locomotion across fields. The trade-off is higher friction, wear, and Cost of transport compared with wheels.

plain: Spotting road signs with a camera and reading what each one means, like a speed limit or a stop sign.
snappy: Detecting and classifying road signs from camera imagery to inform driving decisions.
detail: Traffic sign recognition, abbreviated TSR, both locates signs in the image and classifies them, feeding the rules the vehicle must obey into the planner. It is a standard Advanced driver-assistance systems feature that pairs with Lane detection, and it typically runs Object detection followed by Object recognition on a Convolutional neural network. Detected speed limits can update Adaptive cruise control, and persistent signs may be cross-checked against an HD map.

plain: A planned sequence of positions a robot will pass through, with timing that says when it should be at each one.
snappy: A time-parameterized sequence of poses, velocities, and accelerations that a robot follows.
detail: A trajectory is a Path that has been given timing, so it specifies not just where the robot goes but when and how fast, via Time parameterization. Motion planning produces a path, then Trajectory optimization and smoothing turn it into a feasible, jerk-limited trajectory the controller can execute, after which Trajectory tracking keeps the robot on it. Examples range from a Minimum-snap trajectory for a Quadcopter to a joint-space arm motion produced by MoveIt.

plain: Refining a robot's planned motion by mathematically nudging it toward the smoothest, lowest-effort version that still obeys the robot's limits.
snappy: Computing a motion by minimizing a cost functional subject to dynamics and constraint conditions.
detail: Trajectory optimization formulates motion as minimizing a cost, such as energy, jerk, or path length, while enforcing constraints like collision clearance, joint limits, and the robot's Dynamics. It is often used to refine a rough path from a Rapidly-exploring random tree or to solve Kinodynamic planning directly, and it underlies methods such as CHOMP and STOMP for arms and Minimum-snap trajectory generation for drones. Online variants are closely related to Model predictive control, which re-optimizes a short horizon every Control loop.

plain: Getting a robot to follow a planned path through space while also hitting each point at the right moment in time.
snappy: Control that drives a system to follow a prescribed time-parameterized reference path of states.
detail: Unlike point-to-point Position control, trajectory tracking follows a full reference trajectory with timing, computing commands to minimize the error between actual and desired states along a Trajectory. It is achieved with feedforward plus State feedback, Computed torque control, or Model predictive control, and is graded by tracking error and disturbance rejection. A welding Industrial robot arm tracks a seam, an Autonomous mobile robot tracks a planned route from its Motion planning stack, and a Drone tracks a Minimum-snap trajectory.

plain: Reusing what a robot already learned on one task to get a head start on a new, related task.
snappy: Reapplying knowledge, features, or weights learned on a source task to accelerate learning on a related target task.
detail: Transfer learning is why a manipulation network pretrained on broad Demonstration data fine-tunes quickly to a new gripper or object, improving Sample efficiency. Sim-to-real transfer is a special case moving policies from Simulation to hardware, and a Robot foundation model like RT-2 transfers web-scale knowledge into control. It enables Few-shot learning and a Generalist policy, and overlaps with Multitask learning and Representation learning.

plain: The math that converts a position described in one reference grid into the same position described in another.
snappy: A mathematical mapping that converts a Pose between two coordinate frames via rotation and translation.
detail: A transform expresses where one Coordinate frame sits relative to another, typically as a Homogeneous transformation matrix combining a Rotation matrix and a translation. Robots chain these constantly, for example to relate a camera detection to the Gripper, and ROS organizes them in a Transform tree maintained by the tf library. Correct transforms depend on good Calibration, especially Hand-eye calibration, and underlie Forward kinematics and Localization. Also called a frame transform or coordinate transform.

plain: A continuously updated family tree of all the robot's coordinate viewpoints, showing how each relates to the others.
snappy: A maintained hierarchy of coordinate frames and the time-varying transforms relating them.
detail: A transform tree, known in ROS as the TF tree and provided by tf, tracks every Frame of reference on the robot, from each sensor and joint up to the map, so any Pose can be converted from one frame to another on demand. It stores time-stamped transforms because frames move as the robot's joints and base move, which lets perception expressed in a camera frame be used by a planner working in the world frame. It is foundational to navigation, SLAM, and Visual servoing, and each edge is a Homogeneous transformation matrix.

plain: A type of AI model that learns by paying selective attention to the most relevant parts of its input, now used to power the biggest robot brains.
snappy: An attention-based neural network architecture that weighs relationships across a sequence, underpinning modern robot foundation models.
detail: The transformer uses self-attention to relate every element of an input sequence to every other, which lets it fuse long histories of observations and actions; it is the backbone of a Robot foundation model and a Vision-language-action model such as RT-1, RT-2, and OpenVLA. In robotics it ingests tokenized images, language, and proprioception to output an Action, often combined with Action chunking for smooth control. It is a specialized Neural network and the architecture trained at scale on datasets like Open X-Embodiment for Cross-embodiment learning.

plain: A famous moral puzzle about who to harm when a crash is unavoidable, often raised when discussing self-driving car ethics.
snappy: A thought experiment about allocating unavoidable harm, invoked in debates over how autonomous vehicles should behave in no-win situations.
detail: The trolley problem asks whether a system should, for example, swerve to harm fewer people at the cost of its occupant, and it surfaces constantly in discussions of robot ethics for driving. In practice engineers argue these framings are rare and misleading, since good design focuses on never reaching such states through margin, with frameworks like responsibility-sensitive safety and concepts like minimal risk condition doing the real work. It nonetheless shapes public trust and policy debate around the automated driving system.

plain: A medium-speed four-legged gait where legs on opposite corners move together.
snappy: A quadruped gait in which diagonally opposite legs swing and land as synchronized pairs.
detail: In a trot the front-left and rear-right legs move together, then the front-right and rear-left, giving two support points on a diagonal that keep the Center of mass roughly between them. It is the default cruising Gait of a Quadruped robot like Spot because it is fast yet relies only on modest Dynamic stability. The diagonal pairing contrasts with the slower Crawl gait and the faster, aerial-phase Gallop.

plain: A person's confidence that a robot will do what is expected and behave safely.
snappy: A human's calibrated confidence that a robot will perform reliably and as intended.
detail: Trust governs whether people will actually use and rely on a robot, and it must be calibrated so users neither over-trust a fallible system nor under-use a capable one. In Human-robot interaction, well-designed feedback, predictable motion, and Explainability build appropriate trust, while a single dramatic failure can destroy it. Trust is central to a Service robot in the home and to Shared autonomy, where a Human-in-the-loop must know when to take over.

plain: A single bundle describing both how fast something is spinning and how fast it is sliding through space.
snappy: A six-vector combining the angular and linear velocity of a rigid body.
detail: A twist stacks a body's three angular and three linear velocity components into one six-vector, the velocity counterpart of a Pose. It is the natural output of Differential kinematics, where the Jacobian matrix maps joint velocities to the end-effector twist. Twists are central to Screw theory and live in the tangent space of the Special Euclidean group SE(3); their force-side dual is the Wrench. In ROS, the Twist message commands mobile-robot velocity.

plain: An air-traffic-control-like system specifically for drones, so many of them can fly safely in the same airspace at once.
snappy: An airspace coordination framework that deconflicts and sequences drone flights to enable routine fleet operations at scale.
detail: UAS traffic management (UTM, called U-space in Europe) is the digital layer that lets large numbers of drones share low-altitude airspace without colliding, the precondition for scaling Drone delivery and BVLOS operations. It ingests each Drone's flight plan and Remote ID broadcast, allocates corridors, and issues conflict alerts, complementing onboard Detect and avoid. NASA pioneered the UTM concept and the FAA is integrating it into national airspace; it is the aerial analog of warehouse Fleet management.

plain: A short-range radio technology that measures distance very precisely by timing tiny pulses, used to position robots and tags indoors.
snappy: A short-range RF technology using wide-bandwidth pulses for centimeter-level indoor ranging and positioning.
detail: Ultra-wideband (UWB) sends nanosecond radio pulses across a wide spectrum to measure time-of-flight precisely, giving decimeter-to-centimeter indoor positioning where Global Navigation Satellite System and GPS fail. It is the dominant tag-based localization tech for an Automated guided vehicle in Logistics & Warehouse, for indoor drones, and for asset tracking, and is fused with an Inertial measurement unit and Wheel odometry. UWB anchors act as fixed references much like an RTK base, supporting GPS-denied navigation.

plain: A sensor that measures distance by sending out a sound pulse too high to hear and timing its echo, like a bat.
snappy: A range sensor that measures distance by timing the echo of an emitted ultrasonic pulse.
detail: An ultrasonic sensor, or sonar, emits a high-frequency sound burst and measures the round-trip time of its echo to estimate distance to a surface. It is cheap and works in darkness or on glass, making it common for Obstacle detection and close-range Collision avoidance on a mobile robot, though it is low-resolution and struggles with soft or angled surfaces. For richer ranging robots turn to LiDAR or a Time-of-flight sensor.

plain: The creepy feeling people get when a robot looks almost human but not quite right.
snappy: The dip in human comfort that occurs when a robot or character appears nearly, but not perfectly, human.
detail: Coined by Masahiro Mori, the uncanny valley describes how likeability rises with human-likeness until a near-human appearance produces eeriness instead, a sharp dip before full realism recovers it. It matters for any Android or Humanoid robot meant for Service & Consumer settings, where subtle mismatches in skin, eyes, or motion timing break Trust and harm Human-robot interaction. Designers manage it through stylized Anthropomorphism, avoiding the photoreal middle ground.

plain: The fact that a robot never knows the world or its own state perfectly, only approximately.
snappy: Imperfect or probabilistic knowledge of a robot's state, its sensors, or its environment.
detail: Uncertainty pervades robotics: sensors add Sensor noise, motion has Drift, and the environment is only partially observed. Robots manage it with probabilistic methods like the Kalman filter, the Particle filter, and Monte Carlo localization, which track a belief rather than a single value during State estimation and Localization. Reasoning explicitly about uncertainty is what makes Robustness, safe Collision avoidance, and good decision-making under a Markov decision process possible.

plain: A robot hand whose fingers automatically wrap around an object's shape using fewer motors than they have knuckles.
snappy: A gripper with fewer actuators than joints, so its fingers passively adapt their shape to the object.
detail: An Underactuated gripper exploits Underactuation: a few motors drive many finger joints through linkages or tendons, so unconstrained joints flex passively to envelope whatever they touch. This adaptive behavior gives a robust Power grasp on varied objects without precise Grasp planning, much like a Soft gripper but with rigid links. It is common on humanoid hands and adaptive industrial grippers, and shares its tendon-routing ideas with the Tendon-driven hand and the broader study of Morphological computation.

plain: A design where a machine has fewer motors than the number of independent ways it could move, so some motions happen passively rather than being directly driven.
snappy: A condition in which a system has fewer actuators than degrees of freedom, leaving some motions uncontrolled directly.
detail: An underactuated system cannot command every one of its Degrees of freedom at once, so the controller must exploit dynamics, gravity, or contact to shape the uncontrolled motions. Walking robots are classic examples: a Bipedal robot in flight or single-support has more degrees of freedom than the joints can independently drive, which is why Balance control and Zero moment point reasoning matter. Grippers use it deliberately, where an Underactuated gripper conforms to objects with fewer Actuator channels than fingers.

plain: A Chinese company selling relatively cheap four-legged and human-shaped robots.
snappy: Chinese maker of low-cost quadruped and humanoid robots, including the G1 and H1 platforms.
detail: Unitree Robotics is known for dramatically undercutting Western prices on the Quadruped robot and Humanoid robot market, with the Unitree G1 and Unitree H1 bipeds and the Go-series quadrupeds. Its affordable hardware has made it popular in Research/Frontier labs for Reinforcement learning and Sim-to-real experiments on Legged locomotion. The low cost lets researchers study Learned locomotion and Whole-body control without the budget of a Boston Dynamics platform.

plain: A Danish company that popularized small, safe, easy-to-program robot arms that work next to people.
snappy: Danish maker of UR collaborative robot arms (UR5, UR10) that popularized the cobot category.
detail: Universal Robots largely created the modern Collaborative robot market with its UR series (UR5, UR10), lightweight arms designed for safe Human-robot interaction without fences. The arms use Power and force limiting per ISO/TS 15066, are programmed through an intuitive Teach pendant and Hand guiding, and support a wide ecosystem of End-of-arm tooling. Their ease of deployment made the Cobot accessible to small Manufacturing shops doing Machine tending and Pick and place.

plain: A flying robot with no pilot on board, controlled remotely or flying itself; the formal name for a drone.
snappy: An uncrewed aircraft, the generic engineering term for a drone, flown by remote operator or onboard autonomy.
detail: UAV is the umbrella term that includes the Multirotor drone, Fixed-wing drone, and VTOL drone, all part of a wider Unmanned aircraft system. A UAV carries a Flight controller running stacks like PX4 or ArduPilot, navigates by GNSS positioning and Waypoint navigation, and may fly within Visual line of sight or under BVLOS operations. Civil flight is regulated by the FAA, including Part 107, with Detect and avoid for safe airspace integration.

plain: The whole package needed to fly a drone, including the aircraft, the controls on the ground, and the radio links between them.
snappy: The complete system of an uncrewed aircraft plus its Ground control station and command-and-control links, regulated as one unit.
detail: Regulators such as the FAA define the UAS, not just the airframe, because safe operation depends equally on the Ground control station, the data link (often MAVLink), and the pilot. A typical UAS pairs a Multirotor or Fixed-wing drone running PX4 or ArduPilot with a laptop GCS and a video downlink, and may add Remote ID and Detect and avoid for compliant Beyond visual line of sight flight. The term overlaps with Unmanned aerial vehicle, which refers only to the aircraft itself.

plain: A driverless vehicle that drives over land, often off-road, for military or field jobs with no person on board.
snappy: An uncrewed ground robot built for off-road, military, or field operations, teleoperated or autonomous.
detail: A UGV is the land counterpart to the Unmanned aerial vehicle, ranging from small Defense & Security bomb-disposal Tracked robot platforms to large autonomous trucks used in Agriculture. It may run under Teleoperation, Supervised autonomy, or full Autonomy depending on the mission and Levels of autonomy. DARPA Grand Challenge programs were seminal in advancing UGV navigation and Obstacle avoidance.

plain: A boat with no crew aboard that drives itself across the surface of the water.
snappy: An uncrewed boat robot operating on the water surface, autonomous or remotely operated.
detail: A USV is the marine-surface counterpart of the Unmanned ground vehicle, navigating by GNSS positioning, radar, and Sensor fusion while following maritime collision rules through Obstacle avoidance. It often acts as a communications relay or launch platform for an Autonomous underwater vehicle in Research/Frontier surveys, and serves Defense & Security patrol and mine-hunting roles. Autonomy ranges from Teleoperation to full self-navigation across the Levels of autonomy.

plain: Turning left across oncoming cars at a junction where you have no green arrow to protect you.
snappy: A turn across opposing traffic without a dedicated protective signal phase, requiring the vehicle to judge and accept gaps.
detail: The unprotected left turn (ULT) is a benchmark difficulty for an automated driving system because it demands accurate behavior prediction of oncoming vehicles, gap acceptance, and assertive yet safe motion planning. It combines occlusion, timing, and negotiation, and a vulnerable road user crossing mid-turn raises the stakes further. It is a favorite case for scenario generation and closed-loop simulation, and frequently appears in disengagement reports affecting miles per intervention.

plain: A messy, unpredictable real-world setting that the robot cannot count on staying the same.
snappy: A workspace with uncontrolled layout, lighting, and contents that the robot must perceive and adapt to on the fly.
detail: An unstructured environment, like a home kitchen, a farm field, or a public road, defeats the assumptions of a Structured environment and demands strong Perception, SLAM, and Generalization. It is the natural home of Field robotics and Open world operation, where a Long-tail scenario can appear at any time. Coping with it drives interest in Learning from demonstration, a Foundation model, and Domain randomization to bridge the Reality gap from simulation to reality.

plain: The share of its scheduled working time that a robot is actually running and doing useful work rather than stopped or broken.
snappy: The fraction of scheduled time a deployed robot is operational and productive, also called availability.
detail: Uptime is the reliability KPI customers care about most, because a robot earning its keep only when running directly drives Return on investment. It is degraded by faults, maintenance, and integration stalls, and it is the metric most often guaranteed in a Service-level agreement. Uptime is closely linked to Mean time between failures and Mean time to repair, and it feeds the manufacturing measure Overall equipment effectiveness alongside speed and quality.

plain: A future transport system of small electric aircraft that fly people and cargo on short hops across and around cities.
snappy: Air taxi and cargo operations using electric vertical-takeoff aircraft to serve short intra- and inter-urban routes.
detail: Urban air mobility (UAM) envisions fleets of eVTOL aircraft carrying passengers and freight between rooftops and a Vertiport network, relieving ground congestion on short city routes. The aircraft typically use Distributed electric propulsion and depend on Detect and avoid, dense UAS traffic management, and Beyond visual line of sight autonomy to scale safely. The broader term advanced air mobility (AAM) extends the concept to regional and cargo flights, and it overlaps with Drone delivery infrastructure for Mobility.

plain: A text file that describes a robot's body to software: its parts, how they connect, and what they look like.
snappy: An XML format specifying a robot's links, joints, kinematics, visual meshes, and collision geometry.
detail: A URDF declares each Link and the Joint connecting them, encoding the Kinematics that MoveIt and tf use to compute Forward kinematics and Inverse kinematics. It is loaded by RViz to draw the robot and converted to SDF or MJCF for simulation in Gazebo or MuJoCo. Hand-writing long URDFs is tedious, so engineers generate them with Xacro macros.
