plain: A flexible 3D file format, originally from film, used to assemble large detailed virtual scenes for robots.
snappy: An extensible, composable 3D scene description format (OpenUSD) used in Isaac Sim and digital twins.
detail: Created by Pixar and now open as OpenUSD, USD layers and references many assets into one scene, which suits the photorealistic, large-scale worlds of NVIDIA Isaac and Isaac Sim and the building of a Digital twin. It carries geometry, materials, physics, and sensors, playing the role for Isaac that SDF plays for Gazebo or MJCF for MuJoCo. USD scenes drive Photorealistic rendering and Synthetic data generation.

plain: An estimate of how good a situation is for a robot, measured by how much reward it can expect to collect from there onward.
snappy: An estimate of expected cumulative future reward from a given state or state-action pair.
detail: A value function predicts the long-term Reward an agent can expect from a state (or from taking an action in a state), giving Reinforcement learning a way to compare options without simulating every outcome. State-action values are learned directly in Q-learning, while an Actor-critic architecture pairs a learned value critic with a Policy actor. Accurate value estimates are central within a Markov decision process and improve Sample efficiency by propagating credit across time.

plain: An electronic box that controls how fast an AC electric motor spins by changing the frequency of the power it sends.
snappy: A drive that controls AC motor speed and torque by varying the frequency and voltage of its output.
detail: A VFD (or variable speed drive) sits between the mains and an AC motor, synthesizing a variable-frequency output to smoothly control speed on pumps, fans, conveyors, and spindles. By matching motor speed to demand it saves energy and reduces mechanical stress versus running flat-out, a staple of Industrial automation energy efficiency. A VFD takes commands from a Programmable logic controller or Motion controller over a Fieldbus such as PROFINET or Modbus, and is distinct from a full servo drive used for precise positioning.

plain: A motor-and-spring device that can be made stiff or springy on demand, like tensing or relaxing a muscle.
snappy: An actuator whose mechanical stiffness can be adjusted on the fly during operation.
detail: A variable stiffness actuator (VSA), also called a variable impedance actuator, uses an adjustable elastic element so a robot can be soft and safe during contact yet stiff and precise for fast, accurate motion. This tunability extends the fixed-spring idea of the Series elastic actuator and supports energy-efficient hopping and human-safe interaction in a Humanoid robot. It is a sophisticated Compliant actuator that mechanically realizes adjustable Impedance control.

plain: A model that squeezes a robot's camera images or sensor readings into a few meaningful numbers it can act on, then rebuilds them.
snappy: A generative model that compresses robot observations into a smooth latent distribution, enabling reconstruction and sampling of plausible states or actions.
detail: A VAE maps high-dimensional robot observations such as camera frames into a structured Latent space, a form of Representation learning that gives downstream control a compact state to act on. In robotics it is used to compress observations for a World model, to model the multimodal action distributions seen in human Demonstration data, and as a building block in skill-learning architectures like ACT. It belongs to the same generative family as the Diffusion model but trades sample sharpness for a smooth, samplable latent.

plain: A way for cars to wirelessly talk to other cars, traffic lights, roadside equipment, and even pedestrians' phones to share what is happening around them.
snappy: Wireless communication linking a vehicle with other vehicles, infrastructure, pedestrians, and networks to share safety and traffic information.
detail: Vehicle-to-everything (V2X) is the umbrella for connected-vehicle messaging, encompassing vehicle-to-vehicle communication, vehicle-to-infrastructure communication, and pedestrian links. It lets the ego vehicle receive information beyond its own line of sight, enabling cooperative perception and earlier hazard awareness around blind corners. Implemented over DSRC or Cellular V2X, it augments onboard automotive radar and LiDAR rather than replacing them.

plain: Cars wirelessly talking with roadside equipment like traffic lights and signs to learn things like when a light will turn red.
snappy: Wireless communication between vehicles and roadside infrastructure such as traffic signals, signs, and work zones.
detail: Vehicle-to-infrastructure communication (V2I) is the roadside subset of vehicle-to-everything, letting a vehicle receive signal phase and timing, work-zone alerts, and lane-closure data from connected infrastructure. It supports cooperative perception and smoother behavior planning, for example slowing ahead of a red light it cannot yet see. V2I is essential for automated valet parking, where the garage infrastructure guides the car, and runs over DSRC or Cellular V2X.

plain: Cars wirelessly sending messages straight to each other, like 'I'm braking hard' or 'I'm in your blind spot.'
snappy: Direct wireless data exchange between nearby vehicles sharing position, speed, and intent for cooperative safety.
detail: Vehicle-to-vehicle communication (V2V) is the car-to-car subset of vehicle-to-everything, broadcasting basic safety messages with position, heading, and braking status to neighbors. It enables cooperative perception and platooning, where a self-driving truck convoy shares intent to close gaps safely, and warns of hazards a car's own sensors cannot yet see. Like the rest of V2X it runs over DSRC or Cellular V2X and complements automotive radar and a camera.

plain: Telling a robot joint or motor how fast to spin or move, and keeping it at that speed.
snappy: Closed-loop control that commands and regulates the speed of a joint, wheel, or actuator.
detail: Velocity control regulates rate rather than place, using an Encoder or Resolver to measure speed and a PID controller to hold the Setpoint despite load. It is the natural mode for the wheels of a Differential-drive robot, for Conveyor tracking, and as the inner stage of a Cascade control loop beneath Position control. With Torque control it forms the trio of Servo control modes a Servomotor and its Motor controller can run.

plain: The set of speeds and directions that would eventually crash the robot into a moving object, which the robot is told to avoid choosing.
snappy: The cone of velocities that would lead to a future collision with a moving obstacle, excluded during velocity selection.
detail: A Velocity obstacle reasons in velocity space rather than position space: given another agent's current velocity, it computes the set of the robot's own velocities that would cause a collision at some future time and constrains the planner to pick outside that set. This makes it well suited to dynamic environments with moving people or other robots, where static Obstacle avoidance is insufficient, and it underlies a reactive Local planner for an Autonomous mobile robot. Its multi-robot extension, Optimal Reciprocal Collision Avoidance, splits the avoidance effort between agents.

plain: Two checks on a robot: confirming it was built correctly to its design, and confirming the design actually does the right job in the real world.
snappy: Verification confirms the system was built to spec; validation confirms it meets the real-world need.
detail: Verification and validation (V&V) answers two distinct questions: did we build the system right, and did we build the right system. For an Autonomous vehicle, verification checks the Self-driving stack against requirements, while validation uses Scenario-based testing, Closed-loop simulation, and Log replay to show safe behavior across the Long tail. V&V feeds a Safety case and aligns with functional-safety standards like ISO 26262 and the Safety of the intended functionality framework.

plain: A small airport-like pad where electric air taxis take off and land vertically, with space to charge and board passengers.
snappy: Ground infrastructure with takeoff/landing pads, charging, and passenger handling for eVTOL air-taxi operations.
detail: A vertiport is the eVTOL equivalent of a heliport, providing one or more vertipads, fast charging, passenger flow, and air-traffic interfaces to enable Urban air mobility at scale. Siting and layout must account for downwash, noise, and the precise vertical approaches that Distributed electric propulsion aircraft fly, often using Autonomous docking-style precision guidance on final approach. A network of vertiports is the physical backbone of Mobility air-taxi service and connects to UAS traffic management for sequencing.

plain: Using cameras to let a robot see and understand what is around it.
snappy: The use of cameras and image processing to let a robot perceive its surroundings.
detail: Vision is the dominant sensing channel for most robots, turning Camera images into the spatial and semantic understanding that drives Perception. A mobile robot fuses Vision with Object detection and Semantic segmentation to recognize obstacles, while a manipulator uses Visual servoing to align its end-effector to a target. Vision underpins Visual SLAM and Visual odometry for navigation, and overlaps heavily with Computer vision and Machine vision in industry.

plain: A touch sensor that works by filming a soft gel pad with a tiny camera and watching how the gel squishes against an object.
snappy: A tactile sensor that images a deformable gel surface with an internal camera to reconstruct contact geometry.
detail: A vision-based tactile sensor, such as GelSight, places a soft elastomer over an internal Camera and lights; when the gel presses an object, the camera captures fine surface shape and shear in high resolution. This dense data excels at Slip detection, Tactile servoing, and Contact-rich manipulation, far richer than a simple Capacitive sensor. It is a leading research direction for Dexterous manipulation on an Anthropomorphic hand.

plain: A robot that uses camera images to see where things are and adjust its movements to pick or place them accurately.
snappy: Using camera feedback to compute and correct a robot's position relative to parts in real time, abbreviated VGR.
detail: In VGR a Machine vision system locates a part's Pose and sends corrected coordinates to the Robot controller, letting the arm grasp items that are not precisely fixtured, the basis of Bin picking from a randomly filled tote. It tightly couples perception to motion through Hand-eye calibration so camera coordinates map onto the robot's frame, and at high update rates it becomes Visual servoing. VGR overlaps with AI through learned Object detection and Grasp planning, and it powers flexible Pick and place where rigid Fixturing is impractical.

plain: A single AI model that looks at camera images, reads an instruction in plain language, and directly outputs the moves a robot should make.
snappy: A model that maps visual observations and natural-language instructions directly to robot actions.
detail: A vision-language-action model (VLA) fuses image understanding and language comprehension to output motor commands, enabling Language-conditioned manipulation where a Humanoid robot follows a spoken instruction. VLAs such as RT-2, OpenVLA, and the RT-X family are a type of Robot foundation model trained on large, cross-robot datasets like Open X-Embodiment to achieve broad Generalization. They form a learned Policy that replaces hand-engineered Perception and planning pipelines with end-to-end control.

plain: Trying to make a car drive itself using just cameras, without expensive laser scanners.
snappy: A self-driving approach that relies on cameras for perception, deliberately forgoing lidar and sometimes radar.
detail: Vision-only autonomy bets that cameras plus deep learning can recover depth and geometry well enough to drive, avoiding the cost of LiDAR, an approach championed by Tesla. It leans heavily on Depth estimation, an Occupancy network, and a Bird's-eye-view representation to reconstruct the scene from pixels alone, where lidar-based stacks get range directly. Critics argue it is brittle in glare and rare Edge case lighting, which is why some teams add 4D imaging radar for redundancy rather than going purely camera-only.

plain: Flying a drone close enough that the operator can always see it directly with their own eyes.
snappy: Drone operation that keeps the aircraft within the pilot's unaided sight at all times.
detail: VLOS is the baseline assumption of most drone rules, including FAA Part 107, because the pilot can personally spot and avoid other aircraft and obstacles without onboard Detect and avoid. The pilot may still use an Autopilot for Waypoint navigation or Loiter, but must keep the craft within naked-eye view, optionally aided by a visual observer. Extending operations past this boundary becomes Beyond visual line of sight, which carries far stricter requirements.

plain: Figuring out how a robot has moved by watching how the scene shifts between one camera frame and the next.
snappy: Incremental motion estimation from tracking image features across consecutive camera frames.
detail: Visual odometry (VO) tracks features through successive Camera frames and recovers the Camera's incremental motion via Feature matching and geometry, a key input to Ego-motion estimation and Localization. Fusing it with an Inertial measurement unit yields more robust Visual-inertial odometry, and closing a loop turns it into Visual SLAM. It is widely used in Mobility and on drones where Wheel odometry is unavailable.

plain: Steering a robot continuously by watching live camera images, nudging it until what the camera sees matches the desired view of the target.
snappy: A closed-loop control technique that drives a robot's motion directly from visual feedback to reduce the error between current and desired image features or object pose.
detail: Visual servoing puts a camera inside the Control loop, computing motion commands so that observed image features (image-based) or an estimated target Pose (position-based) converge to a goal, correcting in real time as the scene changes. It depends on a calibrated camera and a Jacobian matrix relating feature motion to robot motion, and is commonly used for Peg-in-hole assembly, Conveyor tracking, and instrument alignment in a Surgical robot. Because it is feedback-driven it tolerates Calibration error and Backlash better than pure open-loop motion, complementing Hand-eye calibration and Pose estimation. In Manufacturing it enables Vision-guided robotics for high-precision insertion and alignment without rigid Fixturing.

plain: Mapping and self-positioning a robot using mainly its cameras instead of laser scanners.
snappy: SLAM that builds a map and tracks pose primarily from camera imagery rather than lidar.
detail: Visual SLAM (vSLAM) tracks features such as ORB features across Camera frames to estimate motion and reconstruct 3D structure, often jointly with a Bundle adjustment back end. It commonly fuses an IMU to become Visual-inertial odometry for robustness, and uses Place recognition for Loop closure. It powers low-cost navigation on drones and AR headsets where LiDAR is too heavy or expensive, though it struggles in textureless or poorly lit scenes.

plain: Tracking how a robot moves by combining what its cameras see with readings from its motion sensor.
snappy: Estimating motion by fusing camera imagery with inertial measurement unit data.
detail: Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) blends visual feature tracking with high-rate accelerometer and gyroscope data from an Inertial measurement unit, giving each sensor's strength: the camera fixes drift while the IMU bridges fast motion and blur. It is a form of Visual odometry tightly coupled through an Extended Kalman filter or a Factor graph, and it underlies tracking on drones and the foundation of many Visual SLAM systems. VIO is favored for GPS-denied navigation indoors and aboard a Quadcopter.

plain: A small, fast-reacting device that moves a short distance back and forth, like the part that pushes a loudspeaker cone.
snappy: A direct-drive electromagnetic actuator producing fast, precise, short-stroke linear motion.
detail: A voice coil actuator (VCM) drives a coil through a fixed magnetic field, producing force in direct proportion to current with essentially no gearing or friction, the hallmark of a Direct drive. Its very high Bandwidth and smooth, backlash-free motion suit hard-disk head positioning, camera autofocus, fine Force control, and active vibration isolation. The trade-off is a short stroke, so it excels at small, rapid, precise moves rather than large travel.

plain: A way of carving up 3D space into a stack of equal-sized cubes, like 3D pixels.
snappy: A representation that discretizes 3D space into a regular lattice of cubic volume cells (voxels).
detail: A voxel grid divides space into uniform cubes, each of which can store occupancy, color, or a learned feature, giving a simple 3D analog of the 2D Occupancy grid. Robotics uses it to downsample a dense Point cloud before Iterative closest point, to build 3D maps, and inside an Occupancy network. The memory-efficient sparse counterpart for mapping is the OctoMap, which adapts cell size with an octree.

plain: An aircraft that rises straight up and lands straight down, so it needs no runway.
snappy: Any aircraft that takes off and lands vertically rather than along a runway.
detail: Every Multirotor is technically a VTOL, but the term is most useful for aircraft that combine vertical lift with efficient forward flight, such as a Hybrid VTOL or a Tiltrotor. VTOL capability is the defining feature of the eVTOL air taxis pursued for Urban air mobility, which operate from a Vertiport rather than an airport. The contrast class is the Fixed-wing drone, which needs a runway or launcher but cruises far more efficiently.

plain: A drone that lifts off and lands straight up like a helicopter, then flies forward efficiently like an airplane.
snappy: An aircraft combining rotor-borne vertical takeoff and hover with efficient fixed-wing forward cruise.
detail: A VTOL drone, also called a Hybrid VTOL, gives the field-friendliness of a Multirotor drone (no runway) with the range of a Fixed-wing drone by transitioning between hover and wing-borne flight, sometimes using a Tiltrotor or Distributed electric propulsion layout. The same VTOL principle scales up to eVTOL air taxis in Urban air mobility, served by a Vertiport. It is valued for Logistics & Warehouse drone delivery and Defense & Security reconnaissance over long ranges.

plain: A person on the road without the protection of a vehicle body, such as someone walking or cycling.
snappy: An unprotected road participant, such as a pedestrian, cyclist, or motorcyclist, requiring heightened care from automated systems.
detail: VRUs are a priority class for an automated driving system because collisions with them carry severe outcomes, so perception must reliably handle pedestrian detection, prediction of erratic motion, and occlusion. Benchmarks like nuScenes and the Waymo Open Dataset label VRUs heavily, and responsibility-sensitive safety frameworks reserve extra margin around them. Handling a cyclist who suddenly enters the ego vehicle path is a canonical hard case for behavior prediction and collision avoidance.

plain: A simple countdown that quietly resets a machine into a safe state if its computer freezes or stops responding.
snappy: A hardware or software timer that triggers a safe action if it is not periodically reset, detecting compute or software hangs.
detail: A Watchdog timer is a core safety and reliability primitive in any Embedded system or Microcontroller running a robot: the software must "kick" the timer periodically, and if a hang or crash stops the kicks, the timer fires to force a reset or a Safety-rated stop. It is widely used in a Flight controller, a Robot controller, and a Real-time operating system to catch deadlocks and infinite loops. Watchdogs are a building block for Fail-safe behavior and contribute to the diagnostic coverage counted toward a Performance Level or Safety Integrity Level.

plain: Google's sister company that runs driverless taxis people can actually hail in some cities.
snappy: Alphabet's autonomous-vehicle company operating a commercial driverless robotaxi service.
detail: Waymo, Alphabet's self-driving unit, operates a commercial Robotaxi service using the Waymo Driver, a Self-driving stack built on LiDAR, Radar, Camera, and HD map data. It runs at Level 4 automation within a defined Operational design domain, publishing the Waymo Open Dataset to advance Autonomous vehicle research. Its sensor-rich, map-reliant approach contrasts with Tesla's Vision-only autonomy bet.

plain: A big set of real self-driving sensor data that Waymo shared publicly so researchers can build and compare autonomy algorithms.
snappy: A large-scale, high-resolution LiDAR-and-camera dataset released by Waymo for perception, prediction, and motion research.
detail: The Waymo Open Dataset (WOD) offers densely labeled 3D object detection and multi-object tracking data plus a separate motion and prediction split with a lane graph, captured across diverse cities and conditions. It is a heavily used benchmark for autonomy research, complementing nuScenes, and its size makes it valuable for training large perception and behavior prediction models. Vulnerable road user labels and long-tail scenes make it a stress test for real-world robustness.

plain: A marked spot along a planned route that a robot aims to pass through on its way to the final destination.
snappy: An intermediate target pose along a route that the robot is commanded to reach in sequence.
detail: A Waypoint breaks a long route into manageable segments, so instead of solving for the whole journey at once the robot performs Waypoint navigation, reaching each point before heading to the next. A warehouse Automated guided vehicle follows waypoints laid out along its aisles, while a Drone executes a mission as an ordered list of GPS waypoints. The Global planner typically outputs the waypoint sequence, and a Local planner or Trajectory tracking controller handles the motion between consecutive waypoints.

plain: Programming a drone to fly itself along a route by visiting a list of GPS map points in order.
snappy: Autonomous flight along a preset route of geographic coordinates managed by the Autopilot.
detail: An operator draws a series of waypoints in a Ground control station, and the Autopilot, fusing GPS with its Inertial measurement unit, flies between them at set speeds and altitudes, optionally triggering camera or sensor actions at each point. It is the backbone of repeatable Agriculture surveys, mapping, and inspection, and is configured identically in PX4 and ArduPilot via MAVLink. For smooth aggressive flight the path can be refined into a Minimum-snap trajectory rather than straight legs.

plain: A UK company building self-driving software that learns to drive directly from experience rather than from hand-written rules.
snappy: British autonomy startup developing end-to-end learned driving models that map sensor input straight to steering and pedal actions.
detail: Wayve pioneered an end-to-end driving approach in which a single neural network learns the full perception-to-control mapping, in contrast to the modular pipeline of a traditional self-driving stack with separate perception, prediction, and planning stages. The company favours camera-centric, vision-only autonomy and trains large driving foundation models, positioning its work alongside the vision-language-action model trend in embodied AI. Its systems are evaluated on disengagement and intervention metrics and tested through closed-loop simulation before fleet deployment in cities.

plain: A free, beginner-friendly robot simulator that comes with ready-made robots and simulated sensors out of the box.
snappy: An open-source robot simulator with bundled robot models, sensor emulation, and multi-language controllers.
detail: Webots ships a library of standard robots and sensors so users can prototype Navigation or Manipulation without authoring every model, and it offers a ROS and ROS 2 bridge. It occupies a middle ground between the lightweight PyBullet and the heavier Gazebo or Isaac Sim, and it is widely used in education and competitions. Like other simulators it relies on a Physics engine and supports Sensor simulation.

plain: Working out how far and which way a robot has moved by counting how much its wheels have turned.
snappy: Pose-change estimation derived from integrating wheel encoder counts and a kinematic model.
detail: Wheel odometry counts rotations from an Encoder on each wheel and applies the robot's drive geometry to estimate incremental Pose change, a form of Dead reckoning common on a Differential drive Autonomous mobile robot in Logistics & Warehouse. Wheel slip and uneven floors cause Sensor drift, so it is fused with an Inertial measurement unit and Visual odometry inside a Kalman filter for reliable State estimation. It is cheap, high-rate, and a backbone input to Localization and SLAM.

plain: Moving on rolling wheels, the efficient way to travel over smooth, flat ground.
snappy: Locomotion using rotating wheels for continuous, low-energy travel over relatively flat terrain.
detail: Wheeled locomotion offers a far lower Cost of transport than Legged locomotion on flat floors, which is why almost every Autonomous mobile robot and Automated guided vehicle in a warehouse rolls rather than walks. Steering schemes range from Differential drive and Skid steering to Ackermann steering and an Omnidirectional drive using a Mecanum wheel. Its weakness is steps and rough ground, which motivates the hybrid Wheeled-legged robot.

plain: A robot that gets around by rolling on wheels, best suited to smooth, flat floors.
snappy: A mobile robot driven by wheels, offering simple, efficient locomotion on flat or paved surfaces.
detail: Wheeled robots are the most common mobile form because Wheeled locomotion is energy-efficient and mechanically simple, powering most of Logistics & Warehouse and Service & Consumer robotics. Steering variants include the Differential-drive robot, Ackermann steering, Skid steering, and the holonomic Omnidirectional robot using a Mecanum wheel or Omni wheel. They underpin platforms from the Delivery robot to the Autonomous mobile robot, though they struggle where a Legged robot or Tracked robot excels.

plain: A robot that has wheels at the ends of its legs, so it can roll fast on smooth ground and step over obstacles when needed.
snappy: A hybrid platform with wheels mounted on articulated legs, combining rolling speed with legged obstacle-crossing agility.
detail: A wheeled-legged robot rolls efficiently like a Wheeled robot on flat ground but lifts and places its wheeled feet like a Legged robot to climb steps or cross gaps, using Whole-body control to manage Balance control. ANYbotics and ETH Zurich research platforms popularized the concept for inspection over mixed terrain. It blends low Cost of transport with Terrain adaptation, sitting between the Quadruped robot and the omnidirectional wheeled base.

plain: Coordinating every joint of a robot at once so it can do a task and stay balanced at the same time.
snappy: A control framework that commands all of a robot's joints together to satisfy task goals and balance simultaneously.
detail: Whole-body control solves, every Control loop, an optimization that distributes a task, like reaching, across all joints while respecting balance, joint limits, and contact constraints. It relies on the robot's full Dynamics, often via Centroidal dynamics and Floating-base dynamics, and frequently sits beneath a Model predictive control planner. A Humanoid robot like Atlas uses WBC to step, push a door, and keep its Zero moment point stable all at once, exploiting Kinematic redundancy and the Null space.

plain: When a robot uses its whole body at once - legs, trunk, and arms together - to move around and do tasks like pushing a door or carrying a load.
snappy: Coordinating legs, torso, and arms together as one system to move the robot while also reaching, bracing, or manipulating, rather than treating walking and arm motion separately.
detail: Instead of locomotion and arm control being separate modules, whole-body locomotion solves them jointly so a Humanoid robot can lean its torso to keep balance while an arm reaches, or brace a hand against a wall to push off. This is the basis of loco-manipulation, where carrying or opening doors changes the robot's own dynamics, and it is implemented with Whole-body control optimizers that respect the Zero moment point, the Support polygon, and joint Torque control limits. It generalizes Bipedal locomotion by folding manipulation, Centroidal dynamics, and Balance control into a single Trajectory optimization.

plain: Recharging a robot's battery through the air, with no plug or metal contacts to connect.
snappy: Transferring power to a robot's battery without physical contacts, typically via inductive coupling.
detail: Wireless charging uses inductive coupling between a floor or wall pad and a coil on the robot, removing the exposed contacts and connector wear that complicate Autonomous docking. It suits a service robot and warehouse Autonomous mobile robot that dock frequently in dirty or wet environments, though it is less efficient and adds Thermal management load. The Battery management system still governs the charge profile and State of charge, and it competes with a Hot-swappable battery approach for minimizing downtime.

plain: All the places a robot's hand can physically reach.
snappy: The set of all poses a robot's end-effector can attain given its joint limits.
detail: A robot's reachable Workspace is bounded by its link lengths, Joint ranges, and overall Reach; the smaller Dexterous workspace is where the End-effector can reach with any orientation. The Workspace shape is determined by the robot's Kinematic chain and the type of Serial manipulator or Parallel manipulator architecture. Planners use the Workspace to verify a target Pose is attainable before solving Inverse kinematics.

plain: A robot's internal mental picture of its surroundings and how things move, which it uses to imagine what will happen before acting.
snappy: A learned or built internal representation of the environment and its dynamics that a robot uses to predict outcomes and plan.
detail: A world model lets a Robot forecast how the environment will respond to its actions, supporting planning without acting blindly in the real world. In Model-based reinforcement learning, the agent learns a world model and rolls it forward to evaluate candidate plans, improving Sample efficiency over Model-free reinforcement learning. World models are central to Embodied AI and increasingly to Generative simulation, where learned dynamics fill in for an expensive Physics engine.

plain: A single bundle describing both a push and a twist that a body applies, combined together.
snappy: A six-vector combining force and torque acting on a body.
detail: A wrench stacks three force and three torque components into one six-vector, the force-side dual of a Twist. A Force/torque sensor at the robot wrist measures the wrench during Force control, Impedance control, or a delicate Peg-in-hole insertion. The transpose of the Jacobian matrix maps an end-effector wrench into the joint torques needed to produce it, which is how arms render Cartesian forces.

plain: A shortcut language that lets engineers write a robot description once with reusable templates instead of repeating themselves.
snappy: A macro preprocessor that generates parameterized, reusable URDF (or SDF) robot descriptions.
detail: Xacro adds variables, math, conditionals, and macros to XML, so a six-legged robot's identical legs are written once and instantiated six times, then expanded into a flat URDF at build time. It dramatically cuts duplication in describing a Manipulator or Quadruped robot and is standard practice in ROS and ROS 2 workflows. The expanded URDF then feeds RViz, tf, MoveIt, and Gazebo.

plain: A Japanese company that makes Motoman factory robots and the motors and controllers that drive them.
snappy: Japanese maker of Motoman industrial robots, servomotors, and motion controllers.
detail: Yaskawa, through its Motoman brand, is one of the 'big four' Industrial robotics suppliers, building the Articulated robot for Robotic welding, painting, and Material handling. The company is also a dominant maker of the Servomotor and Variable frequency drive that power countless other machines, giving it deep Motion control expertise. Its robots use a dedicated Robot controller tuned for high-speed, high-Repeatability work on the Production line.

plain: The spot on the ground where a walking robot's tipping forces cancel out, used to tell whether it stays balanced.
snappy: The point on the ground where the net horizontal torque from foot reaction forces is zero.
detail: The zero moment point (ZMP) coincides with the Center of pressure during balanced contact, and a biped is dynamically balanced as long as its ZMP stays strictly inside the Support polygon. ZMP-based gait generation, often built on the Linear inverted pendulum model, drove early Humanoid robot walking and Bipedal locomotion controllers. It complements newer criteria like the Capture point and Centroidal dynamics that better handle Dynamic walking and recovery steps.

plain: A robot succeeding at a task it was never specifically trained on, with no extra practice.
snappy: Performing an unseen task or handling unseen objects with no task-specific training examples.
detail: Zero-shot generalization is a headline capability of a Vision-language-action model like RT-2, which can act on novel objects described in language thanks to web-scale priors. It is the strongest form of generalization, beyond Few-shot learning, and is the aspiration for any Generalist policy or Robot foundation model. In practice it leans on Transfer learning and rich Representation learning so that a Humanoid robot can attempt instructions outside its Demonstration data.

plain: A well-known rule-of-thumb recipe for setting up a controller by first pushing it until it just starts to oscillate.
snappy: A classic heuristic for tuning PID gains derived from the onset of sustained oscillation.
detail: The Ziegler-Nichols method increases the proportional Gain until the loop oscillates steadily, records that ultimate gain and its period, then plugs them into a lookup table to set PID controller parameters. It is a fast starting point for Gain tuning on Manufacturing process loops and simple motor Servo control, though it tends to produce aggressive responses with noticeable Overshoot that often need manual refinement. It remains a textbook baseline against which modern model-based tuning is compared.

plain: A company that uses small autonomous aircraft to fly medicines and packages directly to people, dropping them by parachute or on a tether.
snappy: Drone-delivery operator flying fixed-wing and hybrid aircraft to deposit medical and retail payloads autonomously.
detail: Zipline built one of the first at-scale Drone delivery networks, originally flying blood and vaccines to clinics across Rwanda and Ghana using a catapult-launched Fixed-wing drone. Its newer platform adds a VTOL hover stage with a lowered delivery droid for precise Last-mile delivery to homes. Operations depend heavily on BVLOS operations approvals, Geofencing, and Detect and avoid systems to share airspace safely.

plain: Amazon's self-driving company building a custom, symmetrical vehicle with no steering wheel.
snappy: Amazon's autonomous-vehicle company building a purpose-built, bidirectional robotaxi.
detail: Zoox, owned by Amazon, designs a ground-up Robotaxi with no steering wheel, bidirectional driving, and four-wheel steering rather than retrofitting an existing car. Its purpose-built vehicle pairs a full Self-driving stack of LiDAR, Radar, and Camera with Level 4 automation inside a chosen Operational design domain. The clean-sheet design lets Zoox optimize the Chassis and sensor placement for the Autonomous vehicle task from the start.
